Floating-point precision          *user_guide-basics-floating-point-precision*

*user_guide-basics-basics-float-precision*

pandas stores real-valued data using 64-bit floating point by default.
Floating-point numbers can represent only a finite set of values: a decimal
number like `0.03` is stored as the nearest representable binary fraction,
and the result of every arithmetic operation is rounded to the nearest
representable value. As a consequence, computations that would give
identical results in exact arithmetic can differ, typically around the 16th
significant digit, depending on how they are carried out:

>python
    In [140]: ser = pd.Series(0.03, index=range(60))

    In [141]: ser.head(20).mean() == ser.mean()
    Out[141]: np.False_
<
Both means display as `0.03` by default, but they are not identical:

>python
    In [142]: means = pd.Series([ser.head(20).mean(), ser.mean()])

    In [143]: with pd.option_context("display.precision", 20):
       .....:     print(means)
       .....: 
    0    0.03000000000000000583
    1    0.03000000000000000236
    dtype: float64
<
This is not specific to pandas: it is inherent to IEEE 754
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754 floating-point arithmetic, which is
used by virtually all modern hardware and software. See the Python tutorial
https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html for an accessible
introduction.

For this reason, avoid relying on exact equality of computed floating-point
values. In particular, using computed floats as labels --- for example
grouping on a column produced by a `mean` --- can split what displays as a
single value into multiple groups:

>python
    In [144]: means.nunique()
    Out[144]: 2
<
If you need to compare or group on computed floats, round them first with
|pandas.Series.round|, compare with `numpy.isclose()`
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.isclose.html#numpy.isclose,
or bin the values with |pandas.cut|:

>python
    In [145]: means.round(10).nunique()
    Out[145]: 1
<

FUNCTION APPLICATION                  *user_guide-basics-function-application*

*user_guide-basics-basics-apply*

To apply your own or another library's functions to pandas objects, you
should be aware of the three methods below. The appropriate method to use
depends on whether your function expects to operate on an entire `DataFrame`
or `Series`, row- or column-wise, or elementwise.

1. |user_guide-basics-tablewise-function-application|:
   |pandas.DataFrame.pipe|
2. |user_guide-basics-row-or-column-wise-function-application|:
   |pandas.DataFrame.apply|
3. |user_guide-basics-aggregation-api|: |pandas.DataFrame.agg| and
   |pandas.DataFrame.transform|
4. |user_guide-basics-applying-elementwise-functions|:
   |pandas.DataFrame.map|

                            *user_guide-basics-tablewise-function-application*
Tablewise function application

*user_guide-basics-basics-pipe*

`DataFrames` and `Series` can be passed into functions. However, if the
function needs to be called in a chain, consider using the
|pandas.DataFrame.pipe| method.

First some setup:

>python
    In [146]: def extract_city_name(df):
       .....:     """
       .....:     Chicago, IL -> Chicago for city_name column
       .....:     """
       .....:     df["city_name"] = df["city_and_code"].str.split(",").str.get(0)
       .....:     return df
       .....: 

    In [147]: def add_country_name(df, country_name=None):
       .....:     """
       .....:     Chicago -> Chicago-US for city_name column
       .....:     """
       .....:     col = "city_name"
       .....:     df["city_and_country"] = df[col] + country_name
       .....:     return df
       .....: 

    In [148]: df_p = pd.DataFrame({"city_and_code": ["Chicago, IL"]})
<
`extract_city_name` and `add_country_name` are functions taking and
returning `DataFrames`.

Now compare the following:

>python
    In [149]: add_country_name(extract_city_name(df_p), country_name="US")
    Out[149]: 
      city_and_code city_name city_and_country
    0   Chicago, IL   Chicago        ChicagoUS
<
Is equivalent to:

>python
    In [150]: df_p.pipe(extract_city_name).pipe(add_country_name, country_name="US")
    Out[150]: 
      city_and_code city_name city_and_country
    0   Chicago, IL   Chicago        ChicagoUS
<
pandas encourages the second style, which is known as method chaining.
`pipe` makes it easy to use your own or another library's functions in
method chains, alongside pandas' methods.

In the example above, the functions `extract_city_name` and
`add_country_name` each expected a `DataFrame` as the first positional
argument. What if the function you wish to apply takes its data as, say, the
second argument? In this case, provide `pipe` with a tuple of
`(callable, data_keyword)`. `.pipe` will route the `DataFrame` to the
argument specified in the tuple.

For example, we can fit a regression using statsmodels. Their API expects a
formula first and a `DataFrame` as the second argument, `data`. We pass in
the function, keyword pair `(sm.ols, 'data')` to `pipe`:

>python
    In [147]: import statsmodels.formula.api as sm

    In [148]: bb = pd.read_csv("data/baseball.csv", index_col="id")

    In [149]: (
       .....:     bb.query("h > 0")
       .....:     .assign(ln_h=lambda df: np.log(df.h))
       .....:     .pipe((sm.ols, "data"), "hr ~ ln_h + year + g + C(lg)")
       .....:     .fit()
       .....:     .summary()
       .....: )
       .....:
    Out[149]:
    <class 'statsmodels.iolib.summary.Summary'>
    """
                               OLS Regression Results
    ==============================================================================
    Dep. Variable:                     hr   R-squared:                       0.685
    Model:                            OLS   Adj. R-squared:                  0.665
    Method:                 Least Squares   F-statistic:                     34.28
    Date:                Tue, 22 Nov 2022   Prob (F-statistic):           3.48e-15
    Time:                        05:34:17   Log-Likelihood:                -205.92
    No. Observations:                  68   AIC:                             421.8
    Df Residuals:                      63   BIC:                             432.9
    Df Model:                           4
    Covariance Type:            nonrobust
    ===============================================================================
                      coef    std err          t      P>|t|      [0.025      0.975]
    -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Intercept   -8484.7720   4664.146     -1.819      0.074   -1.78e+04     835.780
    C(lg)[T.NL]    -2.2736      1.325     -1.716      0.091      -4.922       0.375
    ln_h           -1.3542      0.875     -1.547      0.127      -3.103       0.395
    year            4.2277      2.324      1.819      0.074      -0.417       8.872
    g               0.1841      0.029      6.258      0.000       0.125       0.243
    ==============================================================================
    Omnibus:                       10.875   Durbin-Watson:                   1.999
    Prob(Omnibus):                  0.004   Jarque-Bera (JB):               17.298
    Skew:                           0.537   Prob(JB):                     0.000175
    Kurtosis:                       5.225   Cond. No.                     1.49e+07
    ==============================================================================

    Notes:
    [1] Standard Errors assume that the covariance matrix of the errors is correctly specified.
    [2] The condition number is large, 1.49e+07. This might indicate that there are
    strong multicollinearity or other numerical problems.
    """
<
The pipe method is inspired by unix pipes and more recently dplyr
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr and magrittr
https://github.com/tidyverse/magrittr, which have introduced the popular
`(%>%)` (read pipe) operator for R https://www.r-project.org. The
implementation of `pipe` here is quite clean and feels right at home in
Python. We encourage you to view the source code of |pandas.DataFrame.pipe|.

                   *user_guide-basics-row-or-column-wise-function-application*
Row or column-wise function application

Arbitrary functions can be applied along the axes of a DataFrame using the
|pandas.DataFrame.apply| method, which, like the descriptive statistics
methods, takes an optional `axis` argument:

>python
    In [151]: df.apply(lambda x: np.mean(x))
    Out[151]: 
    one      0.811094
    two      1.360588
    three    0.187958
    dtype: float64

    In [152]: df.apply(lambda x: np.mean(x), axis=1)
    Out[152]: 
    a    1.583749
    b    0.734929
    c    1.133683
    d   -0.166914
    dtype: float64

    In [153]: df.apply(lambda x: x.max() - x.min())
    Out[153]: 
    one      1.051928
    two      1.632779
    three    1.840607
    dtype: float64

    In [154]: df.apply(np.cumsum)
    Out[154]: 
            one       two     three
    a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
    b  1.738035  3.684640 -0.050390
    c  2.433281  5.163008  1.177045
    d       NaN  5.442353  0.563873

    In [155]: df.apply(np.exp)
    Out[155]: 
            one       two     three
    a  4.034899  5.885648       NaN
    b  1.409244  6.767440  0.950858
    c  2.004201  4.385785  3.412466
    d       NaN  1.322262  0.541630
<
  Warning: ~

  For a general Python callable, |pandas.DataFrame.apply| invokes it once
  per column (or once per row with `axis=1`) in a Python-level loop. It is a
  tool for flexibility, not speed: when a vectorized equivalent exists, it
  will generally be much faster. Every example above can be written more
  directly without `apply`:

  >python
      In [156]: df.mean()            # df.apply(lambda x: np.mean(x))
      Out[156]: 
      one      0.811094
      two      1.360588
      three    0.187958
      dtype: float64

      In [157]: df.mean(axis=1)      # df.apply(lambda x: np.mean(x), axis=1)
      Out[157]: 
      a    1.583749
      b    0.734929
      c    1.133683
      d   -0.166914
      dtype: float64

      In [158]: df.max() - df.min()  # df.apply(lambda x: x.max() - x.min())
      Out[158]: 
      one      1.051928
      two      1.632779
      three    1.840607
      dtype: float64

      In [159]: df.cumsum()          # df.apply(np.cumsum)
      Out[159]: 
              one       two     three
      a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
      b  1.738035  3.684640 -0.050390
      c  2.433281  5.163008  1.177045
      d       NaN  5.442353  0.563873

      In [160]: np.exp(df)           # df.apply(np.exp)
      Out[160]: 
              one       two     three
      a  4.034899  5.885648       NaN
      b  1.409244  6.767440  0.950858
      c  2.004201  4.385785  3.412466
      d       NaN  1.322262  0.541630
<
  The first four avoid the per-column loop and are several times faster on a
  wide frame. The last is a NumPy ufunc, which `apply` recognizes and
  applies to the whole frame at once, so the two are equally fast; the
  direct spelling is simply clearer.

  Before reaching for `apply`, look for a vectorized alternative: a
  DataFrame or Series method, an arithmetic or comparison operation (see
  |user_guide-basics-basics-binop|), or an accessor method such as the
  |user_guide-text-text-string-methods| under `.str` or the
  |user_guide-basics-basics-dt-accessors| under `.dt`. Reserve `apply` for
  logic with no vectorized equivalent, such as a function from a third-party
  library that operates on one row or column at a time.

The |pandas.DataFrame.apply| method will also dispatch on a string method
name.

>python
    In [161]: df.apply("mean")
    Out[161]: 
    one      0.811094
    two      1.360588
    three    0.187958
    dtype: float64

    In [162]: df.apply("mean", axis=1)
    Out[162]: 
    a    1.583749
    b    0.734929
    c    1.133683
    d   -0.166914
    dtype: float64
<
The return type of the function passed to |pandas.DataFrame.apply| affects
the type of the final output from `DataFrame.apply` for the default
behaviour:

- If the applied function returns a `Series`, the final output is a
  `DataFrame`. The columns match the index of the `Series` returned by the
  applied function.
- If the applied function returns any other type, the final output is a
  `Series`.

This default behaviour can be overridden using the `result_type`, which
accepts three options: `reduce`, `broadcast`, and `expand`. These will
determine how list-likes return values expand (or not) to a `DataFrame`.

|pandas.DataFrame.apply| combined with some cleverness can be used to answer
many questions about a data set. For example, suppose we wanted to extract
the date where the maximum value for each column occurred:

>python
    In [163]: tsdf = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     np.random.randn(1000, 3),
       .....:     columns=["A", "B", "C"],
       .....:     index=pd.date_range("1/1/2000", periods=1000),
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [164]: tsdf.apply(lambda x: x.idxmax())
    Out[164]: 
    A   2000-08-06
    B   2001-01-18
    C   2001-07-18
    dtype: datetime64[us]
<
(In this case the built-in `tsdf.idxmax()` gives the same result more
simply; `apply` is shown for illustration.)

You may also pass additional arguments and keyword arguments to the
|pandas.DataFrame.apply| method.

>python
    In [165]: def subtract_and_divide(x, sub, divide=1):
       .....:     return (x - sub) / divide
       .....: 

    In [166]: df_udf = pd.DataFrame(np.ones((2, 2)))

    In [167]: df_udf.apply(subtract_and_divide, args=(5,), divide=3)
    Out[167]: 
              0         1
    0 -1.333333 -1.333333
    1 -1.333333 -1.333333
<
Another useful feature is the ability to pass Series methods to carry out
some Series operation on each column or row:

>python
    In [168]: tsdf = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     np.random.randn(10, 3),
       .....:     columns=["A", "B", "C"],
       .....:     index=pd.date_range("1/1/2000", periods=10),
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [169]: tsdf.iloc[3:7] = np.nan

    In [170]: tsdf
    Out[170]: 
                       A         B         C
    2000-01-01 -0.158131 -0.232466  0.321604
    2000-01-02 -1.810340 -3.105758  0.433834
    2000-01-03 -1.209847 -1.156793 -0.136794
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08 -0.653602  0.178875  1.008298
    2000-01-09  1.007996  0.462824  0.254472
    2000-01-10  0.307473  0.600337  1.643950

    In [171]: tsdf.apply(pd.Series.interpolate)
    Out[171]: 
                       A         B         C
    2000-01-01 -0.158131 -0.232466  0.321604
    2000-01-02 -1.810340 -3.105758  0.433834
    2000-01-03 -1.209847 -1.156793 -0.136794
    2000-01-04 -1.098598 -0.889659  0.092225
    2000-01-05 -0.987349 -0.622526  0.321243
    2000-01-06 -0.876100 -0.355392  0.550262
    2000-01-07 -0.764851 -0.088259  0.779280
    2000-01-08 -0.653602  0.178875  1.008298
    2000-01-09  1.007996  0.462824  0.254472
    2000-01-10  0.307473  0.600337  1.643950
<
(Here too, `tsdf.interpolate()` is the idiomatic spelling.)

Finally, |pandas.DataFrame.apply| takes an argument `raw` which is False by
default, which converts each row or column into a Series before applying the
function. When set to True, the passed function will instead receive an
ndarray object, which has positive performance implications if you do not
need the indexing functionality.

Aggregation API                            *user_guide-basics-aggregation-api*

*user_guide-basics-basics-aggregate*

The aggregation API allows one to express possibly multiple aggregation
operations in a single concise way. This API is similar across pandas
objects, see |user_guide-groupby-groupby-aggregate|, the
|user_guide-window-window-overview|, and the
|user_guide-timeseries-timeseries-aggregate|. The entry point for
aggregation is |pandas.DataFrame.aggregate|, or the alias
|pandas.DataFrame.agg|.

We will use a similar starting frame from above:

>python
    In [172]: tsdf = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     np.random.randn(10, 3),
       .....:     columns=["A", "B", "C"],
       .....:     index=pd.date_range("1/1/2000", periods=10),
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [173]: tsdf.iloc[3:7] = np.nan

    In [174]: tsdf
    Out[174]: 
                       A         B         C
    2000-01-01  1.257606  1.004194  0.167574
    2000-01-02 -0.749892  0.288112 -0.757304
    2000-01-03 -0.207550 -0.298599  0.116018
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.814347 -0.257623  0.869226
    2000-01-09 -0.250663 -1.206601  0.896839
    2000-01-10  2.169758 -1.333363  0.283157
<
Using a single function is equivalent to |pandas.DataFrame.apply|. You can
also pass named methods as strings. These will return a `Series` of the
aggregated output:

>python
    In [175]: tsdf.agg(lambda x: np.sum(x))
    Out[175]: 
    A    3.033606
    B   -1.803879
    C    1.575510
    dtype: float64

    In [176]: tsdf.agg("sum")
    Out[176]: 
    A    3.033606
    B   -1.803879
    C    1.575510
    dtype: float64

    # these are equivalent to a ``.sum()`` because we are aggregating
    # on a single function
    In [177]: tsdf.sum()
    Out[177]: 
    A    3.033606
    B   -1.803879
    C    1.575510
    dtype: float64
<
Single aggregations on a `Series` this will return a scalar value:

>python
    In [178]: tsdf["A"].agg("sum")
    Out[178]: np.float64(3.033606102414146)
<

                       *user_guide-basics-aggregating-with-multiple-functions*
Aggregating with multiple functions

You can pass multiple aggregation arguments as a list. The results of each
of the passed functions will be a row in the resulting `DataFrame`. These
are naturally named from the aggregation function.

>python
    In [179]: tsdf.agg(["sum"])
    Out[179]: 
                A         B        C
    sum  3.033606 -1.803879  1.57551
<
Multiple functions yield multiple rows:

>python
    In [180]: tsdf.agg(["sum", "mean"])
    Out[180]: 
                 A         B         C
    sum   3.033606 -1.803879  1.575510
    mean  0.505601 -0.300647  0.262585
<
On a `Series`, multiple functions return a `Series`, indexed by the function
names:

>python
    In [181]: tsdf["A"].agg(["sum", "mean"])
    Out[181]: 
    sum     3.033606
    mean    0.505601
    Name: A, dtype: float64
<
Passing a `lambda` function will yield a `<lambda>` named row:

>python
    In [182]: tsdf["A"].agg(["sum", lambda x: x.mean()])
    Out[182]: 
    sum         3.033606
    <lambda>    0.505601
    Name: A, dtype: float64
<
Passing a named function will yield that name for the row:

>python
    In [183]: def mymean(x):
       .....:     return x.mean()
       .....: 

    In [184]: tsdf["A"].agg(["sum", mymean])
    Out[184]: 
    sum       3.033606
    mymean    0.505601
    Name: A, dtype: float64
<

Aggregating with a dict            *user_guide-basics-aggregating-with-a-dict*

Passing a dictionary of column names to a scalar or a list of scalars, to
`DataFrame.agg` allows you to customize which functions are applied to which
columns. Note that the results are not in any particular order, you can use
an `OrderedDict` instead to guarantee ordering.

>python
    In [185]: tsdf.agg({"A": "mean", "B": "sum"})
    Out[185]: 
    A    0.505601
    B   -1.803879
    dtype: float64
<
Passing a list-like will generate a `DataFrame` output. You will get a
matrix-like output of all of the aggregators. The output will consist of all
unique functions. Those that are not noted for a particular column will be
`NaN`:

>python
    In [186]: tsdf.agg({"A": ["mean", "min"], "B": "sum"})
    Out[186]: 
                 A         B
    mean  0.505601       NaN
    min  -0.749892       NaN
    sum        NaN -1.803879
<

Custom describe                            *user_guide-basics-custom-describe*

*user_guide-basics-basics-aggregation-custom-describe*

With `.agg()` it is possible to easily create a custom describe function,
similar to the built in |user_guide-basics-basics-describe|.

>python
    In [187]: from functools import partial

    In [188]: q_25 = partial(pd.Series.quantile, q=0.25)

    In [189]: q_25.__name__ = "25%"

    In [190]: q_75 = partial(pd.Series.quantile, q=0.75)

    In [191]: q_75.__name__ = "75%"

    In [192]: tsdf.agg(["count", "mean", "std", "min", q_25, "median", q_75, "max"])
    Out[192]: 
                   A         B         C
    count   6.000000  6.000000  6.000000
    mean    0.505601 -0.300647  0.262585
    std     1.103362  0.887508  0.606860
    min    -0.749892 -1.333363 -0.757304
    25%    -0.239885 -0.979600  0.128907
    median  0.303398 -0.278111  0.225365
    75%     1.146791  0.151678  0.722709
    max     2.169758  1.004194  0.896839
<

Transform API                                *user_guide-basics-transform-api*

*user_guide-basics-basics-transform*

The |pandas.DataFrame.transform| method returns an object that is indexed
the same (same size) as the original. This API allows you to provide
multiple operations at the same time rather than one-by-one. Its API is
quite similar to the `.agg` API.

We create a frame similar to the one used in the above sections.

>python
    In [193]: tsdf = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     np.random.randn(10, 3),
       .....:     columns=["A", "B", "C"],
       .....:     index=pd.date_range("1/1/2000", periods=10),
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [194]: tsdf.iloc[3:7] = np.nan

    In [195]: tsdf
    Out[195]: 
                       A         B         C
    2000-01-01 -0.428759 -0.864890 -0.675341
    2000-01-02 -0.168731  1.338144 -1.279321
    2000-01-03 -1.621034  0.438107  0.903794
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.254374 -1.240447 -0.201052
    2000-01-09 -0.157795  0.791197 -1.144209
    2000-01-10 -0.030876  0.371900  0.061932
<
Transform the entire frame. `.transform()` allows input functions as: a
NumPy function, a string function name or a user defined function.

>python
    In [196]: tsdf.transform(np.abs)
    Out[196]: 
                       A         B         C
    2000-01-01  0.428759  0.864890  0.675341
    2000-01-02  0.168731  1.338144  1.279321
    2000-01-03  1.621034  0.438107  0.903794
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.254374  1.240447  0.201052
    2000-01-09  0.157795  0.791197  1.144209
    2000-01-10  0.030876  0.371900  0.061932

    In [197]: tsdf.transform("abs")
    Out[197]: 
                       A         B         C
    2000-01-01  0.428759  0.864890  0.675341
    2000-01-02  0.168731  1.338144  1.279321
    2000-01-03  1.621034  0.438107  0.903794
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.254374  1.240447  0.201052
    2000-01-09  0.157795  0.791197  1.144209
    2000-01-10  0.030876  0.371900  0.061932

    In [198]: tsdf.transform(lambda x: x.abs())
    Out[198]: 
                       A         B         C
    2000-01-01  0.428759  0.864890  0.675341
    2000-01-02  0.168731  1.338144  1.279321
    2000-01-03  1.621034  0.438107  0.903794
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.254374  1.240447  0.201052
    2000-01-09  0.157795  0.791197  1.144209
    2000-01-10  0.030876  0.371900  0.061932
<
Here |pandas.DataFrame.transform| received a single function; this is
equivalent to a ufunc https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/ufuncs.html
application.

>python
    In [199]: np.abs(tsdf)
    Out[199]: 
                       A         B         C
    2000-01-01  0.428759  0.864890  0.675341
    2000-01-02  0.168731  1.338144  1.279321
    2000-01-03  1.621034  0.438107  0.903794
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.254374  1.240447  0.201052
    2000-01-09  0.157795  0.791197  1.144209
    2000-01-10  0.030876  0.371900  0.061932
<
Passing a single function to `.transform()` with a `Series` will yield a
single `Series` in return.

>python
    In [200]: tsdf["A"].transform(np.abs)
    Out[200]: 
    2000-01-01    0.428759
    2000-01-02    0.168731
    2000-01-03    1.621034
    2000-01-04         NaN
    2000-01-05         NaN
    2000-01-06         NaN
    2000-01-07         NaN
    2000-01-08    0.254374
    2000-01-09    0.157795
    2000-01-10    0.030876
    Freq: D, Name: A, dtype: float64
<

                         *user_guide-basics-transform-with-multiple-functions*
Transform with multiple functions

Passing multiple functions will yield a column MultiIndexed DataFrame. The
first level will be the original frame column names; the second level will
be the names of the transforming functions.

>python
    In [201]: tsdf.transform([np.abs, lambda x: x + 1])
    Out[201]: 
                       A                   B                   C          
                absolute  <lambda>  absolute  <lambda>  absolute  <lambda>
    2000-01-01  0.428759  0.571241  0.864890  0.135110  0.675341  0.324659
    2000-01-02  0.168731  0.831269  1.338144  2.338144  1.279321 -0.279321
    2000-01-03  1.621034 -0.621034  0.438107  1.438107  0.903794  1.903794
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.254374  1.254374  1.240447 -0.240447  0.201052  0.798948
    2000-01-09  0.157795  0.842205  0.791197  1.791197  1.144209 -0.144209
    2000-01-10  0.030876  0.969124  0.371900  1.371900  0.061932  1.061932
<
Passing multiple functions to a Series will yield a DataFrame. The resulting
column names will be the transforming functions.

>python
    In [202]: tsdf["A"].transform([np.abs, lambda x: x + 1])
    Out[202]: 
                absolute  <lambda>
    2000-01-01  0.428759  0.571241
    2000-01-02  0.168731  0.831269
    2000-01-03  1.621034 -0.621034
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN

    2000-01-09  0.157795  0.842205
    2000-01-10  0.030876  0.969124

Transforming with a dict          *user_guide-basics-transforming-with-a-dict*

Passing a dict of functions will allow selective transforming per column.

>python
    In [203]: tsdf.transform({"A": np.abs, "B": lambda x: x + 1})
    Out[203]: 
                       A         B
    2000-01-01  0.428759  0.135110
    2000-01-02  0.168731  2.338144
    2000-01-03  1.621034  1.438107
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.254374 -0.240447
    2000-01-09  0.157795  1.791197
    2000-01-10  0.030876  1.371900
<
Passing a dict of lists will generate a MultiIndexed DataFrame with these
selective transforms.

>python
    In [204]: tsdf.transform({"A": np.abs, "B": [lambda x: x + 1, "sqrt"]})
    Out[204]: 
                       A         B          
                absolute  <lambda>      sqrt
    2000-01-01  0.428759  0.135110       NaN
    2000-01-02  0.168731  2.338144  1.156782
    2000-01-03  1.621034  1.438107  0.661897
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-05       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-08  0.254374 -0.240447       NaN
    2000-01-09  0.157795  1.791197  0.889493
    2000-01-10  0.030876  1.371900  0.609836
<

                            *user_guide-basics-applying-elementwise-functions*
Applying elementwise functions

*user_guide-basics-basics-elementwise*

Since not all functions can be vectorized (accept NumPy arrays and return
another array or value), the methods |pandas.DataFrame.map| on DataFrame and
analogously |pandas.Series.map| on Series accept any Python function taking
a single value and returning a single value. For example:

>python
    In [205]: df4 = df.copy()

    In [206]: df4
    Out[206]: 
            one       two     three
    a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
    b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
    c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
    d       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172

    In [207]: def f(x):
       .....:     return len(str(x))
       .....: 

    In [208]: df4["one"].map(f)
    Out[208]: 
    a    18
    b    19
    c    18
    d     3
    Name: one, dtype: int64

    In [209]: df4.map(f)
    Out[209]: 
       one  two  three
    a   18   17      3
    b   19   18     20
    c   18   18     16
    d    3   19     19
<
|pandas.Series.map| has an additional feature; it can be used to easily
“link” or “map” values defined by a secondary series. This is closely
related to |user_guide-merging-merging|:

>python
    In [210]: s = pd.Series(
       .....:     ["six", "seven", "six", "seven", "six"], index=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [211]: t = pd.Series({"six": 6.0, "seven": 7.0})

    In [212]: s
    Out[212]: 
    a      six
    b    seven
    c      six
    d    seven
    e      six
    dtype: str

    In [213]: s.map(t)
    Out[213]: 
    a    6.0
    b    7.0
    c    6.0
    d    7.0
    e    6.0
    dtype: float64
<

                            *user_guide-basics-reindexing-and-altering-labels*
REINDEXING AND ALTERING LABELS

*user_guide-basics-basics-reindexing*

|pandas.Series.reindex| is the fundamental data alignment method in pandas.
It is used to implement nearly all other features relying on label-alignment
functionality. To reindex means to conform the data to match a given set of
labels along a particular axis. This accomplishes several things:

- Reorders the existing data to match a new set of labels
- Inserts missing value (NA) markers in label locations where no data for
  that label existed
- If specified, fill data for missing labels using logic (highly relevant to
  working with time series data)

Here is a simple example:

>python
    In [214]: s = pd.Series(np.random.randn(5), index=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])

    In [215]: s
    Out[215]: 
    a    1.695148
    b    1.328614
    c    1.234686
    d   -0.385845
    e   -1.326508
    dtype: float64

    In [216]: s.reindex(["e", "b", "f", "d"])
    Out[216]: 
    e   -1.326508
    b    1.328614
    f         NaN
    d   -0.385845
    dtype: float64
<
Here, the `f` label was not contained in the Series and hence appears as
`NaN` in the result.

With a DataFrame, you can simultaneously reindex the index and columns:

>python
    In [217]: df
    Out[217]: 
            one       two     three
    a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
    b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
    c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
    d       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172

    In [218]: df.reindex(index=["c", "f", "b"], columns=["three", "two", "one"])
    Out[218]: 
          three       two       one
    c  1.227435  1.478369  0.695246
    f       NaN       NaN       NaN
    b -0.050390  1.912123  0.343054
<
Note that the `Index` objects containing the actual axis labels can be
shared between objects. So if we have a Series and a DataFrame, the
following can be done:

>python
    In [219]: rs = s.reindex(df.index)

    In [220]: rs
    Out[220]: 
    a    1.695148
    b    1.328614
    c    1.234686
    d   -0.385845
    dtype: float64

    In [221]: rs.index is df.index
    Out[221]: True
<
This means that the reindexed Series's index is the same Python object as
the DataFrame's index.

|pandas.DataFrame.reindex| also supports an “axis-style” calling convention,
where you specify a single `labels` argument and the `axis` it applies to.

>python
    In [222]: df.reindex(["c", "f", "b"], axis="index")
    Out[222]: 
            one       two     three
    c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
    f       NaN       NaN       NaN
    b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390

    In [223]: df.reindex(["three", "two", "one"], axis="columns")
    Out[223]: 
          three       two       one
    a       NaN  1.772517  1.394981
    b -0.050390  1.912123  0.343054
    c  1.227435  1.478369  0.695246
    d -0.613172  0.279344       NaN
<
  See also: ~

  |user_guide-advanced-advanced| is an even more concise way of doing
  reindexing.

  Note: ~

  When writing performance-sensitive code, there is a good reason to spend
  some time becoming a reindexing ninja: many operations are faster on
  pre-aligned data. Adding two unaligned DataFrames internally triggers a
  reindexing step. For exploratory analysis you will hardly notice the
  difference (because `reindex` has been heavily optimized), but when CPU
  cycles matter sprinkling a few explicit `reindex` calls here and there can
  have an impact.

                   *user_guide-basics-reindexing-to-align-with-another-object*
Reindexing to align with another object

*user_guide-basics-basics-reindex-like*

You may wish to take an object and reindex its axes to be labeled the same
as another object. While the syntax for this is straightforward albeit
verbose, it is a common enough operation that the
|pandas.DataFrame.reindex_like| method is available to make this simpler:

>python
    In [224]: df2 = df.reindex(["a", "b", "c"], columns=["one", "two"])

    In [225]: df3 = df2 - df2.mean()

    In [226]: df2
    Out[226]: 
            one       two
    a  1.394981  1.772517
    b  0.343054  1.912123
    c  0.695246  1.478369

    In [227]: df3
    Out[227]: 
            one       two
    a  0.583888  0.051514
    b -0.468040  0.191120
    c -0.115848 -0.242634

    In [228]: df.reindex_like(df2)
    Out[228]: 
            one       two
    a  1.394981  1.772517
    b  0.343054  1.912123
    c  0.695246  1.478369
<

               *user_guide-basics-aligning-objects-with-each-other-with-align*
Aligning objects with each other with `align`

*user_guide-basics-basics-align*

The |pandas.Series.align| method is the fastest way to simultaneously align
two objects. It supports a `join` argument (related to
|user_guide-merging-merging|):

  - `join='outer'`: take the union of the indexes (default)
  - `join='left'`: use the calling object's index
  - `join='right'`: use the passed object's index
  - `join='inner'`: intersect the indexes

It returns a tuple with both of the reindexed Series:

>python
    In [229]: s = pd.Series(np.random.randn(5), index=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])

    In [230]: s1 = s[:4]

    In [231]: s2 = s[1:]

    In [232]: s1.align(s2)
    Out[232]: 
    (a   -0.186646
     b   -1.692424
     c   -0.303893
     d   -1.425662
     e         NaN
     dtype: float64,
     a         NaN
     b   -1.692424
     c   -0.303893
     d   -1.425662
     e    1.114285
     dtype: float64)

    In [233]: s1.align(s2, join="inner")
    Out[233]: 
    (b   -1.692424
     c   -0.303893
     d   -1.425662
     dtype: float64,
     b   -1.692424
     c   -0.303893
     d   -1.425662
     dtype: float64)

    In [234]: s1.align(s2, join="left")
    Out[234]: 
    (a   -0.186646
     b   -1.692424
     c   -0.303893
     d   -1.425662
     dtype: float64,
     a         NaN
     b   -1.692424
     c   -0.303893
     d   -1.425662
     dtype: float64)
<
For DataFrames, the join method will be applied to both the index and the
columns by default:

>python
    In [235]: df.align(df2, join="inner")
    Out[235]: 
    (        one       two
     a  1.394981  1.772517
     b  0.343054  1.912123
     c  0.695246  1.478369,
             one       two
     a  1.394981  1.772517
     b  0.343054  1.912123
     c  0.695246  1.478369)
<
You can also pass an `axis` option to only align on the specified axis:

>python
    In [236]: df.align(df2, join="inner", axis=0)
    Out[236]: 
    (        one       two     three
     a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
     b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
     c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435,
             one       two
     a  1.394981  1.772517
     b  0.343054  1.912123
     c  0.695246  1.478369)
<
If you pass a Series to |pandas.DataFrame.align|, you can choose to align
both objects either on the DataFrame's index or columns using the `axis`
argument:

>python
    In [237]: df.align(df2.iloc[0], axis=1)
    Out[237]: 
    (        one     three       two
     a  1.394981       NaN  1.772517
     b  0.343054 -0.050390  1.912123
     c  0.695246  1.227435  1.478369
     d       NaN -0.613172  0.279344,
     one      1.394981
     three         NaN
     two      1.772517
     Name: a, dtype: float64)
<

Filling while reindexing          *user_guide-basics-filling-while-reindexing*

*user_guide-basics-basics-reindex-fill*

|pandas.Series.reindex| takes an optional parameter `method` which is a
filling method chosen from the following table:

Method   Action
-------  ---------------------------------------------------------------------
ffill    Fill values forward
bfill    Fill values backward
nearest  Fill from the nearest index value

We illustrate these fill methods on a simple Series:

>python
    In [238]: rng = pd.date_range("1/3/2000", periods=8)

    In [239]: ts = pd.Series(np.random.randn(8), index=rng)

    In [240]: ts2 = ts.iloc[[0, 3, 6]]

    In [241]: ts
    Out[241]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    0.400528
    2000-01-05   -0.015083
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    1.414806
    2000-01-08    0.118428
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10   -0.936077
    Freq: D, dtype: float64

    In [242]: ts2
    Out[242]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    Freq: 3D, dtype: float64

    In [243]: ts2.reindex(ts.index)
    Out[243]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04         NaN
    2000-01-05         NaN
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07         NaN
    2000-01-08         NaN
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10         NaN
    Freq: D, dtype: float64

    In [244]: ts2.reindex(ts.index, method="ffill")
    Out[244]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    0.183051
    2000-01-05    0.183051
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    2.395489
    2000-01-08    2.395489
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10    0.733639
    Freq: D, dtype: float64

    In [245]: ts2.reindex(ts.index, method="bfill")
    Out[245]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    2.395489
    2000-01-05    2.395489
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    0.733639
    2000-01-08    0.733639
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10         NaN
    Freq: D, dtype: float64

    In [246]: ts2.reindex(ts.index, method="nearest")
    Out[246]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    0.183051
    2000-01-05    2.395489
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    2.395489
    2000-01-08    0.733639
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10    0.733639
    Freq: D, dtype: float64
<
These methods require that the indexes are ordered increasing or decreasing.

Note that the same result could have been achieved using
|user_guide-missing_data-missing-data-fillna| (except for
`method='nearest'`) or |user_guide-missing_data-missing-data-interpolate|:

>python
    In [247]: ts2.reindex(ts.index).ffill()
    Out[247]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    0.183051
    2000-01-05    0.183051
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    2.395489
    2000-01-08    2.395489
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10    0.733639
    Freq: D, dtype: float64
<
|pandas.Series.reindex| will raise a ValueError if the index is not
monotonically increasing or decreasing. |pandas.Series.fillna| and
|pandas.Series.interpolate| will not perform any checks on the order of the
index.

                        *user_guide-basics-limits-on-filling-while-reindexing*
Limits on filling while reindexing

*user_guide-basics-basics-limits-on-reindex-fill*

The `limit` and `tolerance` arguments provide additional control over
filling while reindexing. Limit specifies the maximum count of consecutive
matches:

>python
    In [248]: ts2.reindex(ts.index, method="ffill", limit=1)
    Out[248]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    0.183051
    2000-01-05         NaN
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    2.395489
    2000-01-08         NaN
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10    0.733639
    Freq: D, dtype: float64
<
In contrast, tolerance specifies the maximum distance between the index and
indexer values:

>python
    In [249]: ts2.reindex(ts.index, method="ffill", tolerance="1 day")
    Out[249]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    0.183051
    2000-01-05         NaN
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    2.395489
    2000-01-08         NaN
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10    0.733639
    Freq: D, dtype: float64
<
Notice that when used on a `DatetimeIndex`, `TimedeltaIndex` or
`PeriodIndex`, `tolerance` will coerced into a `Timedelta` if possible. This
allows you to specify tolerance with appropriate strings.

Dropping labels from an axis  *user_guide-basics-dropping-labels-from-an-axis*

*user_guide-basics-basics-drop*

A method closely related to `reindex` is the |pandas.DataFrame.drop|
function. It removes a set of labels from an axis:

>python
    In [250]: df
    Out[250]: 
            one       two     three
    a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
    b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
    c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
    d       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172

    In [251]: df.drop(["a", "d"], axis=0)
    Out[251]: 
            one       two     three
    b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
    c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435

    In [252]: df.drop(["one"], axis=1)
    Out[252]: 
            two     three
    a  1.772517       NaN
    b  1.912123 -0.050390
    c  1.478369  1.227435
    d  0.279344 -0.613172
<
Note that the following also works, but is a bit less obvious / clean:

>python
    In [253]: df.reindex(df.index.difference(["a", "d"]))
    Out[253]: 
            one       two     three
    b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
    c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
<

Renaming / mapping labels          *user_guide-basics-renaming-mapping-labels*

*user_guide-basics-basics-rename*

The |pandas.DataFrame.rename| method allows you to relabel an axis based on
some mapping (a dict or Series) or an arbitrary function.

>python
    In [254]: s
    Out[254]: 
    a   -0.186646
    b   -1.692424
    c   -0.303893
    d   -1.425662
    e    1.114285
    dtype: float64

    In [255]: s.rename(str.upper)
    Out[255]: 
    A   -0.186646
    B   -1.692424
    C   -0.303893
    D   -1.425662
    E    1.114285
    dtype: float64
<
If you pass a function, it must return a value when called with any of the
labels (and must produce a set of unique values). A dict or Series can also
be used:

>python
    In [256]: df.rename(
       .....:     columns={"one": "foo", "two": "bar"},
       .....:     index={"a": "apple", "b": "banana", "d": "durian"},
       .....: )
       .....: 
    Out[256]: 
                 foo       bar     three
    apple   1.394981  1.772517       NaN
    banana  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
    c       0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
    durian       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172
<
If the mapping doesn't include a column/index label, it isn't renamed. Note
that extra labels in the mapping don't throw an error.

|pandas.DataFrame.rename| also supports an “axis-style” calling convention,
where you specify a single `mapper` and the `axis` to apply that mapping to.

>python
    In [257]: df.rename({"one": "foo", "two": "bar"}, axis="columns")
    Out[257]: 
            foo       bar     three
    a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
    b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
    c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
    d       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172

    In [258]: df.rename({"a": "apple", "b": "banana", "d": "durian"}, axis="index")
    Out[258]: 
                 one       two     three
    apple   1.394981  1.772517       NaN
    banana  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
    c       0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
    durian       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172
<
Finally, |pandas.Series.rename| also accepts a scalar or list-like for
altering the `Series.name` attribute.

>python
    In [259]: s.rename("scalar-name")
    Out[259]: 
    a   -0.186646
    b   -1.692424
    c   -0.303893
    d   -1.425662
    e    1.114285
    Name: scalar-name, dtype: float64
<
The methods |pandas.DataFrame.rename_axis| and |pandas.Series.rename_axis|
allow specific names of a `MultiIndex` to be changed (as opposed to the
labels).

>python
    In [260]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], "y": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]},
       .....:     index=pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
       .....:         [["a", "b", "c"], [1, 2]], names=["let", "num"]
       .....:     ),
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [261]: df
    Out[261]: 
             x   y
    let num       
    a   1    1  10
        2    2  20
    b   1    3  30
        2    4  40
    c   1    5  50
        2    6  60

    In [262]: df.rename_axis(index={"let": "abc"})
    Out[262]: 
             x   y
    abc num       
    a   1    1  10
        2    2  20
    b   1    3  30
        2    4  40
    c   1    5  50
        2    6  60

    In [263]: df.rename_axis(index=str.upper)
    Out[263]: 
             x   y
    LET NUM       
    a   1    1  10
        2    2  20
    b   1    3  30
        2    4  40
    c   1    5  50
        2    6  60
<

ITERATION                                        *user_guide-basics-iteration*

*user_guide-basics-basics-iteration*

The behavior of basic iteration over pandas objects depends on the type.
When iterating over a Series, it is regarded as array-like, and basic
iteration produces the values. DataFrames follow the dict-like convention of
iterating over the “keys” of the objects.

In short, basic iteration (`for i in object`) produces:

- Series: values
- DataFrame: column labels

Thus, for example, iterating over a DataFrame gives you the column names:

>python
    In [264]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {"col1": np.random.randn(3), "col2": np.random.randn(3)}, index=["a", "b", "c"]
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [265]: for col in df:
       .....:     print(col)
       .....: 
    col1
    col2
<
pandas objects also have the dict-like |pandas.DataFrame.items| method to
iterate over the (key, value) pairs.

To iterate over the rows of a DataFrame, you can use the following methods:

- |pandas.DataFrame.iterrows|: Iterate over the rows of a DataFrame as
  (index, Series) pairs. This converts the rows to Series objects, which can
  change the dtypes and has some performance implications.
- |pandas.DataFrame.itertuples|: Iterate over the rows of a DataFrame as
  namedtuples of the values. This is a lot faster than
  |pandas.DataFrame.iterrows|, and is in most cases preferable to use to
  iterate over the values of a DataFrame.

  Warning: ~

  Iterating through pandas objects is generally slow. In many cases,
  iterating manually over the rows is not needed and can be avoided with one
  of the following approaches:

  - Look for a vectorized solution: many operations can be performed using
    built-in methods or NumPy functions, (boolean) indexing, ...
  - When you have a function that cannot work on the full DataFrame/Series
    at once, it is better to use |pandas.DataFrame.apply| instead of
    iterating over the values. See the docs on
    |user_guide-basics-basics-apply|.
  - If you need to do iterative manipulations on the values but performance
    is important, consider writing the inner loop with cython or numba. See
    the |user_guide-enhancingperf-enhancingperf| section for some examples
    of this approach.

  Warning: ~

  You should never modify something you are iterating over. This is not
  guaranteed to work in all cases. Depending on the data types, the iterator
  returns a copy and not a view, and writing to it will have no effect!

  For example, in the following case setting the value has no effect:

  >python
      In [266]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": ["a", "b", "c"]})

      In [267]: for index, row in df.iterrows():
         .....:     row["a"] = 10
         .....: 

      In [268]: df
      Out[268]: 
         a  b
      0  1  a
      1  2  b
      2  3  c
<

items                                                *user_guide-basics-items*

Consistent with the dict-like interface, |pandas.DataFrame.items| iterates
through key-value pairs:

- Series: (index, scalar value) pairs
- DataFrame: (column, Series) pairs

For example:

>python
    In [269]: for label, ser in df.items():
       .....:     print(label)
       .....:     print(ser)
       .....: 
    a
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    Name: a, dtype: int64
    b
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    Name: b, dtype: str
<

iterrows                                          *user_guide-basics-iterrows*

*user_guide-basics-basics-iterrows*

|pandas.DataFrame.iterrows| allows you to iterate through the rows of a
DataFrame as Series objects. It returns an iterator yielding each index
value along with a Series containing the data in each row:

>python
    In [270]: for row_index, row in df.iterrows():
       .....:     print(row_index, row, sep="\n")
       .....: 
    0
    a    1
    b    a
    Name: 0, dtype: object
    1
    a    2
    b    b
    Name: 1, dtype: object
    2
    a    3
    b    c
    Name: 2, dtype: object
<
  Note: ~

  Because |pandas.DataFrame.iterrows| returns a Series for each row, it does
  not preserve dtypes across the rows (dtypes are preserved across columns
  for DataFrames). For example,

  >python
      In [271]: df_orig = pd.DataFrame([[1, 1.5]], columns=["int", "float"])

      In [272]: df_orig.dtypes
      Out[272]: 
      int        int64
      float    float64
      dtype: object

      In [273]: row = next(df_orig.iterrows())[1]

      In [274]: row
      Out[274]: 
      int      1.0
      float    1.5
      Name: 0, dtype: float64
<
  All values in `row`, returned as a Series, are now upcasted to floats,
  also the original integer value in column `x`:

  >python
      In [275]: row["int"].dtype
      Out[275]: dtype('float64')

      In [276]: df_orig["int"].dtype
      Out[276]: dtype('int64')
<
  To preserve dtypes while iterating over the rows, it is better to use
  |pandas.DataFrame.itertuples| which returns namedtuples of the values and
  which is generally much faster than |pandas.DataFrame.iterrows|.

For instance, a contrived way to transpose the DataFrame would be:

>python
    In [277]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [4, 5, 6]})

    In [278]: print(df2)
       x  y
    0  1  4
    1  2  5
    2  3  6

    In [279]: print(df2.T)
       0  1  2
    x  1  2  3
    y  4  5  6

    In [280]: df2_t = pd.DataFrame({idx: values for idx, values in df2.iterrows()})

    In [281]: print(df2_t)
       0  1  2
    x  1  2  3
    y  4  5  6
<

itertuples                                      *user_guide-basics-itertuples*

The |pandas.DataFrame.itertuples| method will return an iterator yielding a
namedtuple for each row in the DataFrame. The first element of the tuple
will be the row's corresponding index value, while the remaining values are
the row values.

For instance:

>python
    In [282]: for row in df.itertuples():
       .....:     print(row)
       .....: 
    Pandas(Index=0, a=1, b='a')
    Pandas(Index=1, a=2, b='b')
    Pandas(Index=2, a=3, b='c')
<
This method does not convert the row to a Series object; it merely returns
the values inside a namedtuple. Therefore, |pandas.DataFrame.itertuples|
preserves the data type of the values and is generally faster than
|pandas.DataFrame.iterrows|.

  Note: ~

  The column names will be renamed to positional names if they are invalid
  Python identifiers, repeated, or start with an underscore. With a large
  number of columns (>255), regular tuples are returned.

.DT ACCESSOR                                   *user_guide-basics-dt-accessor*

*user_guide-basics-basics-dt-accessors*

`Series` has an accessor to succinctly return datetime like properties for
the values of the Series, if it is a datetime/period like Series. This will
return a Series, indexed like the existing Series.

>python
    # datetime
    In [283]: s = pd.Series(pd.date_range("20130101 09:10:12", periods=4))

    In [284]: s
    Out[284]: 
    0   2013-01-01 09:10:12
    1   2013-01-02 09:10:12
    2   2013-01-03 09:10:12
    3   2013-01-04 09:10:12
    dtype: datetime64[us]

    In [285]: s.dt.hour
    Out[285]: 
    0    9
    1    9
    2    9
    3    9
    dtype: int32

    In [286]: s.dt.second
    Out[286]: 
    0    12
    1    12
    2    12
    3    12
    dtype: int32

    In [287]: s.dt.day
    Out[287]: 
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    3    4
    dtype: int32
<
This enables nice expressions like this:

>python
    In [288]: s[s.dt.day == 2]
    Out[288]: 
    1   2013-01-02 09:10:12
    dtype: datetime64[us]
<
You can easily produce tz aware transformations:

>python
    In [289]: stz = s.dt.tz_localize("US/Eastern")

    In [290]: stz
    Out[290]: 
    0   2013-01-01 09:10:12-05:00
    1   2013-01-02 09:10:12-05:00
    2   2013-01-03 09:10:12-05:00
    3   2013-01-04 09:10:12-05:00
    dtype: datetime64[us, US/Eastern]

    In [291]: stz.dt.tz
    Out[291]: zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(key='US/Eastern')
<
You can also chain these types of operations:

>python
    In [292]: s.dt.tz_localize("UTC").dt.tz_convert("US/Eastern")
    Out[292]: 
    0   2013-01-01 04:10:12-05:00
    1   2013-01-02 04:10:12-05:00
    2   2013-01-03 04:10:12-05:00
    3   2013-01-04 04:10:12-05:00
    dtype: datetime64[us, US/Eastern]
<
You can also format datetime values as strings with
|pandas.Series.dt.strftime| which supports the same format as the standard
`strftime()`
https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime.strftime.

>python
    # DatetimeIndex
    In [293]: s = pd.Series(pd.date_range("20130101", periods=4))

    In [294]: s
    Out[294]: 
    0   2013-01-01
    1   2013-01-02
    2   2013-01-03
    3   2013-01-04
    dtype: datetime64[us]

    In [295]: s.dt.strftime("%Y/%m/%d")
    Out[295]: 
    0    2013/01/01
    1    2013/01/02
    2    2013/01/03
    3    2013/01/04
    dtype: str
<
>python
    # PeriodIndex
    In [296]: s = pd.Series(pd.period_range("20130101", periods=4))

    In [297]: s
    Out[297]: 
    0    2013-01-01
    1    2013-01-02
    2    2013-01-03
    3    2013-01-04
    dtype: period[D]

    In [298]: s.dt.strftime("%Y/%m/%d")
    Out[298]: 
    0    2013/01/01
    1    2013/01/02
    2    2013/01/03
    3    2013/01/04
    dtype: str
<
The `.dt` accessor works for period and timedelta dtypes.

>python
    # period
    In [299]: s = pd.Series(pd.period_range("20130101", periods=4, freq="D"))

    In [300]: s
    Out[300]: 
    0    2013-01-01
    1    2013-01-02
    2    2013-01-03
    3    2013-01-04
    dtype: period[D]

    In [301]: s.dt.year
    Out[301]: 
    0    2013
    1    2013
    2    2013
    3    2013
    dtype: int64

    In [302]: s.dt.day
    Out[302]: 
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    3    4
    dtype: int64
<
>python
    # timedelta
    In [303]: s = pd.Series(pd.timedelta_range("1 day 00:00:05", periods=4, freq="s"))

    In [304]: s
    Out[304]: 
    0   1 days 00:00:05
    1   1 days 00:00:06
    2   1 days 00:00:07
    3   1 days 00:00:08
    dtype: timedelta64[us]

    In [305]: s.dt.days
    Out[305]: 
    0    1
    1    1
    2    1
    3    1
    dtype: int64

    In [306]: s.dt.seconds
    Out[306]: 
    0    5
    1    6
    2    7
    3    8
    dtype: int32

    In [307]: s.dt.components
    Out[307]: 
       days  hours  minutes  seconds  milliseconds  microseconds  nanoseconds
    0     1      0        0        5             0             0            0
    1     1      0        0        6             0             0            0
    2     1      0        0        7             0             0            0
    3     1      0        0        8             0             0            0
<
  Note: ~

  `Series.dt` will raise a `TypeError` if you access with a
  non-datetime-like values.

VECTORIZED STRING METHODS        *user_guide-basics-vectorized-string-methods*

Series is equipped with a set of string processing methods that make it easy
to operate on each element of the array. Perhaps most importantly, these
methods exclude missing/NA values automatically. These are accessed via the
Series's `str` attribute and generally have names matching the equivalent
(scalar) built-in string methods. For example:

  >python
      In [308]: s = pd.Series(
         .....:     ["A", "B", "C", "Aaba", "Baca", np.nan, "CABA", "dog", "cat"], dtype="string"
         .....: )
         .....: 

      In [309]: s.str.lower()
      Out[309]: 
      0       a
      1       b
      2       c
      3    aaba
      4    baca
      5    <NA>
      6    caba
      7     dog
      8     cat
      dtype: string
<

Powerful pattern-matching methods are provided as well, but note that
pattern-matching generally uses regular expressions
https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html by default (and in some cases
always uses them).

  Note: ~

  Prior to pandas 1.0, string methods were only available on `object` -dtype
  `Series`. pandas 1.0 added the |pandas.StringDtype| which is dedicated to
  strings. See |user_guide-text-text-types| for more.

Please see |user_guide-text-text-string-methods| for a complete description.

SORTING                                            *user_guide-basics-sorting*

*user_guide-basics-basics-sorting*

pandas supports three kinds of sorting: sorting by index labels, sorting by
column values, and sorting by a combination of both.

By index                                          *user_guide-basics-by-index*

*user_guide-basics-basics-sort-index*

The |pandas.Series.sort_index| and |pandas.DataFrame.sort_index| methods are
used to sort a pandas object by its index levels.

>python
    In [310]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {
       .....:         "one": pd.Series(np.random.randn(3), index=["a", "b", "c"]),
       .....:         "two": pd.Series(np.random.randn(4), index=["a", "b", "c", "d"]),
       .....:         "three": pd.Series(np.random.randn(3), index=["b", "c", "d"]),
       .....:     }
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [311]: unsorted_df = df.reindex(
       .....:     index=["a", "d", "c", "b"], columns=["three", "two", "one"]
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [312]: unsorted_df
    Out[312]: 
          three       two       one
    a       NaN -1.152244  0.562973
    d -0.252916 -0.109597       NaN
    c  1.273388 -0.167123  0.640382
    b -0.098217  0.009797 -1.299504

    # DataFrame
    In [313]: unsorted_df.sort_index()
    Out[313]: 
          three       two       one
    a       NaN -1.152244  0.562973
    b -0.098217  0.009797 -1.299504
    c  1.273388 -0.167123  0.640382
    d -0.252916 -0.109597       NaN

    In [314]: unsorted_df.sort_index(ascending=False)
    Out[314]: 
          three       two       one
    d -0.252916 -0.109597       NaN
    c  1.273388 -0.167123  0.640382
    b -0.098217  0.009797 -1.299504
    a       NaN -1.152244  0.562973

    In [315]: unsorted_df.sort_index(axis=1)
    Out[315]: 
            one     three       two
    a  0.562973       NaN -1.152244
    d       NaN -0.252916 -0.109597
    c  0.640382  1.273388 -0.167123
    b -1.299504 -0.098217  0.009797

    # Series
    In [316]: unsorted_df["three"].sort_index()
    Out[316]: 
    a         NaN
    b   -0.098217
    c    1.273388
    d   -0.252916
    Name: three, dtype: float64
<
Sorting by index also supports a `key` parameter that takes a callable
function to apply to the index being sorted. For `MultiIndex` objects, the
key is applied per-level to the levels specified by `level`.

>python
    In [317]: s1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["B", "a", "C"], "b": [1, 2, 3], "c": [2, 3, 4]}).set_index(
       .....:     list("ab")
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [318]: s1
    Out[318]: 
         c
    a b   
    B 1  2
    a 2  3
    C 3  4
<
>python
    In [319]: s1.sort_index(level="a")
    Out[319]: 
         c
    a b   
    B 1  2
    C 3  4
    a 2  3

    In [320]: s1.sort_index(level="a", key=lambda idx: idx.str.lower())
    Out[320]: 
         c
    a b   
    a 2  3
    B 1  2
    C 3  4
<
For information on key sorting by value, see
|user_guide-basics-basics-sort-value-key|.

By values                                        *user_guide-basics-by-values*

*user_guide-basics-basics-sort-values*

The |pandas.Series.sort_values| method is used to sort a `Series` by its
values. The |pandas.DataFrame.sort_values| method is used to sort a
`DataFrame` by its column or row values. The optional `by` parameter to
|pandas.DataFrame.sort_values| may used to specify one or more columns to
use to determine the sorted order.

>python
    In [321]: df1 = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {"one": [2, 1, 1, 1], "two": [1, 3, 2, 4], "three": [5, 4, 3, 2]}
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [322]: df1.sort_values(by="two")
    Out[322]: 
       one  two  three
    0    2    1      5
    2    1    2      3
    1    1    3      4
    3    1    4      2
<
The `by` parameter can take a list of column names, e.g.:

>python
    In [323]: df1[["one", "two", "three"]].sort_values(by=["one", "two"])
    Out[323]: 
       one  two  three
    2    1    2      3
    1    1    3      4
    3    1    4      2
    0    2    1      5
<
These methods have special treatment of NA values via the `na_position`
argument:

>python
    In [324]: s[2] = np.nan

    In [325]: s.sort_values()
    Out[325]: 
    0       A
    3    Aaba
    1       B
    4    Baca
    6    CABA
    8     cat
    7     dog
    2    <NA>
    5    <NA>
    dtype: string

    In [326]: s.sort_values(na_position="first")
    Out[326]: 
    2    <NA>
    5    <NA>
    0       A
    3    Aaba
    1       B
    4    Baca
    6    CABA
    8     cat
    7     dog
    dtype: string
<
Sorting also supports a `key` parameter that takes a callable function to
apply to the values being sorted.

>python
    In [327]: s1 = pd.Series(["B", "a", "C"])
<
>python
    In [328]: s1.sort_values()
    Out[328]: 
    0    B
    2    C
    1    a
    dtype: str

    In [329]: s1.sort_values(key=lambda x: x.str.lower())
    Out[329]: 
    1    a
    0    B
    2    C
    dtype: str
<
`key` will be given the |pandas.Series| of values and should return a
`Series` or array of the same shape with the transformed values. For
`DataFrame` objects, the key is applied per column, so the key should still
expect a Series and return a Series, e.g.

>python
    In [330]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["B", "a", "C"], "b": [1, 2, 3]})
<
>python
    In [331]: df.sort_values(by="a")
    Out[331]: 
       a  b
    0  B  1
    2  C  3
    1  a  2

    In [332]: df.sort_values(by="a", key=lambda col: col.str.lower())
    Out[332]: 
       a  b
    1  a  2
    0  B  1
    2  C  3
<
The name or type of each column can be used to apply different functions to
different columns.

By indexes and values                *user_guide-basics-by-indexes-and-values*

*user_guide-basics-basics-sort-indexes-and-values*

Strings passed as the `by` parameter to |pandas.DataFrame.sort_values| may
refer to either columns or index level names.

>python
    # Build MultiIndex
    In [333]: idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
       .....:     [("a", 1), ("a", 2), ("a", 2), ("b", 2), ("b", 1), ("b", 1)]
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [334]: idx.names = ["first", "second"]

    # Build DataFrame
    In [335]: df_multi = pd.DataFrame({"A": np.arange(6, 0, -1)}, index=idx)

    In [336]: df_multi
    Out[336]: 
                  A
    first second   
    a     1       6
          2       5
          2       4
    b     2       3
          1       2
          1       1
<
Sort by ‘second' (index) and ‘A' (column)

>python
    In [337]: df_multi.sort_values(by=["second", "A"])
    Out[337]: 
                  A
    first second   
    b     1       1
          1       2
    a     1       6
    b     2       3
    a     2       4
          2       5
<
  Note: ~

  If a string matches both a column name and an index level name then a
  warning is issued and the column takes precedence. This will result in an
  ambiguity error in a future version.

searchsorted                                  *user_guide-basics-searchsorted*

*user_guide-basics-basics-searchsorted*

Series has the |pandas.Series.searchsorted| method, which works similarly to
`numpy.ndarray.searchsorted()`
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.searchsorted.html#numpy.ndarray.searchsorted.

>python
    In [338]: ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])

    In [339]: ser.searchsorted([0, 3])
    Out[339]: array([0, 2])

    In [340]: ser.searchsorted([0, 4])
    Out[340]: array([0, 3])

    In [341]: ser.searchsorted([1, 3], side="right")
    Out[341]: array([1, 3])

    In [342]: ser.searchsorted([1, 3], side="left")
    Out[342]: array([0, 2])

    In [343]: ser = pd.Series([3, 1, 2])

    In [344]: ser.searchsorted([0, 3], sorter=np.argsort(ser))
    Out[344]: array([0, 2])
<

smallest / largest values          *user_guide-basics-smallest-largest-values*

*user_guide-basics-basics-nsorted*

`Series` has the |pandas.Series.nsmallest| and |pandas.Series.nlargest|
methods which return the smallest or largest `\(n\)` values. For a large
`Series` this can be much faster than sorting the entire Series and calling
`head(n)` on the result.

>python
    In [345]: s = pd.Series(np.random.permutation(10))

    In [346]: s
    Out[346]: 
    0    2
    1    0
    2    3
    3    7
    4    1
    5    5
    6    9
    7    6
    8    8
    9    4
    dtype: int64

    In [347]: s.sort_values()
    Out[347]: 
    1    0
    4    1
    0    2
    2    3
    9    4
    5    5
    7    6
    3    7
    8    8
    6    9
    dtype: int64

    In [348]: s.nsmallest(3)
    Out[348]: 
    1    0
    4    1
    0    2
    dtype: int64

    In [349]: s.nlargest(3)
    Out[349]: 
    6    9
    8    8
    3    7
    dtype: int64
<
`DataFrame` also has the `nlargest` and `nsmallest` methods.

>python
    In [350]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {
       .....:         "a": [-2, -1, 1, 10, 8, 11, -1],
       .....:         "b": list("abdceff"),
       .....:         "c": [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 3.2, np.nan, 3.0, 4.0],
       .....:     }
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [351]: df.nlargest(3, "a")
    Out[351]: 
        a  b    c
    5  11  f  3.0
    3  10  c  3.2
    4   8  e  NaN

    In [352]: df.nlargest(5, ["a", "c"])
    Out[352]: 
        a  b    c
    5  11  f  3.0
    3  10  c  3.2
    4   8  e  NaN
    2   1  d  4.0
    6  -1  f  4.0

    In [353]: df.nsmallest(3, "a")
    Out[353]: 
       a  b    c
    0 -2  a  1.0
    1 -1  b  2.0
    6 -1  f  4.0

    In [354]: df.nsmallest(5, ["a", "c"])
    Out[354]: 
       a  b    c
    0 -2  a  1.0
    1 -1  b  2.0
    6 -1  f  4.0
    2  1  d  4.0
    4  8  e  NaN
<

                            *user_guide-basics-sorting-by-a-multiindex-column*
Sorting by a MultiIndex column

*user_guide-basics-basics-multiindex-sorting*

You must be explicit about sorting when the column is a MultiIndex, and
fully specify all levels to `by`.

>python
    In [355]: df1.columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
       .....:     [("a", "one"), ("a", "two"), ("b", "three")]
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [356]: df1.sort_values(by=("a", "two"))
    Out[356]: 
        a         b
      one two three
    0   2   1     5
    2   1   2     3
    1   1   3     4
    3   1   4     2
<

COPYING                                            *user_guide-basics-copying*

The |pandas.DataFrame.copy| method on pandas objects copies the underlying
data (though not the axis indexes, since they are immutable) and returns a
new object. Note that it is seldom necessary to copy objects. For example,
there are only a handful of ways to alter a DataFrame in-place:

- Inserting, deleting, or modifying a column.
- Assigning to the `index` or `columns` attributes.
- For homogeneous data, directly modifying the values via the `values`
  attribute or advanced indexing.

To be clear, no pandas method has the side effect of modifying your data;
almost every method returns a new object, leaving the original object
untouched. If the data is modified, it is because you did so explicitly.

DTYPES                                              *user_guide-basics-dtypes*

*user_guide-basics-basics-dtypes*

For the most part, pandas uses NumPy arrays and dtypes for Series or
individual columns of a DataFrame. NumPy provides support for `float`,
`int`, `bool`, `timedelta64[ns]` and `datetime64[ns]` (note that NumPy does
not support timezone-aware datetimes).

pandas and third-party libraries extend NumPy's type system in a few places.
This section describes the extensions pandas has made internally. See
Extension types
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/development/extending.html#extending-extension-types
for how to write your own extension that works with pandas. See
the ecosystem page https://pandas.pydata.org/community/ecosystem.html for a
list of third-party libraries that have implemented an extension.

The following table lists all of pandas extension types. For methods
requiring `dtype` arguments, strings can be specified as indicated. See the
respective documentation sections for more on each type.

Kind of      Data Type         Scalar     Array                 String Aliases
Data
-----------  ----------------  ---------  --------------------  -------------------------------
tz-aware     DatetimeTZDtype   Timestamp  arrays.DatetimeArray  'datetime64[ns, <tz>]'
datetime
Categorical  CategoricalDtype  (none)     Categorical           'category'
period       PeriodDtype       Period     arrays.PeriodArray    'period[<freq>]',
(time                                     'Period[<freq>]'
spans)
sparse       SparseDtype       (none)     arrays.SparseArray    'Sparse', 'Sparse[int]',
                                                                'Sparse[float]'
intervals    IntervalDtype     Interval   arrays.IntervalArray  'interval', 'Interval',
                                                                'Interval[<numpy_dtype>]',
                                                                'Interval[datetime64[ns,
                                                                <tz>]]',
                                                                'Interval[timedelta64[<freq>]]'
nullable     Int64Dtype, ...     (none)     arrays.IntegerArray   'Int8', 'Int16', 'Int32',
integer                                                         'Int64', 'UInt8', 'UInt16',
                                                                'UInt32', 'UInt64'
nullable     Float64Dtype, ...   (none)     arrays.FloatingArray  'Float32', 'Float64'
float
Strings      StringDtype       str        arrays.StringArray    'string'
Boolean      BooleanDtype      bool       arrays.BooleanArray   'boolean'
(with NA)

pandas has two ways to store strings.

1. `object` dtype, which can hold any Python object, including strings.
2. |pandas.StringDtype|, which is dedicated to strings.

Generally, we recommend using |pandas.StringDtype|. See
|user_guide-text-text-types| for more.

Finally, arbitrary objects may be stored using the `object` dtype, but
should be avoided to the extent possible (for performance and
interoperability with other libraries and methods. See
|user_guide-basics-basics-object-conversion|).

A convenient |pandas.DataFrame.dtypes| attribute for DataFrame returns a
Series with the data type of each column.

>python
    In [357]: dft = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {
       .....:         "A": np.random.rand(3),
       .....:         "B": 1,
       .....:         "C": "foo",
       .....:         "D": pd.Timestamp("20010102"),
       .....:         "E": pd.Series([1.0] * 3).astype("float32"),
       .....:         "F": False,
       .....:         "G": pd.Series([1] * 3, dtype="int8"),
       .....:     }
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [358]: dft
    Out[358]: 
              A  B    C          D    E      F  G
    0  0.035962  1  foo 2001-01-02  1.0  False  1
    1  0.701379  1  foo 2001-01-02  1.0  False  1
    2  0.281885  1  foo 2001-01-02  1.0  False  1

    In [359]: dft.dtypes
    Out[359]: 
    A           float64
    B             int64
    C               str
    D    datetime64[us]
    E           float32
    F              bool
    G              int8
    dtype: object
<
On a `Series` object, use the |pandas.Series.dtype| attribute.

>python
    In [360]: dft["A"].dtype
    Out[360]: dtype('float64')
<
If a pandas object contains data with multiple dtypes in a single column,
the dtype of the column will be chosen to accommodate all of the data types
(`object` is the most general).

>python
    # these ints are coerced to floats
    In [361]: pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.0])
    Out[361]: 
    0    1.0
    1    2.0
    2    3.0
    3    4.0
    4    5.0
    5    6.0
    dtype: float64

    # string data forces an ``object`` dtype
    In [362]: pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 6.0, "foo"])
    Out[362]: 
    0      1
    1      2
    2      3
    3    6.0
    4    foo
    dtype: object
<
The number of columns of each type in a `DataFrame` can be found by calling
`DataFrame.dtypes.value_counts()`.

>python
    In [363]: dft.dtypes.value_counts()
    Out[363]: 
    float64           1
    int64             1
    str               1
    datetime64[us]    1
    float32           1
    bool              1
    int8              1
    Name: count, dtype: int64
<
Numeric dtypes will propagate and can coexist in DataFrames. If a dtype is
passed (either directly via the `dtype` keyword, a passed `ndarray`, or a
passed `Series`), then it will be preserved in DataFrame operations.
Furthermore, different numeric dtypes will NOT be combined. The following
example will give you a taste.

>python
    In [364]: df1 = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(8, 1), columns=["A"], dtype="float64")

    In [365]: df1
    Out[365]: 
              A
    0  0.224364
    1  1.890546
    2  0.182879
    3  0.787847
    4 -0.188449
    5  0.667715
    6 -0.011736
    7 -0.399073

    In [366]: df1.dtypes
    Out[366]: 
    A    float64
    dtype: object

    In [367]: df2 = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {
       .....:         "A": pd.Series(np.random.randn(8), dtype="float32"),
       .....:         "B": pd.Series(np.random.randn(8)),
       .....:         "C": pd.Series(np.random.randint(0, 255, size=8), dtype="uint8"),  # [0,255] (range of uint8)
       .....:     }
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [368]: df2
    Out[368]: 
              A         B    C
    0  0.823270  0.256090   26
    1  1.607861  1.426469   86
    2 -0.333669 -0.416203   46
    3 -0.063467  1.139976  212
    4 -1.014637 -1.193477   26
    5  0.678758  0.096706    7
    6 -0.040865 -1.956850  184
    7 -0.357346 -0.714337  206

    In [369]: df2.dtypes
    Out[369]: 
    A    float32
    B    float64
    C      uint8
    dtype: object
<

defaults                                          *user_guide-basics-defaults*

By default integer types are `int64` and float types are `float64`,
regardless of platform (32-bit or 64-bit). The following will all result in
`int64` dtypes.

>python
    In [370]: pd.DataFrame([1, 2], columns=["a"]).dtypes
    Out[370]: 
    a    int64
    dtype: object

    In [371]: pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}).dtypes
    Out[371]: 
    a    int64
    dtype: object

    In [372]: pd.DataFrame({"a": 1}, index=list(range(2))).dtypes
    Out[372]: 
    a    int64
    dtype: object
<
Note that Numpy will choose platform-dependent types when creating arrays.
The following WILL result in `int32` on 32-bit platform.

>python
    In [373]: frame = pd.DataFrame(np.array([1, 2]))
<

upcasting                                        *user_guide-basics-upcasting*

Types can potentially be upcasted when combined with other types, meaning
they are promoted from the current type (e.g. `int` to `float`).

>python
    In [374]: df3 = df1.reindex_like(df2).fillna(value=0.0) + df2

    In [375]: df3
    Out[375]: 
              A         B      C
    0  1.047634  0.256090   26.0
    1  3.498407  1.426469   86.0
    2 -0.150790 -0.416203   46.0
    3  0.724380  1.139976  212.0
    4 -1.203087 -1.193477   26.0
    5  1.346474  0.096706    7.0
    6 -0.052601 -1.956850  184.0
    7 -0.756419 -0.714337  206.0

    In [376]: df3.dtypes
    Out[376]: 
    A    float64
    B    float64
    C    float64
    dtype: object
<
|pandas.DataFrame.to_numpy| will return the lower-common-denominator of the
dtypes, meaning the dtype that can accommodate ALL of the types in the
resulting homogeneous dtyped NumPy array. This can force some upcasting.

>python
    In [377]: df3.to_numpy().dtype
    Out[377]: dtype('float64')
<

astype                                              *user_guide-basics-astype*

You can use the |pandas.DataFrame.astype| method to explicitly convert
dtypes from one to another. These will by default return a copy, even if the
dtype was unchanged (pass `copy=False` to change this behavior). In
addition, they will raise an exception if the astype operation is invalid.

Upcasting is always according to the NumPy rules. If two different dtypes
are involved in an operation, then the more general one will be used as the
result of the operation.

>python
    In [378]: df3
    Out[378]: 
              A         B      C
    0  1.047634  0.256090   26.0
    1  3.498407  1.426469   86.0
    2 -0.150790 -0.416203   46.0
    3  0.724380  1.139976  212.0
    4 -1.203087 -1.193477   26.0
    5  1.346474  0.096706    7.0
    6 -0.052601 -1.956850  184.0
    7 -0.756419 -0.714337  206.0

    In [379]: df3.dtypes
    Out[379]: 
    A    float64
    B    float64
    C    float64
    dtype: object

    # conversion of dtypes
    In [380]: df3.astype("float32").dtypes
    Out[380]: 
    A    float32
    B    float32
    C    float32
    dtype: object
<
Convert a subset of columns to a specified type using
|pandas.DataFrame.astype|.

>python
    In [381]: dft = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6], "c": [7, 8, 9]})

    In [382]: dft[["a", "b"]] = dft[["a", "b"]].astype(np.uint8)

    In [383]: dft
    Out[383]: 
       a  b  c
    0  1  4  7
    1  2  5  8
    2  3  6  9

    In [384]: dft.dtypes
    Out[384]: 
    a    uint8
    b    uint8
    c    int64
    dtype: object
<
Convert certain columns to a specific dtype by passing a dict to
|pandas.DataFrame.astype|.

>python
    In [385]: dft1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 0, 1], "b": [4, 5, 6], "c": [7, 8, 9]})

    In [386]: dft1 = dft1.astype({"a": np.bool_, "c": np.float64})

    In [387]: dft1
    Out[387]: 
           a  b    c
    0   True  4  7.0
    1  False  5  8.0
    2   True  6  9.0

    In [388]: dft1.dtypes
    Out[388]: 
    a       bool
    b      int64
    c    float64
    dtype: object
<
  Note: ~

  When trying to convert a subset of columns to a specified type using
  |pandas.DataFrame.astype| and |pandas.DataFrame.loc|, upcasting occurs.
