  |pandas.DataFrame.loc| tries to fit in what we are assigning to the
  current dtypes, while `[]` will overwrite them taking the dtype from the
  right hand side. Therefore the following piece of code produces the
  unintended result.

  >python
      In [389]: dft = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6], "c": [7, 8, 9]})

      In [390]: dft.loc[:, ["a", "b"]].astype(np.uint8).dtypes
      Out[390]: 
      a    uint8
      b    uint8
      dtype: object

      In [391]: dft.loc[:, ["a", "b"]] = dft.loc[:, ["a", "b"]].astype(np.uint8)

      In [392]: dft.dtypes
      Out[392]: 
      a    int64
      b    int64
      c    int64
      dtype: object
<

object conversion                        *user_guide-basics-object-conversion*

*user_guide-basics-basics-object-conversion*

pandas offers various functions to try to force conversion of types from the
`object` dtype to other types. In cases where the data is already of the
correct type, but stored in an `object` array, the
|pandas.DataFrame.infer_objects| and |pandas.Series.infer_objects| methods
can be used to soft convert to the correct type.

  >python
      In [393]: import datetime

      In [394]: df = pd.DataFrame(
         .....:     [
         .....:         [1, 2],
         .....:         ["a", "b"],
         .....:         [datetime.datetime(2016, 3, 2), datetime.datetime(2016, 3, 2)],
         .....:     ]
         .....: )
         .....: 

      In [395]: df = df.T

      In [396]: df
      Out[396]: 
         0  1                    2
      0  1  a  2016-03-02 00:00:00
      1  2  b  2016-03-02 00:00:00

      In [397]: df.dtypes
      Out[397]: 
      0    object
      1    object
      2    object
      dtype: object
<

Because the data was transposed the original inference stored all columns as
object, which `infer_objects` will correct.

  >python
      In [398]: df.infer_objects().dtypes
      Out[398]: 
      0             int64
      1               str
      2    datetime64[us]
      dtype: object
<

The following functions are available for one dimensional object arrays or
scalars to perform hard conversion of objects to a specified type:

- |pandas.to_numeric| (conversion to numeric dtypes)

  >python
      In [399]: m = ["1.1", 2, 3]

      In [400]: pd.to_numeric(m)
      Out[400]: array([1.1, 2. , 3. ])
<

- |pandas.to_datetime| (conversion to datetime objects)

  >python
      In [401]: import datetime

      In [402]: m = ["2016-07-09", datetime.datetime(2016, 3, 2)]

      In [403]: pd.to_datetime(m)
      Out[403]: DatetimeIndex(['2016-07-09', '2016-03-02'], dtype='datetime64[us]', freq=None)
<

- |pandas.to_timedelta| (conversion to timedelta objects)

  >python
      In [404]: m = ["5us", pd.Timedelta("1day")]

      In [405]: pd.to_timedelta(m)
      Out[405]: 
      TimedeltaIndex(['0 days 00:00:00.000005', '1 days 00:00:00.000000'],
                     dtype='timedelta64[us]', freq=None)
<

To force a conversion, we can pass in an `errors` argument, which specifies
how pandas should deal with elements that cannot be converted to desired
dtype or object. By default, `errors='raise'`, meaning that any errors
encountered will be raised during the conversion process. However, if
`errors='coerce'`, these errors will be ignored and pandas will convert
problematic elements to `pd.NaT` (for datetime and timedelta) or `np.nan`
(for numeric). This might be useful if you are reading in data which is
mostly of the desired dtype (e.g. numeric, datetime), but occasionally has
non-conforming elements intermixed that you want to represent as missing:

>python
    In [406]: import datetime

    In [407]: m = ["apple", datetime.datetime(2016, 3, 2)]

    In [408]: pd.to_datetime(m, errors="coerce")
    Out[408]: DatetimeIndex(['NaT', '2016-03-02'], dtype='datetime64[us]', freq=None)

    In [409]: m = ["apple", 2, 3]

    In [410]: pd.to_numeric(m, errors="coerce")
    Out[410]: array([nan,  2.,  3.])

    In [411]: m = ["apple", pd.Timedelta("1day")]

    In [412]: pd.to_timedelta(m, errors="coerce")
    Out[412]: TimedeltaIndex([NaT, '1 days'], dtype='timedelta64[us]', freq=None)
<
In addition to object conversion, |pandas.to_numeric| provides another
argument `downcast`, which gives the option of downcasting the newly (or
already) numeric data to a smaller dtype, which can conserve memory:

>python
    In [413]: m = ["1", 2, 3]

    In [414]: pd.to_numeric(m, downcast="integer")  # smallest signed int dtype
    Out[414]: array([1, 2, 3], dtype=int8)

    In [415]: pd.to_numeric(m, downcast="signed")  # same as 'integer'
    Out[415]: array([1, 2, 3], dtype=int8)

    In [416]: pd.to_numeric(m, downcast="unsigned")  # smallest unsigned int dtype
    Out[416]: array([1, 2, 3], dtype=uint8)

    In [417]: pd.to_numeric(m, downcast="float")  # smallest float dtype
    Out[417]: array([1., 2., 3.], dtype=float32)
<
As these methods apply only to one-dimensional arrays, lists or scalars;
they cannot be used directly on multi-dimensional objects such as
DataFrames. However, with |pandas.DataFrame.apply|, we can “apply” the
function over each column efficiently:

>python
    In [418]: import datetime

    In [419]: df = pd.DataFrame([["2016-07-09", datetime.datetime(2016, 3, 2)]] * 2, dtype="O")

    In [420]: df
    Out[420]: 
                0                    1
    0  2016-07-09  2016-03-02 00:00:00
    1  2016-07-09  2016-03-02 00:00:00

    In [421]: df.apply(pd.to_datetime)
    Out[421]: 
               0          1
    0 2016-07-09 2016-03-02
    1 2016-07-09 2016-03-02

    In [422]: df = pd.DataFrame([["1.1", 2, 3]] * 2, dtype="O")

    In [423]: df
    Out[423]: 
         0  1  2
    0  1.1  2  3
    1  1.1  2  3

    In [424]: df.apply(pd.to_numeric)
    Out[424]: 
         0  1  2
    0  1.1  2  3
    1  1.1  2  3

    In [425]: df = pd.DataFrame([["5us", pd.Timedelta("1day")]] * 2, dtype="O")

    In [426]: df
    Out[426]: 
         0                1
    0  5us  1 days 00:00:00
    1  5us  1 days 00:00:00

    In [427]: df.apply(pd.to_timedelta)
    Out[427]: 
                           0      1
    0 0 days 00:00:00.000005 1 days
    1 0 days 00:00:00.000005 1 days
<

gotchas                                            *user_guide-basics-gotchas*

Performing selection operations on `integer` type data can easily upcast the
data to `floating`. The dtype of the input data will be preserved in cases
where `nans` are not introduced. See also
|user_guide-gotchas-gotchas-intna|.

>python
    In [428]: dfi = df3.astype("int32")

    In [429]: dfi["E"] = 1

    In [430]: dfi
    Out[430]: 
       A  B    C  E
    0  1  0   26  1
    1  3  1   86  1
    2  0  0   46  1
    3  0  1  212  1
    4 -1 -1   26  1
    5  1  0    7  1
    6  0 -1  184  1
    7  0  0  206  1

    In [431]: dfi.dtypes
    Out[431]: 
    A    int32
    B    int32
    C    int32
    E    int64
    dtype: object

    In [432]: casted = dfi[dfi > 0]

    In [433]: casted
    Out[433]: 
         A    B    C  E
    0  1.0  NaN   26  1
    1  3.0  1.0   86  1
    2  NaN  NaN   46  1
    3  NaN  1.0  212  1
    4  NaN  NaN   26  1
    5  1.0  NaN    7  1
    6  NaN  NaN  184  1
    7  NaN  NaN  206  1

    In [434]: casted.dtypes
    Out[434]: 
    A    float64
    B    float64
    C      int32
    E      int64
    dtype: object
<
While float dtypes are unchanged.

>python
    In [435]: dfa = df3.copy()

    In [436]: dfa["A"] = dfa["A"].astype("float32")

    In [437]: dfa.dtypes
    Out[437]: 
    A    float32
    B    float64
    C    float64
    dtype: object

    In [438]: casted = dfa[df2 > 0]

    In [439]: casted
    Out[439]: 
              A         B      C
    0  1.047634  0.256090   26.0
    1  3.498407  1.426469   86.0
    2       NaN       NaN   46.0
    3       NaN  1.139976  212.0
    4       NaN       NaN   26.0
    5  1.346474  0.096706    7.0
    6       NaN       NaN  184.0
    7       NaN       NaN  206.0

    In [440]: casted.dtypes
    Out[440]: 
    A    float32
    B    float64
    C    float64
    dtype: object
<

                          *user_guide-basics-selecting-columns-based-on-dtype*
SELECTING COLUMNS BASED ON `dtype`

The |pandas.DataFrame.select_dtypes| method implements subsetting of columns
based on their `dtype`.

First, let's create a |pandas.DataFrame| with a slew of different dtypes:

>python
    In [441]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {
       .....:         "string": list("abc"),
       .....:         "int64": list(range(1, 4)),
       .....:         "uint8": np.arange(3, 6).astype("u1"),
       .....:         "float64": np.arange(4.0, 7.0),
       .....:         "bool1": [True, False, True],
       .....:         "bool2": [False, True, False],
       .....:         "dates": pd.date_range("now", periods=3),
       .....:         "category": pd.Series(list("ABC")).astype("category"),
       .....:     }
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [442]: df["tdeltas"] = df.dates.diff()

    In [443]: df["uint64"] = np.arange(3, 6).astype("u8")

    In [444]: df["other_dates"] = pd.date_range("20130101", periods=3)

    In [445]: df["tz_aware_dates"] = pd.date_range("20130101", periods=3, tz="US/Eastern")

    In [446]: df
    Out[446]: 
      string  int64  uint8  ...  uint64 other_dates            tz_aware_dates
    0      a      1      3  ...       3  2013-01-01 2013-01-01 00:00:00-05:00
    1      b      2      4  ...       4  2013-01-02 2013-01-02 00:00:00-05:00
    2      c      3      5  ...       5  2013-01-03 2013-01-03 00:00:00-05:00

    [3 rows x 12 columns]
<
And the dtypes:

>python
    In [447]: df.dtypes
    Out[447]: 
    string                                   str
    int64                                  int64
    uint8                                  uint8
    float64                              float64
    bool1                                   bool
    bool2                                   bool
    dates                         datetime64[us]
    category                            category
    tdeltas                      timedelta64[us]
    uint64                                uint64
    other_dates                   datetime64[us]
    tz_aware_dates    datetime64[us, US/Eastern]
    dtype: object
<
|pandas.DataFrame.select_dtypes| has two parameters `include` and `exclude`
that allow you to say “give me the columns with these dtypes” (`include`)
and/or “give the columns without these dtypes” (`exclude`).

For example, to select `bool` columns:

>python
    In [448]: df.select_dtypes(include=[bool])
    Out[448]: 
       bool1  bool2
    0   True  False
    1  False   True
    2   True  False
<
You can also pass the name of a dtype in the NumPy dtype hierarchy
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/arrays.scalars.html:

>python
    In [449]: df.select_dtypes(include=["bool"])
    Out[449]: 
       bool1  bool2
    0   True  False
    1  False   True
    2   True  False
<
|pandas.DataFrame.select_dtypes| also works with generic dtypes.

For example, to select all numeric and boolean columns while excluding
unsigned integers:

>python
    In [450]: df.select_dtypes(include=["number", "bool"], exclude=["unsignedinteger"])
    Out[450]: 
       int64  float64  bool1  bool2 tdeltas
    0      1      4.0   True  False     NaT
    1      2      5.0  False   True  1 days
    2      3      6.0   True  False  1 days
<
To select string columns include `str`:

>python
    In [451]: df.select_dtypes(include=[str])
    Out[451]: 
      string
    0      a
    1      b
    2      c
<
  Note: ~

  This is a change in pandas 3.0. Previously strings were stored in `object`
  dtype columns, so would be selected with `include=[object]`. See
  |user_guide-migration-string-migration-select-dtypes| for details on how
  to write code that works with both versions.

To see all the child dtypes of a generic `dtype` like `numpy.number` you can
define a function that returns a tree of child dtypes:

>python
    In [452]: def subdtypes(dtype):
       .....:     subs = dtype.__subclasses__()
       .....:     if not subs:
       .....:         return dtype
       .....:     return [dtype, [subdtypes(dt) for dt in subs]]
       .....: 
<
All NumPy dtypes are subclasses of `numpy.generic`:

>python
    In [453]: subdtypes(np.generic)
    Out[453]: 
    [numpy.generic,
     [[numpy.number,
       [[numpy.integer,
         [[numpy.signedinteger,
           [numpy.int8,
            numpy.int16,
            numpy.int32,
            numpy.int64,
            numpy.longlong,
            numpy.timedelta64]],
          [numpy.unsignedinteger,
           [numpy.uint8,
            numpy.uint16,
            numpy.uint32,
            numpy.uint64,
            numpy.ulonglong]]]],
        [numpy.inexact,
         [[numpy.floating,
           [numpy.float16, numpy.float32, numpy.float64, numpy.longdouble]],
          [numpy.complexfloating,
           [numpy.complex64, numpy.complex128, numpy.clongdouble]]]]]],
      [numpy.flexible,
       [[numpy.character, [numpy.bytes_, numpy.str_]],
        [numpy.void, [numpy.record]]]],
      numpy.bool,
      numpy.datetime64,
      numpy.object_]]
<
  Note: ~

  pandas also defines the types `category`, and `datetime64[ns, tz]`, which
  are not integrated into the normal NumPy hierarchy and won't show up with
  the above function.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Nullable Boolean data type                         *pandas-user_guide-boolean*

*user_guide-boolean-boolean*

INDEXING WITH NA VALUES           *user_guide-boolean-indexing-with-na-values*

*user_guide-boolean-boolean-indexing*

pandas allows indexing with `NA` values in a boolean array, which are
treated as `False`.

>python
    In [1]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])

    In [2]: mask = pd.array([True, False, pd.NA], dtype="boolean")

    In [3]: s[mask]
    Out[3]: 
    0    1
    dtype: int64
<
If you would prefer to keep the `NA` values you can manually fill them with
`fillna(True)`.

>python
    In [4]: s[mask.fillna(True)]
    Out[4]: 
    0    1
    2    3
    dtype: int64
<
If you create a column of `NA` values (for example to fill them later) with
`df['new_col'] = pd.NA`, the `dtype` would be set to `object` in the new
column. The performance on this column will be worse than with the
appropriate type. It's better to use
`df['new_col'] = pd.Series(pd.NA, dtype="boolean")` (or another `dtype` that
supports `NA`).

>python
    In [5]: df = pd.DataFrame()

    In [6]: df['objects'] = pd.NA

    In [7]: df.dtypes
    Out[7]: 
    objects    object
    dtype: object
<

KLEENE LOGICAL OPERATIONS       *user_guide-boolean-kleene-logical-operations*

*user_guide-boolean-boolean-kleene*

|pandas.arrays.BooleanArray| implements Kleene Logic
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-valued_logic#Kleene_and_Priest_logics
(sometimes called three-value logic) for logical operations like `&` (and),
`|` (or) and `^` (exclusive-or).

This table demonstrates the results for every combination. These operations
are symmetrical, so flipping the left- and right-hand side makes no
difference in the result.

Expression                                                              Result
----------------------------------------------------------------------  ------
True & True                                                             True
True & False                                                            False
True & NA                                                               NA
False & False                                                           False
False & NA                                                              False
NA & NA                                                                 NA
True | True                                                             True
True | False                                                            True
True | NA                                                               True
False | False                                                           False
False | NA                                                              NA
NA | NA                                                                 NA
True ^ True                                                             False
True ^ False                                                            True
True ^ NA                                                               NA
False ^ False                                                           False
False ^ NA                                                              NA
NA ^ NA                                                                 NA

When an `NA` is present in an operation, the output value is `NA` only if
the result cannot be determined solely based on the other input. For
example, `True | NA` is `True`, because both `True | True` and
`True | False` are `True`. In that case, we don't actually need to consider
the value of the `NA`.

On the other hand, `True & NA` is `NA`. The result depends on whether the
`NA` really is `True` or `False`, since `True & True` is `True`, but
`True & False` is `False`, so we can't determine the output.

This differs from how `np.nan` behaves in logical operations. pandas treated
`np.nan` is always false in the output.

In `or`

>python
    In [8]: pd.Series([True, False, np.nan], dtype="object") | True
    Out[8]: 
    0     True
    1     True
    2    False
    dtype: bool

    In [9]: pd.Series([True, False, np.nan], dtype="boolean") | True
    Out[9]: 
    0    True
    1    True
    2    True
    dtype: boolean
<
In `and`

>python
    In [10]: pd.Series([True, False, np.nan], dtype="object") & True
    Out[10]: 
    0     True
    1    False
    2    False
    dtype: bool

    In [11]: pd.Series([True, False, np.nan], dtype="boolean") & True
    Out[11]: 
    0     True
    1    False
    2     <NA>
    dtype: boolean
<

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Categorical data                               *pandas-user_guide-categorical*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical*

This is an introduction to pandas categorical data type, including a short
comparison with R's `factor`.

`Categoricals` are a pandas data type corresponding to categorical variables
in statistics. A categorical variable takes on a limited, and usually fixed,
number of possible values (`categories`; `levels` in R). Examples are
gender, social class, blood type, country affiliation, observation time or
rating via Likert scales.

In contrast to statistical categorical variables, categorical data might
have an order (e.g. ‘strongly agree' vs ‘agree' or ‘first observation' vs.
‘second observation'), but numerical operations (additions, divisions, ...)
are not possible.

All values of categorical data are either in `categories` or `np.nan`. Order
is defined by the order of `categories`, not lexical order of the values.
Internally, the data structure consists of a `categories` array and an
integer array of `codes` which point to the real value in the `categories`
array.

The categorical data type is useful in the following cases:

- A string variable consisting of only a few different values. Converting
  such a string variable to a categorical variable will save some memory,
  see section |user_guide-categorical-categorical-memory|.
- The lexical order of a variable is not the same as the logical order
  (“one”, “two”, “three”). By converting to a categorical and specifying an
  order on the categories, sorting and min/max will use the logical order
  instead of the lexical order, see section
  |user_guide-categorical-categorical-sort|.
- As a signal to other Python libraries that this column should be treated
  as a categorical variable (e.g. to use suitable statistical methods or
  plot types).

See also the |reference-arrays-api-arrays-categorical|.

OBJECT CREATION                       *user_guide-categorical-object-creation*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-objectcreation*

Series creation                       *user_guide-categorical-series-creation*

Categorical `Series` or columns in a `DataFrame` can be created in several
ways:

By specifying `dtype="category"` when constructing a `Series`:

>python
    In [1]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category")

    In [2]: s
    Out[2]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    3    a
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
<
By converting an existing `Series` or column to a `category` dtype:

>python
    In [3]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": ["a", "b", "c", "a"]})

    In [4]: df["B"] = df["A"].astype("category")

    In [5]: df
    Out[5]: 
       A  B
    0  a  a
    1  b  b
    2  c  c
    3  a  a
<
By using special functions, such as |pandas.cut|, which groups data into
discrete bins. See the |user_guide-reshaping-reshaping-tile-cut| in the
docs.

>python
    In [6]: df = pd.DataFrame({"value": np.random.randint(0, 100, 20)})

    In [7]: labels = ["{0} - {1}".format(i, i + 9) for i in range(0, 100, 10)]

    In [8]: df["group"] = pd.cut(df.value, range(0, 105, 10), right=False, labels=labels)

    In [9]: df.head(10)
    Out[9]: 
       value    group
    0     65  60 - 69
    1     49  40 - 49
    2     56  50 - 59
    3     43  40 - 49
    4     43  40 - 49
    5     91  90 - 99
    6     32  30 - 39
    7     87  80 - 89
    8     36  30 - 39
    9      8    0 - 9
<
By passing a |pandas.Categorical| object to a `Series` or assigning it to a
`DataFrame`.

>python
    In [10]: raw_cat = pd.Categorical(
       ....:     [None, "b", "c", None], categories=["b", "c", "d"], ordered=False
       ....: )
       ....: 

    In [11]: s = pd.Series(raw_cat)

    In [12]: s
    Out[12]: 
    0    NaN
    1      b
    2      c
    3    NaN
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'd']

    In [13]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": ["a", "b", "c", "a"]})

    In [14]: df["B"] = raw_cat

    In [15]: df
    Out[15]: 
       A    B
    0  a  NaN
    1  b    b
    2  c    c
    3  a  NaN
<
Categorical data has a specific `category`
|user_guide-basics-basics-dtypes|:

>python
    In [16]: df.dtypes
    Out[16]: 
    A         str
    B    category
    dtype: object
<

DataFrame creation                 *user_guide-categorical-dataframe-creation*

Similar to the previous section where a single column was converted to
categorical, all columns in a `DataFrame` can be batch converted to
categorical either during or after construction.

This can be done during construction by specifying `dtype="category"` in the
`DataFrame` constructor:

>python
    In [17]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": list("abca"), "B": list("bccd")}, dtype="category")

    In [18]: df.dtypes
    Out[18]: 
    A    category
    B    category
    dtype: object
<
Note that the categories present in each column differ; the conversion is
done column by column, so only labels present in a given column are
categories:

>python
    In [19]: df["A"]
    Out[19]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    3    a
    Name: A, dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']

    In [20]: df["B"]
    Out[20]: 
    0    b
    1    c
    2    c
    3    d
    Name: B, dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'd']
<
Analogously, all columns in an existing `DataFrame` can be batch converted
using |pandas.DataFrame.astype|:

>python
    In [21]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": list("abca"), "B": list("bccd")})

    In [22]: df_cat = df.astype("category")

    In [23]: df_cat.dtypes
    Out[23]: 
    A    category
    B    category
    dtype: object
<
This conversion is likewise done column by column:

>python
    In [24]: df_cat["A"]
    Out[24]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    3    a
    Name: A, dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']

    In [25]: df_cat["B"]
    Out[25]: 
    0    b
    1    c
    2    c
    3    d
    Name: B, dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'd']
<

Controlling behavior             *user_guide-categorical-controlling-behavior*

In the examples above where we passed `dtype='category'`, we used the
default behavior:

1. Categories are inferred from the data.
2. Categories are unordered.

To control those behaviors, instead of passing `'category'`, use an instance
of `CategoricalDtype`.

>python
    In [26]: from pandas.api.types import CategoricalDtype

    In [27]: s = pd.Series([None, "b", "c", None])

    In [28]: cat_type = CategoricalDtype(categories=["b", "c", "d"], ordered=True)

    In [29]: s_cat = s.astype(cat_type)

    In [30]: s_cat
    Out[30]: 
    0    NaN
    1      b
    2      c
    3    NaN
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['b' < 'c' < 'd']
<
Similarly, a `CategoricalDtype` can be used with a `DataFrame` to ensure
that categories are consistent among all columns.

>python
    In [31]: from pandas.api.types import CategoricalDtype

    In [32]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": list("abca"), "B": list("bccd")})

    In [33]: cat_type = CategoricalDtype(categories=list("abcd"), ordered=True)

    In [34]: df_cat = df.astype(cat_type)

    In [35]: df_cat["A"]
    Out[35]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    3    a
    Name: A, dtype: category
    Categories (4, str): ['a' < 'b' < 'c' < 'd']

    In [36]: df_cat["B"]
    Out[36]: 
    0    b
    1    c
    2    c
    3    d
    Name: B, dtype: category
    Categories (4, str): ['a' < 'b' < 'c' < 'd']
<
  Note: ~

  To perform table-wise conversion, where all labels in the entire
  `DataFrame` are used as categories for each column, the `categories`
  parameter can be determined programmatically by
  `categories = pd.unique(df.to_numpy().ravel())`.

If you already have `codes` and `categories`, you can use the
|pandas.Categorical.from_codes| constructor to save the factorize step
during normal constructor mode:

>python
    In [37]: splitter = np.random.choice([0, 1], 5, p=[0.5, 0.5])

    In [38]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical.from_codes(splitter, categories=["train", "test"]))
<

Regaining original data       *user_guide-categorical-regaining-original-data*

To get back to the original `Series` or NumPy array, use
`Series.astype(original_dtype)` or `np.asarray(categorical)`:

>python
    In [39]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"])

    In [40]: s
    Out[40]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    3    a
    dtype: str

    In [41]: s2 = s.astype("category")

    In [42]: s2
    Out[42]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    3    a
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']

    In [43]: s2.astype(str)
    Out[43]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    3    a
    dtype: str

    In [44]: np.asarray(s2)
    Out[44]: array(['a', 'b', 'c', 'a'], dtype=object)
<
  Note: ~

  In contrast to R's `factor` function, categorical data is not converting
  input values to strings; categories will end up the same data type as the
  original values.

  Note: ~

  In contrast to R's `factor` function, there is currently no way to
  assign/change labels at creation time. Use `categories` to change the
  categories after creation time.

CATEGORICALDTYPE                     *user_guide-categorical-categoricaldtype*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-categoricaldtype*

A categorical's type is fully described by

1. `categories`: a sequence of unique values and no missing values
2. `ordered`: a boolean

This information can be stored in a `CategoricalDtype`. The `categories`
argument is optional, which implies that the actual categories should be
inferred from whatever is present in the data when the |pandas.Categorical|
is created. The categories are assumed to be unordered by default.

>python
    In [45]: from pandas.api.types import CategoricalDtype

    In [46]: CategoricalDtype(["a", "b", "c"])
    Out[46]: CategoricalDtype(categories=['a', 'b', 'c'], ordered=False, categories_dtype=str)

    In [47]: CategoricalDtype(["a", "b", "c"], ordered=True)
    Out[47]: CategoricalDtype(categories=['a', 'b', 'c'], ordered=True, categories_dtype=str)

    In [48]: CategoricalDtype()
    Out[48]: CategoricalDtype(categories=None, ordered=False, categories_dtype=None)
<
A `CategoricalDtype` can be used in any place pandas expects a `dtype`. For
example |pandas.read_csv|, |pandas.DataFrame.astype|, or in the `Series`
constructor.

  Note: ~

  As a convenience, you can use the string `'category'` in place of a
  `CategoricalDtype` when you want the default behavior of the categories
  being unordered, and equal to the set values present in the array. In
  other words, `dtype='category'` is equivalent to
  `dtype=CategoricalDtype()`.

Equality semantics                 *user_guide-categorical-equality-semantics*

Two instances of `CategoricalDtype` compare equal whenever they have the
same categories and order. When comparing two unordered categoricals, the
order of the `categories` is not considered. Note that categories with
different dtypes are not the same.

>python
    In [49]: c1 = CategoricalDtype(["a", "b", "c"], ordered=False)

    # Equal, since order is not considered when ordered=False
    In [50]: c1 == CategoricalDtype(["b", "c", "a"], ordered=False)
    Out[50]: True

    # Unequal, since the second CategoricalDtype is ordered
    In [51]: c1 == CategoricalDtype(["a", "b", "c"], ordered=True)
    Out[51]: False
<
All instances of `CategoricalDtype` compare equal to the string
`'category'`.

>python
    In [52]: c1 == "category"
    Out[52]: True
<
Notice that the `categories_dtype` should be considered, especially when
comparing with two empty `CategoricalDtype` instances.

>python
    In [53]: c2 = pd.Categorical(np.array([], dtype=object))

    In [54]: c3 = pd.Categorical(np.array([], dtype=float))

    In [55]: c2.dtype == c3.dtype
    Out[55]: False
<

DESCRIPTION                               *user_guide-categorical-description*

Using |pandas.DataFrame.describe| on categorical data will produce similar
output to a `Series` or `DataFrame` of type `string`.

>python
    In [56]: cat = pd.Categorical(["a", "c", "c", np.nan], categories=["b", "a", "c"])

    In [57]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cat": cat, "s": ["a", "c", "c", np.nan]})

    In [58]: df.describe()
    Out[58]: 
           cat  s
    count    3  3
    unique   2  2
    top      c  c
    freq     2  2

    In [59]: df["cat"].describe()
    Out[59]: 
    count     3
    unique    2
    top       c
    freq      2
    Name: cat, dtype: object
<

WORKING WITH CATEGORIES       *user_guide-categorical-working-with-categories*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-cat*

Categorical data has a `categories` and a `ordered` property, which list
their possible values and whether the ordering matters or not. These
properties are exposed as `s.cat.categories` and `s.cat.ordered`. If you
don't manually specify categories and ordering, they are inferred from the
passed arguments.

>python
    In [60]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category")

    In [61]: s.cat.categories
    Out[61]: Index(['a', 'b', 'c'], dtype='str')

    In [62]: s.cat.ordered
    Out[62]: False
<
It's also possible to pass in the categories in a specific order:

>python
    In [63]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c", "a"], categories=["c", "b", "a"]))

    In [64]: s.cat.categories
    Out[64]: Index(['c', 'b', 'a'], dtype='str')

    In [65]: s.cat.ordered
    Out[65]: False
<
  Note: ~

  New categorical data are not automatically ordered. You must explicitly
  pass `ordered=True` to indicate an ordered `Categorical`.

  Note: ~

  The result of |pandas.Series.unique| is not always the same as
  `Series.cat.categories`, because `Series.unique()` has a couple of
  guarantees, namely that it returns categories in the order of appearance,
  and it only includes values that are actually present.

  >python
      In [66]: s = pd.Series(list("babc")).astype(CategoricalDtype(list("abcd")))

      In [67]: s
      Out[67]: 
      0    b
      1    a
      2    b
      3    c
      dtype: category
      Categories (4, str): ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']

      # categories
      In [68]: s.cat.categories
      Out[68]: Index(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], dtype='str')

      # uniques
      In [69]: s.unique()
      Out[69]: 
      ['b', 'a', 'c']
      Categories (4, str): ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
<

Renaming categories               *user_guide-categorical-renaming-categories*

Renaming categories is done by using the
|pandas.Categorical.rename_categories| method:

>python
    In [70]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category")

    In [71]: s
    Out[71]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    c
    3    a
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']

    In [72]: new_categories = ["Group %s" % g for g in s.cat.categories]

    In [73]: s = s.cat.rename_categories(new_categories)

    In [74]: s
    Out[74]: 
    0    Group a
    1    Group b
    2    Group c
    3    Group a
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['Group a', 'Group b', 'Group c']

    # You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming
    In [75]: s = s.cat.rename_categories({"Group a": "x", "Group b": "y", "Group c": "z"})

    In [76]: s
    Out[76]: 
    0    x
    1    y
    2    z
    3    x
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['x', 'y', 'z']
<
  Note: ~

  In contrast to R's `factor`, categorical data can have categories of other
  types than string.

Categories must be unique or a `ValueError` is raised:

>python
    In [77]: try:
       ....:     s = s.cat.rename_categories([1, 1, 1])
       ....: except ValueError as e:
       ....:     print("ValueError:", str(e))
       ....: 
    ValueError: Categorical categories must be unique
<
Categories must also not be `NaN` or a `ValueError` is raised:

>python
    In [78]: try:
       ....:     s = s.cat.rename_categories([1, 2, np.nan])
       ....: except ValueError as e:
       ....:     print("ValueError:", str(e))
       ....: 
    ValueError: Categorical categories cannot be null
<
To merge several categories into one, use |pandas.Series.replace| to replace
the values and then drop the categories that are no longer used with
|pandas.Series.cat.remove_unused_categories|:

>python
    In [79]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category")

    In [80]: s = s.replace({"a": "b"}).cat.remove_unused_categories()

    In [81]: s
    Out[81]: 
    0    b
    1    b
    2    c
    3    b
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, str): ['b', 'c']
<

Appending new categories     *user_guide-categorical-appending-new-categories*

Appending categories can be done by using the
|pandas.Categorical.add_categories| method:

>python
    In [82]: s = s.cat.add_categories([4])

    In [83]: s.cat.categories
    Out[83]: Index(['b', 'c', 4], dtype='object')

    In [84]: s
    Out[84]: 
    0    b
    1    b
    2    c
    3    b
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, object): ['b', 'c', 4]
<

Removing categories               *user_guide-categorical-removing-categories*

Removing categories can be done by using the
|pandas.Categorical.remove_categories| method. Values which are removed are
replaced by `np.nan`.:

>python
    In [85]: s = s.cat.remove_categories([4])

    In [86]: s
    Out[86]: 
    0    b
    1    b
    2    c
    3    b
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, object): ['b', 'c']
<

Removing unused categories *user_guide-categorical-removing-unused-categories*

Removing unused categories can also be done:

>python
    In [87]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "a"], categories=["a", "b", "c", "d"]))

    In [88]: s
    Out[88]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    a
    dtype: category
    Categories (4, str): ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']

    In [89]: s.cat.remove_unused_categories()
    Out[89]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    a
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']
<

Setting categories                 *user_guide-categorical-setting-categories*

If you want to do remove and add new categories in one step (which has some
speed advantage), or simply set the categories to a predefined scale, use
|pandas.Categorical.set_categories|.

>python
    In [90]: s = pd.Series(["one", "two", "four", "-"], dtype="category")

    In [91]: s
    Out[91]: 
    0     one
    1     two
    2    four
    3       -
    dtype: category
    Categories (4, str): ['-', 'four', 'one', 'two']

    In [92]: s = s.cat.set_categories(["one", "two", "three", "four"])

    In [93]: s
    Out[93]: 
    0     one
    1     two
    2    four
    3     NaN
    dtype: category
    Categories (4, str): ['one', 'two', 'three', 'four']
<
  Note: ~

  Be aware that |pandas.Categorical.set_categories| cannot know whether some
  category is omitted intentionally or because it is misspelled or (under
  Python3) due to a type difference (e.g., NumPy S1 dtype and Python
  strings). This can result in surprising behaviour!

SORTING AND ORDER                   *user_guide-categorical-sorting-and-order*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-sort*

If categorical data is ordered (`s.cat.ordered == True`), then the order of
the categories has a meaning and certain operations are possible. If the
categorical is unordered, `.min()/.max()` will raise a `TypeError`.

>python
    In [94]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c", "a"], ordered=False))

    In [95]: s = s.sort_values()

    In [96]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"]).astype(CategoricalDtype(ordered=True))

    In [97]: s = s.sort_values()

    In [98]: s
    Out[98]: 
    0    a
    3    a
    1    b
    2    c
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a' < 'b' < 'c']

    In [99]: s.min(), s.max()
    Out[99]: ('a', 'c')
<
You can set categorical data to be ordered by using `as_ordered()` or
unordered by using `as_unordered()`. These will by default return a new
object.

>python
    In [100]: s.cat.as_ordered()
    Out[100]: 
    0    a
    3    a
    1    b
    2    c
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a' < 'b' < 'c']

    In [101]: s.cat.as_unordered()
    Out[101]: 
    0    a
    3    a
    1    b
    2    c
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
<
Sorting will use the order defined by categories, not any lexical order
present on the data type. This is even true for strings and numeric data:

>python
    In [102]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 1], dtype="category")

    In [103]: s = s.cat.set_categories([2, 3, 1], ordered=True)

    In [104]: s
    Out[104]: 
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    3    1
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, int64): [2 < 3 < 1]

    In [105]: s = s.sort_values()

    In [106]: s
    Out[106]: 
    1    2
    2    3
    0    1
    3    1
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, int64): [2 < 3 < 1]

    In [107]: s.min(), s.max()
    Out[107]: (np.int64(2), np.int64(1))
<

Reordering                                 *user_guide-categorical-reordering*

Reordering the categories is possible via the
|pandas.Categorical.reorder_categories| and the
|pandas.Categorical.set_categories| methods. For
|pandas.Categorical.reorder_categories|, all old categories must be included
in the new categories and no new categories are allowed. This will
necessarily make the sort order the same as the categories order.

>python
    In [108]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 1], dtype="category")

    In [109]: s = s.cat.reorder_categories([2, 3, 1], ordered=True)

    In [110]: s
    Out[110]: 
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    3    1
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, int64): [2 < 3 < 1]

    In [111]: s = s.sort_values()

    In [112]: s
    Out[112]: 
    1    2
    2    3
    0    1
    3    1
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, int64): [2 < 3 < 1]

    In [113]: s.min(), s.max()
    Out[113]: (np.int64(2), np.int64(1))
<
  Note: ~

  Note the difference between assigning new categories and reordering the
  categories: the first renames categories and therefore the individual
  values in the `Series`, but if the first position was sorted last, the
  renamed value will still be sorted last. Reordering means that the way
  values are sorted is different afterwards, but not that individual values
  in the `Series` are changed.

  Note: ~

  If the `Categorical` is not ordered, |pandas.Series.min| and
  |pandas.Series.max| will raise `TypeError`. Numeric operations like `+`,
  `-`, `*`, `/` and operations based on them (e.g. |pandas.Series.median|,
  which would need to compute the mean between two values if the length of
  an array is even) do not work and raise a `TypeError`.

Multi column sorting             *user_guide-categorical-multi-column-sorting*

A categorical dtyped column will participate in a multi-column sort in a
similar manner to other columns. The ordering of the categorical is
determined by the `categories` of that column.

>python
    In [114]: dfs = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {
       .....:         "A": pd.Categorical(
       .....:             list("bbeebbaa"),
       .....:             categories=["e", "a", "b"],
       .....:             ordered=True,
       .....:         ),
       .....:         "B": [1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1],
       .....:     }
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [115]: dfs.sort_values(by=["A", "B"])
    Out[115]: 
       A  B
    2  e  1
    3  e  2
    7  a  1
    6  a  2
    0  b  1
    5  b  1
    1  b  2
    4  b  2
<
Reordering the `categories` changes a future sort.

>python
    In [116]: dfs["A"] = dfs["A"].cat.reorder_categories(["a", "b", "e"])

    In [117]: dfs.sort_values(by=["A", "B"])
    Out[117]: 
       A  B
    7  a  1
    6  a  2
    0  b  1
    5  b  1
    1  b  2
    4  b  2
    2  e  1
    3  e  2
<

COMPARISONS                               *user_guide-categorical-comparisons*

Comparing categorical data with other objects is possible in three cases:

- Comparing equality (`==` and `!=`) to a list-like object (list, Series,
  array, ...) of the same length as the categorical data.
- All comparisons (`==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, and `<=`) of categorical data
  to another categorical Series, when `ordered==True` and the `categories`
  are the same.
- All comparisons of a categorical data to a scalar.

All other comparisons, especially “non-equality” comparisons of two
categoricals with different categories or a categorical with any list-like
object, will raise a `TypeError`.

  Note: ~

  Any “non-equality” comparisons of categorical data with a `Series`,
  `np.array`, `list` or categorical data with different categories or
  ordering will raise a `TypeError` because custom categories ordering could
  be interpreted in two ways: one with taking into account the ordering and
  one without.

>python
    In [118]: cat = pd.Series([1, 2, 3]).astype(CategoricalDtype([3, 2, 1], ordered=True))

    In [119]: cat_base = pd.Series([2, 2, 2]).astype(CategoricalDtype([3, 2, 1], ordered=True))

    In [120]: cat_base2 = pd.Series([2, 2, 2]).astype(CategoricalDtype(ordered=True))

    In [121]: cat
    Out[121]: 
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, int64): [3 < 2 < 1]

    In [122]: cat_base
    Out[122]: 
    0    2
    1    2
    2    2
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, int64): [3 < 2 < 1]

    In [123]: cat_base2
    Out[123]: 
    0    2
    1    2
    2    2
    dtype: category
    Categories (1, int64): [2]
<
Comparing to a categorical with the same categories and ordering or to a
scalar works:

>python
    In [124]: cat > cat_base
    Out[124]: 
    0     True
    1    False
    2    False
    dtype: bool

    In [125]: cat > 2
    Out[125]: 
    0     True
    1    False
    2    False
    dtype: bool
<
Equality comparisons work with any list-like object of same length and
scalars:

>python
    In [126]: cat == cat_base
    Out[126]: 
    0    False
    1     True
    2    False
    dtype: bool

    In [127]: cat == np.array([1, 2, 3])
    Out[127]: 
    0    True
    1    True
    2    True
    dtype: bool

    In [128]: cat == 2
    Out[128]: 
    0    False
    1     True
    2    False
    dtype: bool
<
This doesn't work because the categories are not the same:

>python
    In [129]: try:
       .....:     cat > cat_base2
       .....: except TypeError as e:
       .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
       .....: 
    TypeError: Categoricals can only be compared if 'categories' are the same.
<
If you want to do a “non-equality” comparison of a categorical series with a
list-like object which is not categorical data, you need to be explicit and
convert the categorical data back to the original values:

>python
    In [130]: base = np.array([1, 2, 3])

    In [131]: try:
       .....:     cat > base
       .....: except TypeError as e:
       .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
       .....: 
    TypeError: Cannot compare a Categorical for op __gt__ with type <class 'numpy.ndarray'>.
    If you want to compare values, use 'np.asarray(cat) <op> other'.

    In [132]: np.asarray(cat) > base
    Out[132]: array([False, False, False])
<
When you compare two unordered categoricals with the same categories, the
order is not considered:

>python
    In [133]: c1 = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"], categories=["a", "b"], ordered=False)

    In [134]: c2 = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"], categories=["b", "a"], ordered=False)

    In [135]: c1 == c2
    Out[135]: array([ True,  True])
<

OPERATIONS                                 *user_guide-categorical-operations*

Apart from |pandas.Series.min|, |pandas.Series.max| and
|pandas.Series.mode|, the following operations are possible with categorical
data:

`Series` methods like |pandas.Series.value_counts| will use all categories,
even if some categories are not present in the data:

>python
    In [136]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c", "c"], categories=["c", "a", "b", "d"]))

    In [137]: s.value_counts()
    Out[137]: 
    c    2
    a    1
    b    1
    d    0
    Name: count, dtype: int64
<
`DataFrame` methods like |pandas.DataFrame.sum| also show “unused”
categories when `observed=False`.

>python
    In [138]: columns = pd.Categorical(
       .....:     ["One", "One", "Two"], categories=["One", "Two", "Three"], ordered=True
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [139]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     data=[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]],
       .....:     columns=pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([["A", "B", "B"], columns]),
       .....: ).T
       .....: 

    In [140]: df.groupby(level=1, observed=False).sum()
    Out[140]: 
           0  1
    One    3  9
    Two    3  6
    Three  0  0
<
Groupby will also show “unused” categories when `observed=False`:

>python
    In [141]: cats = pd.Categorical(
       .....:     ["a", "b", "b", "b", "c", "c", "c"], categories=["a", "b", "c", "d"]
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [142]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cats": cats, "values": [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5]})

    In [143]: df.groupby("cats", observed=False).mean()
    Out[143]: 
          values
    cats        
    a        1.0
    b        2.0
    c        4.0
    d        NaN

    In [144]: cats2 = pd.Categorical(["a", "a", "b", "b"], categories=["a", "b", "c"])

    In [145]: df2 = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {
       .....:         "cats": cats2,
       .....:         "B": ["c", "d", "c", "d"],
       .....:         "values": [1, 2, 3, 4],
       .....:     }
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [146]: df2.groupby(["cats", "B"], observed=False).mean()
    Out[146]: 
            values
    cats B        
    a    c     1.0
         d     2.0
    b    c     3.0
         d     4.0
    c    c     NaN
         d     NaN
<
Pivot tables:

>python
    In [147]: raw_cat = pd.Categorical(["a", "a", "b", "b"], categories=["a", "b", "c"])

    In [148]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": raw_cat, "B": ["c", "d", "c", "d"], "values": [1, 2, 3, 4]})

    In [149]: pd.pivot_table(df, values="values", index=["A", "B"], observed=False)
    Out[149]: 
         values
    A B        
    a c     1.0
      d     2.0
    b c     3.0
      d     4.0
<

DATA MUNGING                             *user_guide-categorical-data-munging*

The optimized pandas data access methods `.loc`, `.iloc`, `.at`, and `.iat`,
work as normal. The only difference is the return type (for getting) and
that only values already in `categories` can be assigned.

Getting                                       *user_guide-categorical-getting*

If the slicing operation returns either a `DataFrame` or a column of type
`Series`, the `category` dtype is preserved.

>python
    In [150]: idx = pd.Index(["h", "i", "j", "k", "l", "m", "n"])

    In [151]: cats = pd.Series(["a", "b", "b", "b", "c", "c", "c"], dtype="category", index=idx)

    In [152]: values = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5]

    In [153]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cats": cats, "values": values}, index=idx)

    In [154]: df.iloc[2:4, :]
    Out[154]: 
      cats  values
    j    b       2
    k    b       2

    In [155]: df.iloc[2:4, :].dtypes
    Out[155]: 
    cats      category
    values       int64
    dtype: object

    In [156]: df.loc["h":"j", "cats"]
    Out[156]: 
    h    a
    i    b
    j    b
    Name: cats, dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']

    In [157]: df[df["cats"] == "b"]
    Out[157]: 
      cats  values
    i    b       2
    j    b       2
    k    b       2
<
An example where the category type is not preserved is if you take one
single row: the resulting `Series` is of dtype `object`:

>python
    # get the complete "h" row as a Series
    In [158]: df.loc["h", :]
    Out[158]: 
    cats      a
    values    1
    Name: h, dtype: object
<
Returning a single item from categorical data will also return the value,
not a categorical of length “1”.

>python
    In [159]: df.iat[0, 0]
    Out[159]: 'a'

    In [160]: df["cats"] = df["cats"].cat.rename_categories(["x", "y", "z"])

    In [161]: df.at["h", "cats"]  # returns a string
    Out[161]: 'x'
<
  Note: ~

  This is in contrast to R's `factor` function, where `factor(c(1,2,3))[1]`
  returns a single value `factor`.

To get a single value `Series` of type `category`, you pass in a list with a
single value:

>python
    In [162]: df.loc[["h"], "cats"]
    Out[162]: 
    h    x
    Name: cats, dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['x', 'y', 'z']
<

                        *user_guide-categorical-string-and-datetime-accessors*
String and datetime accessors

The accessors `.dt` and `.str` will work if the `s.cat.categories` are of an
appropriate type:

>python
    In [163]: str_s = pd.Series(list("aabb"))

    In [164]: str_cat = str_s.astype("category")

    In [165]: str_cat
    Out[165]: 
    0    a
    1    a
    2    b
    3    b
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']

    In [166]: str_cat.str.contains("a")
    Out[166]: 
    0     True
    1     True
    2    False
    3    False
    dtype: bool

    In [167]: date_s = pd.Series(pd.date_range("1/1/2015", periods=5))

    In [168]: date_cat = date_s.astype("category")

    In [169]: date_cat
    Out[169]: 
    0   2015-01-01
    1   2015-01-02
    2   2015-01-03
    3   2015-01-04
    4   2015-01-05
    dtype: category
    Categories (5, datetime64[us]): [2015-01-01, 2015-01-02, 2015-01-03, 2015-01-04,
                                     2015-01-05]

    In [170]: date_cat.dt.day
    Out[170]: 
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    3    4
    4    5
    dtype: int32
<
  Note: ~

  The returned `Series` (or `DataFrame`) is of the same type as if you used
  the `.str.<method>` / `.dt.<method>` on a `Series` of that type (and not
  of type `category`!).

That means, that the returned values from methods and properties on the
accessors of a `Series` and the returned values from methods and properties
on the accessors of this `Series` transformed to one of type `category` will
be equal:

>python
    In [171]: ret_s = str_s.str.contains("a")

    In [172]: ret_cat = str_cat.str.contains("a")

    In [173]: ret_s.dtype == ret_cat.dtype
    Out[173]: True

    In [174]: ret_s == ret_cat
    Out[174]: 
    0    True
    1    True
    2    True
    3    True
    dtype: bool
<
  Note: ~

  The work is done on the `categories` and then a new `Series` is
  constructed. This has some performance implication if you have a `Series`
  of type string, where lots of elements are repeated (i.e. the number of
  unique elements in the `Series` is a lot smaller than the length of the
  `Series`). In this case it can be faster to convert the original `Series`
  to one of type `category` and use `.str.<method>` or `.dt.<property>` on
  that.

Setting                                       *user_guide-categorical-setting*

Setting values in a categorical column (or `Series`) works as long as the
value is included in the `categories`:

>python
    In [175]: idx = pd.Index(["h", "i", "j", "k", "l", "m", "n"])

    In [176]: cats = pd.Categorical(["a", "a", "a", "a", "a", "a", "a"], categories=["a", "b"])

    In [177]: values = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]

    In [178]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cats": cats, "values": values}, index=idx)

    In [179]: df.iloc[2:4, :] = [["b", 2], ["b", 2]]

    In [180]: df
    Out[180]: 
      cats  values
    h    a       1
    i    a       1
    j    b       2
    k    b       2
    l    a       1
    m    a       1
    n    a       1

    In [181]: try:
       .....:     df.iloc[2:4, :] = [["c", 3], ["c", 3]]
       .....: except TypeError as e:
       .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
       .....: 
    TypeError: Cannot setitem on a Categorical with a new category, set the categories first
<
Setting values by assigning categorical data will also check that the
`categories` match:

>python
    In [182]: df.loc["j":"k", "cats"] = pd.Categorical(["a", "a"], categories=["a", "b"])

    In [183]: df
    Out[183]: 
      cats  values
    h    a       1
    i    a       1
    j    a       2
    k    a       2
    l    a       1
    m    a       1
    n    a       1

    In [184]: try:
       .....:     df.loc["j":"k", "cats"] = pd.Categorical(["b", "b"], categories=["a", "b", "c"])
       .....: except TypeError as e:
       .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
       .....: 
    TypeError: Cannot set a Categorical with another, without identical categories
<
Assigning a `Categorical` to parts of a column of other types will use the
values:

>python
    In [185]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 1, 1, 1, 1], "b": ["a", "a", "a", "a", "a"]})

    In [186]: df.loc[1:2, "a"] = pd.Categorical([2, 2], categories=[2, 3])

    In [187]: df.loc[2:3, "b"] = pd.Categorical(["b", "b"], categories=["a", "b"])

    In [188]: df
    Out[188]: 
       a  b
    0  1  a
    1  2  a
    2  2  b
    3  1  b
    4  1  a

    In [189]: df.dtypes
    Out[189]: 
    a    int64
    b      str
    dtype: object
<
  Note: ~

  The examples above use `.loc` / `.iloc` to set values within an existing
  categorical column, which preserves the `category` dtype. Assigning to a
  full column with `df["cats"] = value` instead replaces the column, so the
  dtype is inferred from `value` rather than kept. See
  |user_guide-indexing-indexing-column-assignment-vs-in-place| for details.

Merging / concatenation         *user_guide-categorical-merging-concatenation*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-merge*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-concat*

By default, combining `Series` or `DataFrames` which contain the same
categories results in `category` dtype, otherwise results will depend on the
dtype of the underlying categories. Merges that result in non-categorical
dtypes will likely have higher memory usage. Use `union_categories=True`,
`.astype` or `union_categoricals` to ensure `category` results.

>python
    In [190]: from pandas.api.types import union_categoricals

    # same categories
    In [191]: s1 = pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype="category")

    In [192]: s2 = pd.Series(["a", "b", "a"], dtype="category")

    In [193]: pd.concat([s1, s2])
    Out[193]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    0    a
    1    b
    2    a
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']

    # different categories
    In [194]: s3 = pd.Series(["b", "c"], dtype="category")

    In [195]: pd.concat([s1, s3])
    Out[195]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    0    b
    1    c
    dtype: str

    # Output dtype is inferred based on categories values
    In [196]: int_cats = pd.Series([1, 2], dtype="category")

    In [197]: float_cats = pd.Series([3.0, 4.0], dtype="category")

    In [198]: pd.concat([int_cats, float_cats])
    Out[198]: 
    0    1.0
    1    2.0
    0    3.0
    1    4.0
    dtype: float64

    In [199]: pd.concat([s1, s3], union_categories=True)
    Out[199]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    0    b
    1    c
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']

    In [200]: pd.concat([int_cats, float_cats], union_categories=True)
    Out[200]: 
    0    1.0
    1    2.0
    0    3.0
    1    4.0
    dtype: category
    Categories (4, float64): [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]

    In [201]: pd.concat([s1, s3]).astype("category")
    Out[201]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    0    b
    1    c
    dtype: category
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']

    In [202]: union_categoricals([s1.array, s3.array])
    Out[202]: 
    ['a', 'b', 'b', 'c']
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
<
The following table summarizes the results of merging `Categoricals`:

arg1               arg2               identical  result
-----------------  -----------------  ---------  -----------------------------
category           category           True       category
category (object)  category (object)  False      object (dtype is inferred)
category (int)     category (float)   False      float (dtype is inferred)

Unioning                                     *user_guide-categorical-unioning*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-union*

If you want to combine categoricals that do not necessarily have the same
categories, the |pandas.api.types.union_categoricals| function will combine
a list-like of categoricals. The new categories will be the union of the
categories being combined.

>python
    In [203]: from pandas.api.types import union_categoricals

    In [204]: a = pd.Categorical(["b", "c"])

    In [205]: b = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"])

    In [206]: union_categoricals([a, b])
    Out[206]: 
    ['b', 'c', 'a', 'b']
    Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'a']
<
By default, the resulting categories will be ordered as they appear in the
data. If you want the categories to be lexsorted, use `sort_categories=True`
argument.

>python
    In [207]: union_categoricals([a, b], sort_categories=True)
    Out[207]: 
    ['b', 'c', 'a', 'b']
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
<
`union_categoricals` also works with the “easy” case of combining two
categoricals of the same categories and order information (e.g. what you
could also `append` for).

>python
    In [208]: a = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"], ordered=True)

    In [209]: b = pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "a"], ordered=True)

    In [210]: union_categoricals([a, b])
    Out[210]: 
    ['a', 'b', 'a', 'b', 'a']
    Categories (2, str): ['a' < 'b']
<
The below raises `TypeError` because the categories are ordered and not
identical.

>python
    In [211]: a = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"], ordered=True)

    In [212]: b = pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c"], ordered=True)

    In [213]: union_categoricals([a, b])
    ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
    TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
    Cell In[213], line 1
    ----> 1 union_categoricals([a, b])

    File ~/work/pandas/pandas/pandas/core/dtypes/concat.py:393, in union_categoricals(to_union, sort_categories, ignore_order)
        391     if all(c.ordered for c in to_union):
        392         msg = "to union ordered Categoricals, all categories must be the same"
    --> 393         raise TypeError(msg)
        394     raise TypeError("Categorical.ordered must be the same")
        396 if ignore_order:

    TypeError: to union ordered Categoricals, all categories must be the same
<
Ordered categoricals with different categories or orderings can be combined
by using the `ignore_order=True` argument.

>python
    In [214]: a = pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c"], ordered=True)

    In [215]: b = pd.Categorical(["c", "b", "a"], ordered=True)

    In [216]: union_categoricals([a, b], ignore_order=True)
    Out[216]: 
    ['a', 'b', 'c', 'c', 'b', 'a']
    Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
<
|pandas.api.types.union_categoricals| also works with a `CategoricalIndex`,
or `Series` containing categorical data, but note that the resulting array
will always be a plain `Categorical`:

>python
    In [217]: a = pd.Series(["b", "c"], dtype="category")

    In [218]: b = pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype="category")

    In [219]: union_categoricals([a, b])
    Out[219]: 
    ['b', 'c', 'a', 'b']
    Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'a']
<
  Note: ~

  `union_categoricals` may recode the integer codes for categories when
  combining categoricals. This is likely what you want, but if you are
  relying on the exact numbering of the categories, be aware.

  >python
      In [220]: c1 = pd.Categorical(["b", "c"])

      In [221]: c2 = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"])

      In [222]: c1
      Out[222]: 
      ['b', 'c']
      Categories (2, str): ['b', 'c']

      # "b" is coded to 0
      In [223]: c1.codes
      Out[223]: array([0, 1], dtype=int8)

      In [224]: c2
      Out[224]: 
      ['a', 'b']
      Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']

      # "b" is coded to 1
      In [225]: c2.codes
      Out[225]: array([0, 1], dtype=int8)

      In [226]: c = union_categoricals([c1, c2])

      In [227]: c
      Out[227]: 
      ['b', 'c', 'a', 'b']
      Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'a']

      # "b" is coded to 0 throughout, same as c1, different from c2
      In [228]: c.codes
      Out[228]: array([0, 1, 2, 0], dtype=int8)
<

GETTING DATA IN/OUT               *user_guide-categorical-getting-data-in-out*

You can write data that contains `category` dtypes to a `HDFStore`. See
|user_guide-io-io-hdf5-categorical| for an example and caveats.

It is also possible to write data to and reading data from Stata format
files. See |user_guide-io-io-stata-categorical| for an example and caveats.

Writing to a CSV file will convert the data, effectively removing any
information about the categorical (categories and ordering). So if you read
back the CSV file you have to convert the relevant columns back to
`category` and assign the right categories and categories ordering.

>python
    In [229]: import io

    In [230]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "b", "a", "a", "d"]))

    # rename the categories
    In [231]: s = s.cat.rename_categories(["very good", "good", "bad"])

    # reorder the categories and add missing categories
    In [232]: s = s.cat.set_categories(["very bad", "bad", "medium", "good", "very good"])

    In [233]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cats": s, "vals": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]})

    In [234]: csv = io.StringIO()

    In [235]: df.to_csv(csv)

    In [236]: df2 = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv.getvalue()))

    In [237]: df2.dtypes
    Out[237]: 
    Unnamed: 0    int64
    cats            str
    vals          int64
    dtype: object

    In [238]: df2["cats"]
    Out[238]: 
    0    very good
    1         good
    2         good
    3    very good
    4    very good
    5          bad
    Name: cats, dtype: str

    # Redo the category
    In [239]: df2["cats"] = df2["cats"].astype("category")

    In [240]: df2["cats"] = df2["cats"].cat.set_categories(
       .....:     ["very bad", "bad", "medium", "good", "very good"]
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [241]: df2.dtypes
    Out[241]: 
    Unnamed: 0       int64
    cats          category
    vals             int64
    dtype: object

    In [242]: df2["cats"]
    Out[242]: 
    0    very good
    1         good
    2         good
    3    very good
    4    very good
    5          bad
    Name: cats, dtype: category
    Categories (5, str): ['very bad', 'bad', 'medium', 'good', 'very good']
<
The same holds for writing to a SQL database with `to_sql`.

MISSING DATA                             *user_guide-categorical-missing-data*

pandas primarily uses the value `np.nan` to represent missing data. It is by
default not included in computations. See
|user_guide-missing_data-missing-data|.

Missing values should not be included in the Categorical's `categories`,
only in the `values`. Instead, it is understood that NaN is different, and
is always a possibility. When working with the Categorical's `codes`,
missing values will always have a code of `-1`.

>python
    In [243]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", np.nan, "a"], dtype="category")

    # only two categories
    In [244]: s
    Out[244]: 
    0      a
    1      b
    2    NaN
    3      a
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']

    In [245]: s.cat.codes
    Out[245]: 
    0    0
    1    1
    2   -1
    3    0
    dtype: int8
<
Methods for working with missing data, e.g. |pandas.Series.isna|,
|pandas.Series.fillna|, |pandas.Series.dropna|, all work normally:

>python
    In [246]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", np.nan], dtype="category")

    In [247]: s
    Out[247]: 
    0      a
    1      b
    2    NaN
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']

    In [248]: pd.isna(s)
    Out[248]: 
    0    False
    1    False
    2     True
    dtype: bool

    In [249]: s.fillna("a")
    Out[249]: 
    0    a
    1    b
    2    a
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']
<

DIFFERENCES TO R'S `factor` *user_guide-categorical-differences-to-r-s-factor*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-rfactor*

The following differences to R's factor functions can be observed:

- R's `levels` are named `categories`.
- R's `levels` are always of type string, while `categories` in pandas can
  be of any dtype.
- It's not possible to specify labels at creation time. Use
  `s.cat.rename_categories(new_labels)` afterwards.
- In contrast to R's `factor` function, using categorical data as the sole
  input to create a new categorical series will not remove unused categories
  but create a new categorical series which is equal to the passed in one!
- R allows for missing values to be included in its `levels` (pandas'
  `categories`). pandas does not allow `NaN` categories, but missing values
  can still be in the `values`.

GOTCHAS                                       *user_guide-categorical-gotchas*

Memory usage                             *user_guide-categorical-memory-usage*

*user_guide-categorical-categorical-memory*

The memory usage of a `Categorical` is proportional to the number and size
of categories plus the length of the data. In contrast, an `object` dtype is
proportional to the size of the objects times the length of the data.

>python
    In [250]: s = pd.Series(["foo", "bar"] * 1000, dtype="object")

    # object dtype
    In [251]: s.memory_usage(deep=True)
    Out[251]: 104132

    # category dtype
    In [252]: s.astype("category").memory_usage(deep=True)
    Out[252]: 2155
<
  Note: ~

  If the number of categories approaches the length of the data, the
  `Categorical` will use nearly the same or more memory than an equivalent
  `object` dtype representation.

  >python
      In [253]: s = pd.Series(["foo%04d" % i for i in range(2000)], dtype="object")

      # object dtype
      In [254]: s.memory_usage(deep=True)
      Out[254]: 112132

      # category dtype
      In [255]: s.astype("category").memory_usage(deep=True)
      Out[255]: 34382
<

                     *user_guide-categorical-categorical-is-not-a-numpy-array*
`Categorical` is not a `numpy` array

Currently, categorical data and the underlying `Categorical` is implemented
as a Python object and not as a low-level NumPy array dtype. This leads to
some problems.

NumPy itself doesn't know about the new `dtype`:

>python
    In [256]: try:
       .....:     np.dtype("category")
       .....: except TypeError as e:
       .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
       .....: 
    TypeError: data type 'category' not understood

    In [257]: dtype = pd.Categorical(["a"]).dtype

    In [258]: try:
       .....:     np.dtype(dtype)
       .....: except TypeError as e:
       .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
       .....: 
    TypeError: Cannot interpret 'CategoricalDtype(categories=['a'], ordered=False, categories_dtype=str)' as a data type
<
Dtype comparisons work:

>python
    In [259]: dtype == np.str_
    Out[259]: False

    In [260]: np.str_ == dtype
    Out[260]: False
<
To check if a Series contains Categorical data, use `hasattr(s, 'cat')`:

>python
    In [261]: hasattr(pd.Series(["a"], dtype="category"), "cat")
    Out[261]: True

    In [262]: hasattr(pd.Series(["a"]), "cat")
    Out[262]: False
<
Using NumPy functions on a `Series` of type `category` should not work as
`Categoricals` are not numeric data (even in the case that `.categories` is
numeric).

>python
    In [263]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical([1, 2, 3, 4]))

    In [264]: try:
       .....:     np.sum(s)
       .....: except TypeError as e:
       .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
       .....: 
    TypeError: 'Categorical' with dtype category does not support operation 'sum'
<
  Note: ~

  If such a function works, please file a bug at pandas-dev/pandas
  https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas!

dtype in apply                         *user_guide-categorical-dtype-in-apply*

pandas currently does not preserve the dtype in apply functions: If you
apply along rows you get a `Series` of `object` `dtype` (same as getting a
row -> getting one element will return a basic type) and applying along
columns will also convert to object. `NaN` values are unaffected. You can
use `fillna` to handle missing values before applying a function.

>python
    In [265]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       .....:     {
       .....:         "a": [1, 2, 3, 4],
       .....:         "b": ["a", "b", "c", "d"],
       .....:         "cats": pd.Categorical([1, 2, 3, 2]),
       .....:     }
       .....: )
       .....: 

    In [266]: df.apply(lambda row: type(row["cats"]), axis=1)
    Out[266]: 
    0    <class 'int'>
    1    <class 'int'>
    2    <class 'int'>
    3    <class 'int'>
    dtype: object

    In [267]: df.apply(lambda col: col.dtype, axis=0)
    Out[267]: 
    a          int64
    b            str
    cats    category
    dtype: object
<

Categorical index                   *user_guide-categorical-categorical-index*

`CategoricalIndex` is a type of index that is useful for supporting indexing
with duplicates. This is a container around a `Categorical` and allows
efficient indexing and storage of an index with a large number of duplicated
elements. See the |user_guide-advanced-advanced-categoricalindex| for a more
detailed explanation.

Setting the index will create a `CategoricalIndex`:

>python
    In [268]: cats = pd.Categorical([1, 2, 3, 4], categories=[4, 2, 3, 1])

    In [269]: strings = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]

    In [270]: values = [4, 2, 3, 1]

    In [271]: df = pd.DataFrame({"strings": strings, "values": values}, index=cats)

    In [272]: df.index
    Out[272]: 
    CategoricalIndex([1, 2, 3, 4], categories=[4, 2, 3, 1], ordered=False,
                     dtype='category')

    # This now sorts by the categories order
    In [273]: df.sort_index()
    Out[273]: 
      strings  values
    4       d       1
    2       b       2
    3       c       3
    1       a       4
<

If-then...                                       *user_guide-cookbook-if-then*

An if-then on one column

>python
    In [3]: df.loc[df.AAA >= 5, "BBB"] = -1

    In [4]: df
    Out[4]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
    1    5   -1   50
    2    6   -1  -30
    3    7   -1  -50
<
An if-then with assignment to 2 columns:

>python
    In [5]: df.loc[df.AAA >= 5, ["BBB", "CCC"]] = 555

    In [6]: df
    Out[6]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
    1    5  555  555
    2    6  555  555
    3    7  555  555
<
Add another line with different logic, to do the -else

>python
    In [7]: df.loc[df.AAA < 5, ["BBB", "CCC"]] = 2000

    In [8]: df
    Out[8]: 
       AAA   BBB   CCC
    0    4  2000  2000
    1    5   555   555
    2    6   555   555
    3    7   555   555
<
Or use pandas where after you've set up a mask

>python
    In [9]: df_mask = pd.DataFrame(
       ...:     {"AAA": [True] * 4, "BBB": [False] * 4, "CCC": [True, False] * 2}
       ...: )
       ...: 

    In [10]: df.where(df_mask, -1000)
    Out[10]: 
       AAA   BBB   CCC
    0    4 -1000  2000
    1    5 -1000 -1000
    2    6 -1000   555
    3    7 -1000 -1000
<

    In [11]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       ....:     {"AAA": [4, 5, 6, 7], "BBB": [10, 20, 30, 40], "CCC": [100, 50, -30, -50]}
       ....: )
       ....:

    Out[12]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
    1    5   20   50

    In [13]: df["logic"] = np.where(df["AAA"] > 5, "high", "low")

    In [14]: df
    Out[14]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC logic
    0    4   10  100   low

Building criteria                      *user_guide-cookbook-building-criteria*

Select with multi-column criteria
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/15315452/selecting-with-complex-criteria-from-pandas-dataframe

>python
    In [19]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       ....:     {"AAA": [4, 5, 6, 7], "BBB": [10, 20, 30, 40], "CCC": [100, 50, -30, -50]}
       ....: )
       ....: 

    In [20]: df
    Out[20]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
    1    5   20   50
    2    6   30  -30
    3    7   40  -50
<
...and (without assignment returns a Series)

>python
    In [21]: df.loc[(df["BBB"] < 25) & (df["CCC"] >= -40), "AAA"]
    Out[21]: 
    0    4
    1    5
    Name: AAA, dtype: int64
<
...or (without assignment returns a Series)

>python
    In [22]: df.loc[(df["BBB"] > 25) | (df["CCC"] >= -40), "AAA"]
    Out[22]: 
    0    4
    1    5
    2    6
    3    7
    Name: AAA, dtype: int64
<
...or (with assignment modifies the DataFrame.)

>python
    In [23]: df.loc[(df["BBB"] > 25) | (df["CCC"] >= 75), "AAA"] = 999

    In [24]: df
    Out[24]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0  999   10  100
    1    5   20   50
    2  999   30  -30
    3  999   40  -50
<
Select rows with data closest to certain value using argsort
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/17758023/return-rows-in-a-dataframe-closest-to-a-user-defined-number

>python
    In [25]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       ....:     {"AAA": [4, 5, 6, 7], "BBB": [10, 20, 30, 40], "CCC": [100, 50, -30, -50]}
       ....: )
       ....: 

    In [26]: df
    Out[26]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
    1    5   20   50
    2    6   30  -30
    3    7   40  -50

    In [27]: aValue = 43.0

    In [28]: df.loc[(df.CCC - aValue).abs().argsort()]
    Out[28]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    1    5   20   50
    0    4   10  100
    2    6   30  -30
    3    7   40  -50
<
Dynamically reduce a list of criteria using a binary operators
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/21058254/pandas-boolean-operation-in-a-python-list/21058331

>python
    In [29]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       ....:     {"AAA": [4, 5, 6, 7], "BBB": [10, 20, 30, 40], "CCC": [100, 50, -30, -50]}
       ....: )
       ....: 

    In [30]: df
    Out[30]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
    1    5   20   50
    2    6   30  -30
    3    7   40  -50

    In [31]: Crit1 = df.AAA <= 5.5

    In [32]: Crit2 = df.BBB == 10.0

    In [33]: Crit3 = df.CCC > -40.0
<
One could hard code:

>python
    In [34]: AllCrit = Crit1 & Crit2 & Crit3
<
...Or it can be done with a list of dynamically built criteria

>python
    In [35]: import functools

    In [36]: CritList = [Crit1, Crit2, Crit3]

    In [37]: AllCrit = functools.reduce(lambda x, y: x & y, CritList)

    In [38]: df[AllCrit]
    Out[38]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
<

Repeating rows or columns      *user_guide-cookbook-repeating-rows-or-columns*

Unlike |pandas.Series.repeat|, `DataFrame` has no `repeat` method. The same
result can be achieved by repeating the row (or column) labels and passing
them to |pandas.DataFrame.reindex|. This requires the labels on the repeated
axis to be unique GH 42943 https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/42943

>python
    In [39]: df = pd.DataFrame({"AAA": [1, 2], "BBB": [3, 4]})

    In [40]: df.reindex(df.index.repeat(2))
    Out[40]: 
       AAA  BBB
    0    1    3
    0    1    3
    1    2    4
    1    2    4

    In [41]: df.reindex(df.index.repeat(2)).reset_index(drop=True)
    Out[41]: 
       AAA  BBB
    0    1    3
    1    1    3
    2    2    4
    3    2    4

    In [42]: df.reindex(columns=df.columns.repeat([1, 2]))
    Out[42]: 
       AAA  BBB  BBB
    0    1    3    3
    1    2    4    4
<
Repeating positions with |pandas.DataFrame.iloc| instead works whether or
not the labels are unique:

>python
    In [43]: df.iloc[np.repeat(np.arange(len(df)), 2)]
    Out[43]: 
       AAA  BBB
    0    1    3
    0    1    3
    1    2    4
    1    2    4
<

Expanding ranges into rows    *user_guide-cookbook-expanding-ranges-into-rows*

Given columns of `start` and `stop` values, expand each row into one row per
value in `range(start, stop)`. Applying `range` row-wise and calling
|pandas.Series.explode| is simple but slow for large inputs; a vectorized
construction with `numpy.repeat()`
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.repeat.html#numpy.repeat
is much faster, especially when there are many rows to expand GH 39630
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/39630

>python
    In [44]: df = pd.DataFrame({"start": [10, 27, 30], "stop": [15, 31, 31]})

    In [45]: start = df["start"].to_numpy()

    In [46]: stop = df["stop"].to_numpy()

    In [47]: counts = stop - start

    In [48]: offsets = np.arange(counts.sum()) - np.repeat(counts.cumsum() - counts, counts)

    In [49]: pd.Series(np.repeat(start, counts) + offsets, index=df.index.repeat(counts))
    Out[49]: 
    0    10
    0    11
    0    12
    0    13
    0    14
    1    27
    1    28
    1    29
    1    30
    2    30
    dtype: int64
<

SELECTION                                      *user_guide-cookbook-selection*

*user_guide-cookbook-cookbook-selection*

DataFrames                                    *user_guide-cookbook-dataframes*

The |user_guide-indexing-indexing| docs.

Using both row labels and value conditionals
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14725068/pandas-using-row-labels-in-boolean-indexing

>python
    In [50]: df = pd.DataFrame(
       ....:     {"AAA": [4, 5, 6, 7], "BBB": [10, 20, 30, 40], "CCC": [100, 50, -30, -50]}
       ....: )
       ....: 

    In [51]: df
    Out[51]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
    1    5   20   50
    2    6   30  -30
    3    7   40  -50

    In [52]: df[(df.AAA <= 6) & (df.index.isin([0, 2, 4]))]
    Out[52]: 
       AAA  BBB  CCC
    0    4   10  100
