----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Indexing and selecting data                       *pandas-user_guide-indexing*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing*

The axis labeling information in pandas objects serves many purposes:

- Identifies data (i.e. provides metadata) using known indicators, important
  for analysis, visualization, and interactive console display.
- Enables automatic and explicit data alignment.
- Allows intuitive getting and setting of subsets of the data set.

In this section, we will focus on the final point: namely, how to slice,
dice, and generally get and set subsets of pandas objects. The primary focus
will be on Series and DataFrame as they have received more development
attention in this area.

  Note: ~

  The Python and NumPy indexing operators `[]` and attribute operator `.`
  provide quick and easy access to pandas data structures across a wide
  range of use cases. This makes interactive work intuitive, as there's
  little new to learn if you already know how to deal with Python
  dictionaries and NumPy arrays. However, since the type of the data to be
  accessed isn't known in advance, directly using standard operators has
  some optimization limits. For production code, we recommended that you
  take advantage of the optimized pandas data access methods exposed in this
  chapter.

See the |user_guide-advanced-advanced| for `MultiIndex` and more advanced
indexing documentation.

See the |user_guide-cookbook-cookbook-selection| for some advanced
strategies.

                          *user_guide-indexing-different-choices-for-indexing*
DIFFERENT CHOICES FOR INDEXING

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-choice*

Object selection has had a number of user-requested additions in order to
support more explicit location based indexing. pandas now supports three
types of multi-axis indexing.

- `.loc` is primarily label based, but may also be used with a boolean
  array. `.loc` will raise `KeyError` when the items are not found. Allowed
  inputs are:

    - A single label, e.g. `5` or `'a'` (Note that `5` is interpreted as a
      label of the index. This use is not an integer position along the
      index.).
    - A list or array of labels `['a', 'b', 'c']`.
    - A slice object with labels `'a':'f'` (Note that contrary to usual
      Python slices, both the start and the stop are included, when present
      in the index! See |user_guide-indexing-indexing-slicing-with-labels|
      and |user_guide-advanced-advanced-endpoints-are-inclusive|.)
    - A boolean array (any `NA` values will be treated as `False`).
    - A `callable` function with one argument (the calling Series or
      DataFrame) and that returns valid output for indexing (one of the
      above).
    - A tuple of row (and column) indices whose elements are one of the
      above inputs.

  See more at |user_guide-indexing-indexing-label|.

- `.iloc` is primarily integer position based (from `0` to `length-1` of the
  axis), but may also be used with a boolean array. `.iloc` will raise
  `IndexError` if a requested indexer is out-of-bounds, except slice
  indexers which allow out-of-bounds indexing. (this conforms with
  Python/NumPy slice semantics). Allowed inputs are:

    - An integer e.g. `5`.
    - A list or array of integers `[4, 3, 0]`.
    - A slice object with ints `1:7`.
    - A boolean array (any `NA` values will be treated as `False`).
    - A `callable` function with one argument (the calling Series or
      DataFrame) and that returns valid output for indexing (one of the
      above).
    - A tuple of row (and column) indices whose elements are one of the
      above inputs.

  See more at |user_guide-indexing-indexing-integer|,
  |user_guide-advanced-advanced| and
  |user_guide-advanced-advanced-advanced-hierarchical|.

- `.loc`, `.iloc`, and also `[]` indexing can accept a `callable` as
  indexer. See more at |user_guide-indexing-indexing-callable|.

    Note: ~

    Destructuring tuple keys into row (and column) indexes occurs before
    callables are applied, so you cannot return a tuple from a callable to
    index both rows and columns.

Getting values from an object with multi-axes selection uses the following
notation (using `.loc` as an example, but the following applies to `.iloc`
as well). Any of the axes accessors may be the null slice `:`. Axes left out
of the specification are assumed to be `:`, e.g. `p.loc['a']` is equivalent
to `p.loc['a', :]`.

>python
    In [1]: ser = pd.Series(range(5), index=list("abcde"))

    In [2]: ser.loc[["a", "c", "e"]]
    Out[2]: 
    a    0
    c    2
    e    4
    dtype: int64

    In [3]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(25).reshape(5, 5), index=list("abcde"), columns=list("abcde"))

    In [4]: df.loc[["a", "c", "e"], ["b", "d"]]
    Out[4]: 
        b   d
    a   1   3
    c  11  13
    e  21  23
<

BASICS                                            *user_guide-indexing-basics*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-basics*

As mentioned when introducing the data structures in the
|user_guide-basics-basics|, the primary function of indexing with `[]`
(a.k.a. `__getitem__` for those familiar with implementing class behavior in
Python) is selecting out lower-dimensional slices. The following table shows
return type values when indexing pandas objects with `[]`:

Object Type  Selection                Return Value Type
-----------  -----------------------  ----------------------------------------
Series       series[label]            scalar value
DataFrame    frame[colname]           Series corresponding to colname
DataFrame    frame[[colname]]         DataFrame with columns corresponding to
                                      [colname]
DataFrame    frame[list_of_colnames]  DataFrame with columns corresponding to
                                      list_of_colnames

The same principle applies to label-based selection with `.loc`: a list-like
of labels preserves the corresponding axis (so `df.loc[:, ["A"]]` returns a
`DataFrame`, even when the list contains a single label), while a scalar
label reduces the axis when labels on that axis are unique (so
`df.loc[:, "A"]` typically returns a `Series`; if `"A"` is duplicated on the
axis, a `DataFrame` is returned instead). See
|user_guide-indexing-indexing-label| for details.

Here we construct a simple time series data set to use for illustrating the
indexing functionality:

>python
    In [5]: dates = pd.date_range('1/1/2000', periods=8)

    In [6]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(8, 4),
       ...:                   index=dates, columns=['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'])
       ...: 

    In [7]: df
    Out[7]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863 -1.509059 -1.135632
    2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209 -1.044236
    2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929  1.071804
    2000-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771 -1.039575  0.271860
    2000-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020  0.276232 -1.087401
    2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648 -1.478427  0.524988
    2000-01-07  0.404705  0.577046 -1.715002 -1.039268
    2000-01-08 -0.370647 -1.157892 -1.344312  0.844885
<
  Note: ~

  None of the indexing functionality is time series specific unless
  specifically stated.

Thus, as per above, we have the most basic indexing using `[]`:

>python
    In [8]: s = df['A']

    In [9]: s[dates[5]]
    Out[9]: np.float64(-0.6736897080883706)
<
You can pass a list of columns to `[]` to select columns in that order. If a
column is not contained in the DataFrame, an exception will be raised.
Multiple columns can also be set in this manner:

>python
    In [10]: df
    Out[10]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863 -1.509059 -1.135632
    2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209 -1.044236
    2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929  1.071804
    2000-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771 -1.039575  0.271860
    2000-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020  0.276232 -1.087401
    2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648 -1.478427  0.524988
    2000-01-07  0.404705  0.577046 -1.715002 -1.039268
    2000-01-08 -0.370647 -1.157892 -1.344312  0.844885

    In [11]: df[['B', 'A']] = df[['A', 'B']]

    In [12]: df
    Out[12]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112 -1.509059 -1.135632
    2000-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112  0.119209 -1.044236
    2000-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849 -0.494929  1.071804
    2000-01-04 -0.706771  0.721555 -1.039575  0.271860
    2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972  0.276232 -1.087401
    2000-01-06  0.113648 -0.673690 -1.478427  0.524988
    2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268
    2000-01-08 -1.157892 -0.370647 -1.344312  0.844885
<
You may find this useful for applying a transform (in-place) to a subset of
the columns.

  Warning: ~

  pandas aligns all AXES when setting `Series` and `DataFrame` from `.loc`.

  This will not modify `df` because the column alignment is before value
  assignment.

  >python
      In [13]: df[['A', 'B']]
      Out[13]: 
                         A         B
      2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112
      2000-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112
      2000-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849
      2000-01-04 -0.706771  0.721555
      2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972
      2000-01-06  0.113648 -0.673690
      2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705
      2000-01-08 -1.157892 -0.370647

      In [14]: df.loc[:, ['B', 'A']] = df[['A', 'B']]

      In [15]: df[['A', 'B']]
      Out[15]: 
                         A         B
      2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112
      2000-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112
      2000-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849
      2000-01-04 -0.706771  0.721555
      2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972
      2000-01-06  0.113648 -0.673690
      2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705
      2000-01-08 -1.157892 -0.370647
<
  The correct way to swap column values is by using raw values:

  >python
      In [16]: df.loc[:, ['B', 'A']] = df[['A', 'B']].to_numpy()

      In [17]: df[['A', 'B']]
      Out[17]: 
                         A         B
      2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863
      2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215
      2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569
      2000-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
      2000-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020
      2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648
      2000-01-07  0.404705  0.577046
      2000-01-08 -0.370647 -1.157892
<
  However, pandas does not align AXES when setting `Series` and `DataFrame`
  from `.iloc` because `.iloc` operates by position.

  This will modify `df` because the column alignment is not done before
  value assignment.

  >python
      In [18]: df[['A', 'B']]
      Out[18]: 
                         A         B
      2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863
      2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215
      2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569
      2000-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
      2000-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020
      2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648
      2000-01-07  0.404705  0.577046
      2000-01-08 -0.370647 -1.157892

      In [19]: df.iloc[:, [1, 0]] = df[['A', 'B']]

      In [20]: df[['A','B']]
      Out[20]: 
                         A         B
      2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112
      2000-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112
      2000-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849
      2000-01-04 -0.706771  0.721555
      2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972
      2000-01-06  0.113648 -0.673690
      2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705
      2000-01-08 -1.157892 -0.370647
<

                           *user_guide-indexing-selecting-columns-with-select*
Selecting columns with `select`

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-select*

|pandas.DataFrame.select| returns a DataFrame with the requested columns in
the given order, similar to passing a list of columns to `[]`. As a method,
it can be used within a chain of operations. Columns can be given as
individual arguments or as a single list:

>python
    In [21]: df.select('B', 'A')
    Out[21]: 
                       B         A
    2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863
    2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215
    2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569
    2000-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
    2000-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020
    2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648
    2000-01-07  0.404705  0.577046
    2000-01-08 -0.370647 -1.157892

    In [22]: df.select(['B', 'A'])
    Out[22]: 
                       B         A
    2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863
    2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215
    2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569
    2000-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
    2000-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020
    2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648
    2000-01-07  0.404705  0.577046
    2000-01-08 -0.370647 -1.157892
<
In addition to existing columns, computed columns can be included via
|pandas.col| expressions or callables. A positional expression keeps the
name of the underlying column, while a keyword argument names the resulting
column. Later arguments can refer to columns computed earlier in the same
call:

>python
    In [23]: df.select('A', pd.col('B') * 2, C=pd.col('A') + pd.col('B'), D=pd.col('C') > 0)
    Out[23]: 
                       A         B         C      D
    2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.938225  0.655361   True
    2000-01-02 -0.173215  2.424224  2.251009   True
    2000-01-03 -2.104569 -1.723698 -3.828267  False
    2000-01-04 -0.706771  1.443110  0.736339   True
    2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.849945 -0.282924  False
    2000-01-06  0.113648 -1.347379 -1.233731  False
    2000-01-07  0.577046  0.809410  1.386456   True
    2000-01-08 -1.157892 -0.741294 -1.899186  False
<
A computed column with the same name as an existing column replaces it for
later arguments. It does not replace a column that was already selected, so
the result can contain duplicate column labels:

>python
    In [24]: df.select('A', A=pd.col('A') * 2, E=pd.col('A'))
    Out[24]: 
                       A         A         E
    2000-01-01 -0.282863 -0.565727 -0.565727
    2000-01-02 -0.173215 -0.346429 -0.346429
    2000-01-03 -2.104569 -4.209138 -4.209138
    2000-01-04 -0.706771 -1.413542 -1.413542
    2000-01-05  0.567020  1.134041  1.134041
    2000-01-06  0.113648  0.227297  0.227297
    2000-01-07  0.577046  1.154092  1.154092
    2000-01-08 -1.157892 -2.315785 -2.315785
<

ATTRIBUTE ACCESS                        *user_guide-indexing-attribute-access*

You may access an index on a `Series` or column on a `DataFrame` directly as
an attribute:

>python
    In [25]: sa = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=list('abc'))

    In [26]: dfa = df.copy()
<
>python
    In [27]: sa.b
    Out[27]: np.int64(2)

    In [28]: dfa.A
    Out[28]: 
    2000-01-01   -0.282863
    2000-01-02   -0.173215
    2000-01-03   -2.104569
    2000-01-04   -0.706771
    2000-01-05    0.567020
    2000-01-06    0.113648
    2000-01-07    0.577046
    2000-01-08   -1.157892
    Freq: D, Name: A, dtype: float64
<
>python
    In [29]: sa.a = 5

    In [30]: sa
    Out[30]: 
    a    5
    b    2
    c    3
    dtype: int64

    In [31]: dfa.A = list(range(len(dfa.index)))  # ok if A already exists

    In [32]: dfa
    Out[32]: 
                A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01  0  0.469112 -1.509059 -1.135632
    2000-01-02  1  1.212112  0.119209 -1.044236
    2000-01-03  2 -0.861849 -0.494929  1.071804
    2000-01-04  3  0.721555 -1.039575  0.271860
    2000-01-05  4 -0.424972  0.276232 -1.087401
    2000-01-06  5 -0.673690 -1.478427  0.524988
    2000-01-07  6  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268
    2000-01-08  7 -0.370647 -1.344312  0.844885

    In [33]: dfa['A'] = list(range(len(dfa.index)))  # use this form to create a new column

    In [34]: dfa
    Out[34]: 
                A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01  0  0.469112 -1.509059 -1.135632
    2000-01-02  1  1.212112  0.119209 -1.044236
    2000-01-03  2 -0.861849 -0.494929  1.071804
    2000-01-04  3  0.721555 -1.039575  0.271860
    2000-01-05  4 -0.424972  0.276232 -1.087401
    2000-01-06  5 -0.673690 -1.478427  0.524988
    2000-01-07  6  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268
    2000-01-08  7 -0.370647 -1.344312  0.844885
<
  Warning: ~

  - You can use this access only if the index element is a valid Python
    identifier, e.g. `s.1` is not allowed. See
    here for an explanation of valid identifiers
    https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#identifiers.
  - The attribute will not be available if it conflicts with an existing
    method name, e.g. `s.min` is not allowed, but `s['min']` is possible.
  - Similarly, the attribute will not be available if it conflicts with any
    of the following list: `index`, `major_axis`, `minor_axis`, `items`.
  - In any of these cases, standard indexing will still work, e.g. `s['1']`,
    `s['min']`, and `s['index']` will access the corresponding element or
    column.

If you are using the IPython environment, you may also use tab-completion to
see these accessible attributes.

You can also assign a `dict` to a row of a `DataFrame`:

>python
    In [35]: x = pd.DataFrame({'x': [1, 2, 3], 'y': [3, 4, 5]})

    In [36]: x.iloc[1] = {'x': 9, 'y': 99}

    In [37]: x
    Out[37]: 
       x   y
    0  1   3
    1  9  99
    2  3   5
<
You can use attribute access to modify an existing element of a Series or
column of a DataFrame, but be careful; if you try to use attribute access to
create a new column, it creates a new attribute rather than a new column and
will this raise a `UserWarning`:

>python
    In [38]: df_new = pd.DataFrame({'one': [1., 2., 3.]})

    In [39]: df_new.two = [4, 5, 6]

    In [40]: df_new
    Out[40]: 
       one
    0  1.0
    1  2.0
    2  3.0
<

SLICING RANGES                            *user_guide-indexing-slicing-ranges*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-columns-multiple*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-df-cols*

The most robust and consistent way of slicing ranges along arbitrary axes is
described in the |user_guide-indexing-indexing-integer| section detailing
the `.iloc` method. For now, we explain the semantics of slicing using the
`[]` operator.

    Note: ~

    When the |pandas.Series| has float indices, slicing will select by
    position.

With Series, the syntax works exactly as with an ndarray, returning a slice
of the values and the corresponding labels:

>python
    In [41]: s[:5]
    Out[41]: 
    2000-01-01    0.469112
    2000-01-02    1.212112
    2000-01-03   -0.861849
    2000-01-04    0.721555
    2000-01-05   -0.424972
    Freq: D, Name: A, dtype: float64

    In [42]: s[::2]
    Out[42]: 
    2000-01-01    0.469112
    2000-01-03   -0.861849
    2000-01-05   -0.424972
    2000-01-07    0.404705
    Freq: 2D, Name: A, dtype: float64

    In [43]: s[::-1]
    Out[43]: 
    2000-01-08   -0.370647
    2000-01-07    0.404705
    2000-01-06   -0.673690
    2000-01-05   -0.424972
    2000-01-04    0.721555
    2000-01-03   -0.861849
    2000-01-02    1.212112
    2000-01-01    0.469112
    Freq: -1D, Name: A, dtype: float64
<
Note that setting works as well:

>python
    In [44]: s2 = s.copy()

    In [45]: s2[:5] = 0

    In [46]: s2
    Out[46]: 
    2000-01-01    0.000000
    2000-01-02    0.000000
    2000-01-03    0.000000
    2000-01-04    0.000000
    2000-01-05    0.000000
    2000-01-06   -0.673690
    2000-01-07    0.404705
    2000-01-08   -0.370647
    Freq: D, Name: A, dtype: float64
<
With DataFrame, slicing inside of `[]` slices the rows. This is provided
largely as a convenience since it is such a common operation.

>python
    In [47]: df[:3]
    Out[47]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112 -1.509059 -1.135632
    2000-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112  0.119209 -1.044236
    2000-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849 -0.494929  1.071804

    In [48]: df[::-1]
    Out[48]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-08 -1.157892 -0.370647 -1.344312  0.844885
    2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268
    2000-01-06  0.113648 -0.673690 -1.478427  0.524988
    2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972  0.276232 -1.087401

  String likes in slicing can be convertible to the type of the index and
  lead to natural slicing.

  >python
      In [52]: dfl.loc['20130102':'20130104']
      Out[52]: 
                         A         B         C         D
      2013-01-02  0.357021 -0.674600 -1.776904 -0.968914
      2013-01-03 -1.294524  0.413738  0.276662 -0.472035
      2013-01-04 -0.013960 -0.362543 -0.006154 -0.923061
<

pandas provides a suite of methods in order to have purely label based
indexing. This is a strict inclusion based protocol. Every label asked for
must be in the index, or a `KeyError` will be raised. When slicing, both the
start bound AND the stop bound are included, if present in the index.
Integers are valid labels, but they refer to the label and not the position.

The `.loc` attribute is the primary access method. The following are valid
inputs:

- A single label, e.g. `5` or `'a'` (Note that `5` is interpreted as a label
  of the index. This use is not an integer position along the index.).
- A list or array of labels `['a', 'b', 'c']`.
- A slice object with labels `'a':'f'`. Note that contrary to usual Python
  slices, both the start and the stop are included, when present in the
  index! See |user_guide-indexing-indexing-slicing-with-labels|.
- A boolean array.
- A `callable`, see |user_guide-indexing-indexing-callable|.

>python
    In [53]: s1 = pd.Series(np.random.randn(6), index=list('abcdef'))

    In [54]: s1
    Out[54]: 
    a    1.431256
    b    1.340309
    c   -1.170299
    d   -0.226169
    e    0.410835
    f    0.813850
    dtype: float64

    In [55]: s1.loc['c':]
    Out[55]: 
    c   -1.170299
    d   -0.226169
    e    0.410835
    f    0.813850
    dtype: float64

    In [56]: s1.loc['b']
    Out[56]: np.float64(1.3403088497993827)
<
Note that setting works as well:

>python
    In [57]: s1.loc['c':] = 0

    In [58]: s1
    Out[58]: 
    a    1.431256
    b    1.340309
    c    0.000000
    d    0.000000
    e    0.000000
    f    0.000000
    dtype: float64
<

Slicing with labels                  *user_guide-indexing-slicing-with-labels*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-slicing-with-labels*

When using `.loc` with slices, if both the start and the stop labels are
present in the index, then elements located between the two (including them)
are returned:

>python
    In [70]: s = pd.Series(list('abcde'), index=[0, 3, 2, 5, 4])

    In [71]: s.loc[3:5]
    Out[71]: 
    3    b
    2    c
    5    d
    dtype: str
<
If the index is sorted, and can be compared against start and stop labels,
then slicing will still work as expected, by selecting labels which rank
between the two:

>python
    In [72]: s.sort_index()
    Out[72]: 
    0    a
    2    c
    3    b
    4    e
    5    d
    dtype: str

    In [73]: s.sort_index().loc[1:6]
    Out[73]: 
    2    c
    3    b
    4    e
    5    d
    dtype: str
<
However, if at least one of the two is absent and the index is not sorted,
an error will be raised (since doing otherwise would be computationally
expensive, as well as potentially ambiguous for mixed type indexes). For
instance, in the above example, `s.loc[1:6]` would raise `KeyError`.

For the rationale behind this behavior, see
|user_guide-advanced-advanced-endpoints-are-inclusive|.

>python
    In [74]: s = pd.Series(list('abcdef'), index=[0, 3, 2, 5, 4, 2])

    In [75]: s.loc[3:5]
    Out[75]: 
    3    b
    2    c
    5    d
    dtype: str
<
Also, if the index has duplicate labels and either the start or the stop
label is duplicated, an error will be raised. For instance, in the above
example, `s.loc[2:5]` would raise a `KeyError`.

For more information about duplicate labels, see
|user_guide-duplicates-duplicates|.

When using a slice with a step, such as `.loc[start:stop:step]`, note that
start and stop are interpreted as labels, while step is applied over the
positional index within that label range. This means a stepped slice will
behave differently than using the labels `range(start, stop, step)` when the
index is not contiguous integers.

For example, in a `Series` with a non-contiguous integer index:

>python
    In [76]: s = pd.Series(range(10), index=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45])

    In [77]: s.loc[10:50:5]              # (10), then skip 5 positions → 35 only
    Out[77]: 
    10    2
    35    7
    dtype: int64

    In [78]: s.loc[[10, 15, 20, 25]]     # explicit label selection
    Out[78]: 
    10    2
    15    3
    20    4
    25    5
    dtype: int64
<
The first applies step across positional locations between the start/stop
labels. The second selects each label directly.

Similarly, with a string-based index, the behavior is identical:

>python
    In [79]: s = pd.Series(range(10), index=['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g', 'h', 'i', 'j'])

    In [80]: s.loc['b':'i':2]            # Start at 'b' (position 1), stop at 'i' (position 8), step 2 positions → 'b', 'd', 'f', 'h'
    Out[80]: 
    b    1
    d    3
    f    5
    h    7
    dtype: int64

    In [81]: s.loc[['b', 'd', 'f', 'h']] # explicit label selection
    Out[81]: 
    b    1
    d    3
    f    5
    h    7
    dtype: int64
<
In both cases, start and stop determine the label boundaries (inclusive),
while step skips positions within that range, regardless of the index type.

SELECTION BY POSITION              *user_guide-indexing-selection-by-position*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-integer*

pandas provides a suite of methods in order to get purely integer based
indexing. The semantics follow closely Python and NumPy slicing. These are
`0-based` indexing. When slicing, the start bound is included, while the
upper bound is excluded. Trying to use a non-integer, even a valid label
will raise an `IndexError`.

The `.iloc` attribute is the primary access method. The following are valid
inputs:

- An integer e.g. `5`.
- A list or array of integers `[4, 3, 0]`.
- A slice object with ints `1:7`.
- A boolean array.
- A `callable`, see |user_guide-indexing-indexing-callable|.
- A tuple of row (and column) indexes, whose elements are one of the above
  types.

>python
    In [82]: s1 = pd.Series(np.random.randn(5), index=list(range(0, 10, 2)))

    In [83]: s1
    Out[83]: 
    0    0.695775
    2    0.341734
    4    0.959726
    6   -1.110336
    8   -0.619976
    dtype: float64

    In [84]: s1.iloc[:3]
    Out[84]: 
    0    0.695775
    2    0.341734
    4    0.959726
    dtype: float64

    In [85]: s1.iloc[3]
    Out[85]: np.float64(-1.110336102891167)
<
Note that setting works as well:

>python
    In [86]: s1.iloc[:3] = 0

    In [87]: s1
    Out[87]: 
    0    0.000000
    2    0.000000
    4    0.000000
    6   -1.110336
    8   -0.619976
    dtype: float64
<

Out of range slice indexes are handled gracefully just as in Python/NumPy.

SELECTION BY CALLABLE              *user_guide-indexing-selection-by-callable*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-callable*

`.loc`, `.iloc`, and also `[]` indexing can accept a `callable` as indexer.
The `callable` must be a function with one argument (the calling Series or
DataFrame) that returns valid output for indexing.

  Note: ~

  For `.iloc` indexing, returning a tuple from the callable is not
  supported, since tuple destructuring for row and column indexes occurs
  before applying callables.

>python
    In [112]: df1 = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(6, 4),
       .....:                    index=list('abcdef'),
       .....:                    columns=list('ABCD'))
       .....: 

    In [113]: df1
    Out[113]: 
              A         B         C         D
    a -0.023688  2.410179  1.450520  0.206053
    b -0.251905 -2.213588  1.063327  1.266143
    c  0.299368 -0.863838  0.408204 -1.048089
    d -0.025747 -0.988387  0.094055  1.262731
    e  1.289997  0.082423 -0.055758  0.536580
    f -0.489682  0.369374 -0.034571 -2.484478

    In [114]: df1.loc[lambda df: df['A'] > 0, :]
    Out[114]: 
              A         B         C         D
    c  0.299368 -0.863838  0.408204 -1.048089
    e  1.289997  0.082423 -0.055758  0.536580

    In [115]: df1.loc[:, lambda df: ['A', 'B']]
    Out[115]: 
              A         B
    a -0.023688  2.410179
    b -0.251905 -2.213588
    c  0.299368 -0.863838
    d -0.025747 -0.988387
    e  1.289997  0.082423
    f -0.489682  0.369374

    In [116]: df1.iloc[:, lambda df: [0, 1]]
    Out[116]: 
              A         B
    a -0.023688  2.410179
    b -0.251905 -2.213588
    c  0.299368 -0.863838
    d -0.025747 -0.988387
    e  1.289997  0.082423
    f -0.489682  0.369374

    In [117]: df1[lambda df: df.columns[0]]
    Out[117]: 
    a   -0.023688
    b   -0.251905
    c    0.299368
    d   -0.025747
    e    1.289997
    f   -0.489682
    Name: A, dtype: float64
<
You can use callable indexing in `Series`.

>python
    In [118]: df1['A'].loc[lambda s: s > 0]
    Out[118]: 
    c    0.299368
    e    1.289997
    Name: A, dtype: float64
<
Using these methods / indexers, you can chain data selection operations
without using a temporary variable.

>python
    In [119]: bb = pd.read_csv('data/baseball.csv', index_col='id')

    In [120]: (bb.groupby(['year', 'team']).sum(numeric_only=True)
       .....:    .loc[lambda df: df['r'] > 100])
       .....:

           *user_guide-indexing-combining-positional-and-label-based-indexing*
COMBINING POSITIONAL AND LABEL-BASED INDEXING

*user_guide-indexing-id1*

If you wish to get the 0th and the 2nd elements from the index in the ‘A'
column, you can do:

>python
    In [121]: dfd = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3],
       .....:                     'B': [4, 5, 6]},
       .....:                    index=list('abc'))
       .....: 

    In [122]: dfd
    Out[122]: 
       A  B
    a  1  4
    b  2  5
    c  3  6

    In [123]: dfd.loc[dfd.index[[0, 2]], 'A']
    Out[123]: 
    a    1
    c    3
    Name: A, dtype: int64
<
This can also be expressed using `.iloc`, by explicitly getting locations on
the indexers, and using positional indexing to select things.

>python
    In [124]: dfd.iloc[[0, 2], dfd.columns.get_loc('A')]
    Out[124]: 
    a    1
    c    3
    Name: A, dtype: int64
<
For getting multiple indexers, using `.get_indexer`:

>python
    In [125]: dfd.iloc[[0, 2], dfd.columns.get_indexer(['A', 'B'])]
    Out[125]: 
       A  B
    a  1  4
    c  3  6
<

Reindexing                                    *user_guide-indexing-reindexing*

The idiomatic way to achieve selecting potentially not-found elements is via
`.reindex()`. See also the section on |user_guide-basics-basics-reindexing|.

>python
    In [126]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])

    In [127]: s.reindex([1, 2, 3])
    Out[127]: 
    1    2.0
    2    3.0
    3    NaN
    dtype: float64
<
Alternatively, if you want to select only valid keys, the following is
idiomatic and efficient; it is guaranteed to preserve the dtype of the
selection.

>python
    In [128]: labels = [1, 2, 3]

    In [129]: s.loc[s.index.intersection(labels)]
    Out[129]: 
    1    2
    2    3
    dtype: int64
<

    In [130]: s = pd.Series(np.arange(4), index=['a', 'a', 'b', 'c'])

SELECTING RANDOM SAMPLES        *user_guide-indexing-selecting-random-samples*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-basics-partial-setting*

A random selection of rows or columns from a Series or DataFrame with the
|pandas.DataFrame.sample| method. The method will sample rows by default,
and accepts a specific number of rows/columns to return, or a fraction of
rows.

>python
    In [136]: s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

    # When no arguments are passed, returns 1 row.
    In [137]: s.sample()
    Out[137]: 
    4    4
    dtype: int64

    # One may specify either a number of rows:
    In [138]: s.sample(n=3)
    Out[138]: 
    0    0
    4    4
    1    1
    dtype: int64

    # Or a fraction of the rows:
    In [139]: s.sample(frac=0.5)
    Out[139]: 
    5    5
    3    3
    1    1
    dtype: int64
<
By default, `sample` will return each row at most once, but one can also
sample with replacement using the `replace` option:

>python
    In [140]: s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

    # Without replacement (default):
    In [141]: s.sample(n=6, replace=False)
    Out[141]: 
    0    0
    1    1
    5    5
    3    3
    2    2
    4    4
    dtype: int64

    # With replacement:
    In [142]: s.sample(n=6, replace=True)
    Out[142]: 
    0    0
    4    4
    3    3
    2    2
    4    4
    4    4
    dtype: int64
<
By default, each row has an equal probability of being selected, but if you
want rows to have different probabilities, you can pass the `sample`
function sampling weights as `weights`. These weights can be a list, a NumPy
array, or a Series, but they must be of the same length as the object you
are sampling. Missing values will be treated as a weight of zero, and inf
values are not allowed. If weights do not sum to 1, they will be
re-normalized by dividing all weights by the sum of the weights. For
example:

>python
    In [143]: s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

    In [144]: example_weights = [0, 0, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.4]

    In [145]: s.sample(n=2, weights=example_weights)
    Out[145]: 
    5    5
    4    4
    dtype: int64

    # Weights will be re-normalized automatically
    In [146]: example_weights2 = [0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]

    In [147]: s.sample(n=1, weights=example_weights2)
    Out[147]: 
    0    0
    dtype: int64
<
When applied to a DataFrame, you can use a column of the DataFrame as
sampling weights (provided you are sampling rows and not columns) by simply
passing the name of the column as a string.

>python
    In [148]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({'col1': [9, 8, 7, 6],
       .....:                     'weight_column': [0.5, 0.4, 0.1, 0]})
       .....: 

    In [149]: df2.sample(n=2, weights='weight_column')
    Out[149]: 
       col1  weight_column
    0     9            0.5
    1     8            0.4
<
`sample` also allows users to sample columns instead of rows using the
`axis` argument.

>python
    In [150]: df3 = pd.DataFrame({'col1': [1, 2, 3], 'col2': [2, 3, 4]})

    In [151]: df3.sample(n=1, axis=1)
    Out[151]: 
       col2
    0     2
    1     3
    2     4
<
Finally, one can also set a seed for `sample`'s random number generator
using the `random_state` argument, which will accept either an integer (as a
seed) or a NumPy RandomState object.

>python
    In [152]: df4 = pd.DataFrame({'col1': [1, 2, 3], 'col2': [2, 3, 4]})

    # With a given seed, the sample will always draw the same rows.
    In [153]: df4.sample(n=2, random_state=2)
    Out[153]: 
       col1  col2
    2     3     4
    1     2     3

    In [154]: df4.sample(n=2, random_state=2)
    Out[154]: 
       col1  col2
    2     3     4
    1     2     3
<

SETTING WITH ENLARGEMENT        *user_guide-indexing-setting-with-enlargement*

The `.loc/[]` operations can perform enlargement when setting a non-existent
key for that axis.

In the `Series` case this is effectively an appending operation.

>python
    In [155]: se = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])

    In [156]: se
    Out[156]: 
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    dtype: int64

    In [157]: se[5] = 5.

    In [158]: se
    Out[158]: 
    0    1
    1    2
    2    3
    5    5
    dtype: int64
<
A `DataFrame` can be enlarged on either axis via `.loc`.

>python
    In [159]: dfi = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2),
       .....:                    columns=['A', 'B'])
       .....: 

    In [160]: dfi
    Out[160]: 
       A  B
    0  0  1
    1  2  3
    2  4  5

    In [161]: dfi.loc[:, 'C'] = dfi.loc[:, 'A']

    In [162]: dfi
    Out[162]: 
       A  B  C
    0  0  1  0
    1  2  3  2
    2  4  5  4
<
This is like an `append` operation on the `DataFrame`.

>python
    In [163]: dfi.loc[3] = 5

    In [164]: dfi
    Out[164]: 
       A  B  C
    0  0  1  0
    1  2  3  2
    2  4  5  4
    3  5  5  5
<

                   *user_guide-indexing-fast-scalar-value-getting-and-setting*
FAST SCALAR VALUE GETTING AND SETTING

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-basics-get-value*

Since indexing with `[]` must handle a lot of cases (single-label access,
slicing, boolean indexing, etc.), it has a bit of overhead in order to
figure out what you're asking for. If you only want to access a scalar
value, the fastest way is to use the `at` and `iat` methods, which are
implemented on all of the data structures.

Similarly to `loc`, `at` provides label based scalar lookups, while, `iat`
provides integer based lookups analogously to `iloc`

>python
    In [165]: s.iat[5]
    Out[165]: np.int64(5)

    In [166]: df.at[dates[5], 'A']
    Out[166]: np.float64(0.1136484096888855)

    In [167]: df.iat[3, 0]
    Out[167]: np.float64(-0.7067711336300845)
<
You can also set using these same indexers.

>python
    In [168]: df.at[dates[5], 'A'] = 7

    In [169]: df.iat[3, 0] = 7
<
`at` previously could enlarge the object in-place if the indexer was
missing, but this behavior is deprecated. Use `.loc` instead for setting
values with new keys:

>python
    In [170]: df.loc[dates[-1] + pd.Timedelta('1 day'), 0] = 7

    In [171]: df
    Out[171]: 
                       A         B         C         D    0
    2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112 -1.509059 -1.135632  NaN
    2000-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112  0.119209 -1.044236  NaN
    2000-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849 -0.494929  1.071804  NaN
    2000-01-04  7.000000  0.721555 -1.039575  0.271860  NaN
    2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972  0.276232 -1.087401  NaN
    2000-01-06  7.000000 -0.673690 -1.478427  0.524988  NaN
    2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268  NaN
    2000-01-08 -1.157892 -0.370647 -1.344312  0.844885  NaN
    2000-01-09       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN  7.0
<

BOOLEAN INDEXING                        *user_guide-indexing-boolean-indexing*

Another common operation is the use of boolean vectors to filter the data.
The operators are: `|` for `or`, `&` for `and`, and `~` for `not`. These
must be grouped by using parentheses, since by default Python will evaluate
an expression such as `df['A'] > 2 & df['B'] < 3` as
`df['A'] > (2 & df['B']) < 3`, while the desired evaluation order is
`(df['A'] > 2) & (df['B'] < 3)`.

Using a boolean vector to index a Series works exactly as in a NumPy
ndarray:

>python
    In [172]: s = pd.Series(range(-3, 4))

    In [173]: s
    Out[173]: 
    0   -3
    1   -2
    2   -1
    3    0
    4    1
    5    2
    6    3
    dtype: int64

    In [174]: s[s > 0]
    Out[174]: 
    4    1
    5    2
    6    3
    dtype: int64

    In [175]: s[(s < -1) | (s > 0.5)]
    Out[175]: 
    0   -3
    1   -2
    4    1
    5    2
    6    3
    dtype: int64

    In [176]: s[~(s < 0)]
    Out[176]: 
    3    0
    4    1
    5    2
    6    3
    dtype: int64
<
You may select rows from a DataFrame using a boolean vector the same length
as the DataFrame's index (for example, something derived from one of the
columns of the DataFrame):

>python
    In [177]: df[df['A'] > 0]
    Out[177]: 
                       A         B         C         D   0
    2000-01-04  7.000000  0.721555 -1.039575  0.271860 NaN
    2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972  0.276232 -1.087401 NaN
    2000-01-06  7.000000 -0.673690 -1.478427  0.524988 NaN
    2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268 NaN
<
List comprehensions and the `map` method of Series can also be used to
produce more complex criteria:

>python
    In [178]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({'a': ['one', 'one', 'two', 'three', 'two', 'one', 'six'],
       .....:                     'b': ['x', 'y', 'y', 'x', 'y', 'x', 'x'],
       .....:                     'c': np.random.randn(7)})
       .....: 

    # only want 'two' or 'three'
    In [179]: criterion = df2['a'].map(lambda x: x.startswith('t'))

    In [180]: df2[criterion]
    Out[180]: 
           a  b         c
    2    two  y  2.543083
    3  three  x  0.831311
    4    two  y -0.816973

    # equivalent but slower
    In [181]: df2[[x.startswith('t') for x in df2['a']]]
    Out[181]: 
           a  b         c
    2    two  y  2.543083
    3  three  x  0.831311
    4    two  y -0.816973

    # Multiple criteria
    In [182]: df2[criterion & (df2['b'] == 'x')]
    Out[182]: 
           a  b         c
    3  three  x  0.831311
<
With the choice methods |user_guide-indexing-indexing-label|,
|user_guide-indexing-indexing-integer|, and |user_guide-advanced-advanced|
you may select along more than one axis using boolean vectors combined with
other indexing expressions.

>python
    In [183]: df2.loc[criterion & (df2['b'] == 'x'), 'b':'c']
    Out[183]: 
       b         c
    3  x  0.831311
<
  Warning: ~

  While `loc` supports two kinds of boolean indexing, `iloc` only supports
  indexing with a boolean array. If the indexer is a boolean `Series`, an
  error will be raised. For instance, in the following example,
  `df.iloc[s.values, 1]` is ok. The boolean indexer is an array. But
  `df.iloc[s, 1]` would raise `ValueError`.

  >python
      In [184]: df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]],
         .....:                   index=list('abc'),
         .....:                   columns=['A', 'B'])
         .....: 

      In [185]: s = (df['A'] > 2)

      In [186]: s
      Out[186]: 
      a    False
      b     True
      c     True
      Name: A, dtype: bool

      In [187]: df.loc[s, 'B']
      Out[187]: 
      b    4
      c    6
      Name: B, dtype: int64

      In [188]: df.iloc[s.values, 1]
      Out[188]: 
      b    4
      c    6
      Name: B, dtype: int64
<

                         *user_guide-indexing-filtering-with-dataframe-filter*
Filtering with `DataFrame.filter`

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-boolean-filter*

  Added in version 3.1.0.: ~

|pandas.DataFrame.filter| and |pandas.Series.filter| also accept a boolean
mask through the `cond` keyword, keeping the rows where the mask is True. A
|pandas.Series| mask is aligned on the index; any other array-like must have
the same length as the index.

>python
    In [189]: df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3], 'B': [4, 5, 6]}, index=list('abc'))

    In [190]: df.filter(cond=df['A'] > 1)
    Out[190]: 
       A  B
    b  2  5
    c  3  6
<
`cond` may also be a callable that returns a boolean mask, or an expression
created with |pandas.col|. These two forms may be passed positionally, which
is convenient in a method chain where the intermediate object has no name:

>python
    In [191]: df.filter(pd.col('A') > 1)
    Out[191]: 
       A  B
    b  2  5
    c  3  6

    In [192]: df.assign(C=pd.col('A') + pd.col('B')).filter(lambda df: df['C'] > 5)
    Out[192]: 
       A  B  C
    b  2  5  7
    c  3  6  9
<
Pass `axis=1` to filter columns instead of rows:

>python
    In [193]: df.filter(cond=df.columns.str.startswith('A'), axis=1)
    Out[193]: 
       A
    a  1
    b  2
    c  3
<
Missing values in the mask are treated as False by default, matching
`df[mask]` for a mask with nullable boolean dtype. Pass `na=True` to keep
the corresponding rows instead, or `na="raise"` to raise an error:

>python
    In [194]: mask = pd.array([True, None, False], dtype="boolean")

    In [195]: df.filter(cond=mask)
    Out[195]: 
       A  B
    a  1  4

    In [196]: df.filter(cond=mask, na=True)
    Out[196]: 
       A  B
    a  1  4
    b  2  5
<

INDEXING WITH ISIN                    *user_guide-indexing-indexing-with-isin*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-basics-indexing-isin*

Consider the |pandas.Series.isin| method of `Series`, which returns a
boolean vector that is true wherever the `Series` elements exist in the
passed list. This allows you to select rows where one or more columns have
values you want:

>python
    In [197]: s = pd.Series(np.arange(5), index=np.arange(5)[::-1], dtype='int64')

    In [198]: s
    Out[198]: 
    4    0
    3    1
    2    2
    1    3
    0    4
    dtype: int64

    In [199]: s.isin([2, 4, 6])
    Out[199]: 
    4    False
    3    False
    2     True
    1    False
    0     True
    dtype: bool

    In [200]: s[s.isin([2, 4, 6])]
    Out[200]: 
    2    2
    0    4
    dtype: int64
<
The same method is available for `Index` objects and is useful for the cases
when you don't know which of the sought labels are in fact present:

>python
    In [201]: s[s.index.isin([2, 4, 6])]
    Out[201]: 
    4    0
    2    2
    dtype: int64

    # compare it to the following
    In [202]: s.reindex([2, 4, 6])
    Out[202]: 
    2    2.0
    4    0.0
    6    NaN
    dtype: float64
<
In addition to that, `MultiIndex` allows selecting a separate level to use
in the membership check:

>python
    In [203]: s_mi = pd.Series(np.arange(6),
       .....:                  index=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([[0, 1], ['a', 'b', 'c']]))
       .....: 

    In [204]: s_mi
    Out[204]: 
    0  a    0
       b    1
       c    2
    1  a    3
       b    4
       c    5
    dtype: int64

    In [205]: s_mi.iloc[s_mi.index.isin([(1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (0, 'c')])]
    Out[205]: 
    0  c    2
    1  a    3
    dtype: int64

    In [206]: s_mi.iloc[s_mi.index.isin(['a', 'c', 'e'], level=1)]
    Out[206]: 
    0  a    0
       c    2
    1  a    3
       c    5
    dtype: int64
<
DataFrame also has an |pandas.DataFrame.isin| method. When calling `isin`,
pass a set of values as either an array or dict. If values is an array,
`isin` returns a DataFrame of booleans that is the same shape as the
original DataFrame, with True wherever the element is in the sequence of
values.

>python
    In [207]: df = pd.DataFrame({'vals': [1, 2, 3, 4], 'ids': ['a', 'b', 'f', 'n'],
       .....:                    'ids2': ['a', 'n', 'c', 'n']})
       .....: 

    In [208]: values = ['a', 'b', 1, 3]

    In [209]: df.isin(values)
    Out[209]: 
        vals    ids   ids2
    0   True   True   True
    1  False   True  False
    2   True  False  False
    3  False  False  False
<
Oftentimes you'll want to match certain values with certain columns. Just
make values a `dict` where the key is the column, and the value is a list of
items you want to check for.

>python
    In [210]: values = {'ids': ['a', 'b'], 'vals': [1, 3]}

    In [211]: df.isin(values)
    Out[211]: 
        vals    ids   ids2
    0   True   True  False
    1  False   True  False
    2   True  False  False
    3  False  False  False
<
To return the DataFrame of booleans where the values are not in the original
DataFrame, use the `~` operator:

>python
    In [212]: values = {'ids': ['a', 'b'], 'vals': [1, 3]}

    In [213]: ~df.isin(values)
    Out[213]: 
        vals    ids  ids2
    0  False  False  True
    1   True  False  True
    2  False   True  True
    3   True   True  True
<
Combine DataFrame's `isin` with the `any()` and `all()` methods to quickly
select subsets of your data that meet a given criteria. To select a row
where each column meets its own criterion:

>python
    In [214]: values = {'ids': ['a', 'b'], 'ids2': ['a', 'c'], 'vals': [1, 3]}

    In [215]: row_mask = df.isin(values).all(axis=1)

    In [216]: df[row_mask]
    Out[216]: 
       vals ids ids2
    0     1   a    a
<

                            *user_guide-indexing-the-where-method-and-masking*
THE WHERE() METHOD AND MASKING

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-where-mask*

Selecting values from a Series with a boolean vector generally returns a
subset of the data. To guarantee that selection output has the same shape as
the original data, you can use the `where` method in `Series` and
`DataFrame`.

To return only the selected rows:

>python
    In [217]: s[s > 0]
    Out[217]: 
    3    1
    2    2
    1    3
    0    4
    dtype: int64
<
To return a Series of the same shape as the original:

>python
    In [218]: s.where(s > 0)
    Out[218]: 
    4    NaN
    3    1.0
    2    2.0
    1    3.0
    0    4.0
    dtype: float64
<
Selecting values from a DataFrame with a boolean criterion now also
preserves input data shape. `where` is used under the hood as the
implementation. The code below is equivalent to `df.where(df < 0)`.

>python
    In [219]: dates = pd.date_range('1/1/2000', periods=8)

    In [220]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(8, 4),
       .....:                   index=dates, columns=['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'])
       .....: 

    In [221]: df[df < 0]
    Out[221]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01       NaN       NaN -0.250643 -1.350999
    2000-01-02       NaN -0.026679       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-03       NaN -1.112060       NaN -1.281223
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN -0.592066 -0.650567
    2000-01-05 -0.374599       NaN -1.133167       NaN
    2000-01-06 -1.254148       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07 -0.524443 -0.712053 -0.267772       NaN
    2000-01-08 -0.076848       NaN -1.819296 -1.122503
<
In addition, `where` takes an optional `other` argument for replacement of
values where the condition is False, in the returned copy.

>python
    In [222]: df.where(df < 0, -df)
    Out[222]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01 -0.368085 -0.224661 -0.250643 -1.350999
    2000-01-02 -0.142692 -0.026679 -1.345835 -0.938848
    2000-01-03 -0.509624 -1.112060 -1.648517 -1.281223
    2000-01-04 -0.553689 -0.359996 -0.592066 -0.650567
    2000-01-05 -0.374599 -0.592071 -1.133167 -0.661259
    2000-01-06 -1.254148 -0.627193 -0.411295 -1.282903
    2000-01-07 -0.524443 -0.712053 -0.267772 -1.762567
    2000-01-08 -0.076848 -2.431230 -1.819296 -1.122503
<
You may wish to set values based on some boolean criteria. This can be done
intuitively like so:

>python
    In [223]: s2 = s.copy()

    In [224]: s2[s2 < 0] = 0

    In [225]: s2
    Out[225]: 
    4    0
    3    1
    2    2
    1    3
    0    4
    dtype: int64

    In [226]: df2 = df.copy()

    In [227]: df2[df2 < 0] = 0

    In [228]: df2
    Out[228]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01  0.368085  0.224661  0.000000  0.000000
    2000-01-02  0.142692  0.000000  1.345835  0.938848
    2000-01-03  0.509624  0.000000  1.648517  0.000000
    2000-01-04  0.553689  0.359996  0.000000  0.000000
    2000-01-05  0.000000  0.592071  0.000000  0.661259
    2000-01-06  0.000000  0.627193  0.411295  1.282903
    2000-01-07  0.000000  0.000000  0.000000  1.762567
    2000-01-08  0.000000  2.431230  0.000000  0.000000
<
`where` returns a modified copy of the data.

  Note: ~

  The signature for |pandas.DataFrame.where| differs from `numpy.where()`
  https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.where.html#numpy.where.
  Roughly `df1.where(m, df2)` is equivalent to `np.where(m, df1, df2)`.

  >python
      In [229]: df.where(df < 0, -df) == np.where(df < 0, df, -df)
      Out[229]: 
                     A     B     C     D
      2000-01-01  True  True  True  True
      2000-01-02  True  True  True  True
      2000-01-03  True  True  True  True
      2000-01-04  True  True  True  True
      2000-01-05  True  True  True  True
      2000-01-06  True  True  True  True
      2000-01-07  True  True  True  True
      2000-01-08  True  True  True  True
<

Alignment

Furthermore, `where` aligns the input boolean condition (ndarray or
DataFrame), such that partial selection with setting is possible. This is
analogous to partial setting via `.loc` (but on the contents rather than the
axis labels).

>python
    In [230]: df2 = df.copy()

    In [231]: df2[df2[1:4] > 0] = 3

    In [232]: df2
    Out[232]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01  0.368085  0.224661 -0.250643 -1.350999
    2000-01-02  3.000000 -0.026679  3.000000  3.000000
    2000-01-03  3.000000 -1.112060  3.000000 -1.281223
    2000-01-04  3.000000  3.000000 -0.592066 -0.650567
    2000-01-05 -0.374599  0.592071 -1.133167  0.661259
    2000-01-06 -1.254148  0.627193  0.411295  1.282903
    2000-01-07 -0.524443 -0.712053 -0.267772  1.762567
    2000-01-08 -0.076848  2.431230 -1.819296 -1.122503
<
Where can also accept `axis` and `level` parameters to align the input when
performing the `where`.

>python
    In [233]: df2 = df.copy()

    In [234]: df2.where(df2 > 0, df2['A'], axis='index')
    Out[234]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01  0.368085  0.224661  0.368085  0.368085
    2000-01-02  0.142692  0.142692  1.345835  0.938848
    2000-01-03  0.509624  0.509624  1.648517  0.509624
    2000-01-04  0.553689  0.359996  0.553689  0.553689
    2000-01-05 -0.374599  0.592071 -0.374599  0.661259
    2000-01-06 -1.254148  0.627193  0.411295  1.282903
    2000-01-07 -0.524443 -0.524443 -0.524443  1.762567
    2000-01-08 -0.076848  2.431230 -0.076848 -0.076848
<
This is equivalent to (but faster than) the following.

>python
    In [235]: df2 = df.copy()

    In [236]: df.apply(lambda x, y: x.where(x > 0, y), y=df['A'])
    Out[236]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01  0.368085  0.224661  0.368085  0.368085
    2000-01-02  0.142692  0.142692  1.345835  0.938848
    2000-01-03  0.509624  0.509624  1.648517  0.509624
    2000-01-04  0.553689  0.359996  0.553689  0.553689
    2000-01-05 -0.374599  0.592071 -0.374599  0.661259
    2000-01-06 -1.254148  0.627193  0.411295  1.282903
    2000-01-07 -0.524443 -0.524443 -0.524443  1.762567
    2000-01-08 -0.076848  2.431230 -0.076848 -0.076848
<
`where` can accept a callable as condition and `other` arguments. The
function must be with one argument (the calling Series or DataFrame) and
that returns valid output as condition and `other` argument.

>python
    In [237]: df3 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3],
       .....:                     'B': [4, 5, 6],
       .....:                     'C': [7, 8, 9]})
       .....: 

    In [238]: df3.where(lambda x: x > 4, lambda x: x + 10)
    Out[238]: 
        A   B  C
    0  11  14  7
    1  12   5  8
    2  13   6  9
<

Mask                                                *user_guide-indexing-mask*

|pandas.DataFrame.mask| is the inverse boolean operation of `where`.

>python
    In [239]: s.mask(s >= 0)
    Out[239]: 
    4   NaN
    3   NaN
    2   NaN
    1   NaN
    0   NaN
    dtype: float64

    In [240]: df.mask(df >= 0)
    Out[240]: 
                       A         B         C         D
    2000-01-01       NaN       NaN -0.250643 -1.350999
    2000-01-02       NaN -0.026679       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-03       NaN -1.112060       NaN -1.281223
    2000-01-04       NaN       NaN -0.592066 -0.650567
    2000-01-05 -0.374599       NaN -1.133167       NaN
    2000-01-06 -1.254148       NaN       NaN       NaN
    2000-01-07 -0.524443 -0.712053 -0.267772       NaN
    2000-01-08 -0.076848       NaN -1.819296 -1.122503
<

      *user_guide-indexing-setting-with-enlargement-conditionally-using-numpy*
SETTING WITH ENLARGEMENT CONDITIONALLY USING `numpy()`

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-np-where*

An alternative to |pandas.DataFrame.where| is to use `numpy.where()`
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.where.html#numpy.where.
Combined with setting a new column, you can use it to enlarge a DataFrame
where the values are determined conditionally.

Consider you have two choices to choose from in the following DataFrame. And
you want to set a new column color to ‘green' when the second column has
‘Z'. You can do the following:

>python
    In [241]: df = pd.DataFrame({'col1': list('ABBC'), 'col2': list('ZZXY')})

    In [242]: df['color'] = np.where(df['col2'] == 'Z', 'green', 'red')

    In [243]: df
    Out[243]: 
      col1 col2  color
    0    A    Z  green
    1    B    Z  green
    2    B    X    red
    3    C    Y    red
<
If you have multiple conditions, you can use `numpy.select()`
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.select.html#numpy.select
to achieve that. Say corresponding to three conditions there are three
choice of colors, with a fourth color as a fallback, you can do the
following.

>python
    In [244]: conditions = [
       .....:     (df['col2'] == 'Z') & (df['col1'] == 'A'),
       .....:     (df['col2'] == 'Z') & (df['col1'] == 'B'),
       .....:     (df['col1'] == 'B')
       .....: ]
       .....: 

    In [245]: choices = ['yellow', 'blue', 'purple']

    In [246]: df['color'] = np.select(conditions, choices, default='black')

    In [247]: df
    Out[247]: 
      col1 col2   color
    0    A    Z  yellow
    1    B    Z    blue
    2    B    X  purple
    3    C    Y   black
<

THE QUERY() METHOD                      *user_guide-indexing-the-query-method*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-query*

|pandas.DataFrame| objects have a |pandas.DataFrame.query| method that
allows selection using an expression.

You can get the value of the frame where column `b` has values between the
values of columns `a` and `c`. For example:

>python
    In [248]: n = 10

    In [249]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(n, 3), columns=list('abc'))

    In [250]: df
    Out[250]: 
              a         b         c
    0  0.977227  0.727376  0.630865
    1  0.076462  0.474453  0.438921
    2  0.118680  0.863670  0.138138
    3  0.577363  0.686602  0.595307
    4  0.564592  0.520630  0.913052
    5  0.926075  0.616184  0.078718
    6  0.854477  0.898725  0.076404
    7  0.523211  0.591538  0.792342
    8  0.216974  0.564056  0.397890
    9  0.454131  0.915716  0.074315

    # pure python
    In [251]: df[(df['a'] < df['b']) & (df['b'] < df['c'])]
    Out[251]: 
              a         b         c
    7  0.523211  0.591538  0.792342

    # query
    In [252]: df.query('(a < b) & (b < c)')
    Out[252]: 
              a         b         c
    7  0.523211  0.591538  0.792342
<
Do the same thing but fall back on a named index if there is no column with
the name `a`.

>python
    In [253]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randint(n / 2, size=(n, 2)), columns=list('bc'))

    In [254]: df.index.name = 'a'

    In [255]: df
    Out[255]: 
       b  c
    a      
    0  0  0
    1  3  1
    2  3  4
    3  0  4
    4  0  1
    5  3  4
    6  4  3
    7  1  4
    8  0  3
    9  0  1

    In [256]: df.query('a < b and b < c')
    Out[256]: 
       b  c
    a      
    2  3  4
<
If instead you don't want to or cannot name your index, you can use the name
`index` in your query expression:

>python
    In [257]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randint(n, size=(n, 2)), columns=list('bc'))

    In [258]: df
    Out[258]: 
       b  c
    0  2  3
    1  9  1
    2  3  1
    3  3  0
    4  5  6
    5  5  2
    6  7  4
    7  0  1
    8  2  5
    9  0  1

    In [259]: df.query('index < b < c')
    Out[259]: 
       b  c
    0  2  3
    4  5  6
<
  Note: ~

  If the name of your index overlaps with a column name, the column name is
  given precedence. For example,

  >python
      In [260]: df = pd.DataFrame({'a': np.random.randint(5, size=5)})

      In [261]: df.index.name = 'a'

      In [262]: df.query('a > 2')  # uses the column 'a', not the index
      Out[262]: 
         a
      a   
      3  3
<
  You can still use the index in a query expression by using the special
  identifier ‘index':

  >python
      In [263]: df.query('index > 2')
      Out[263]: 
         a
      a   
      3  3
      4  1
<
  If for some reason you have a column named `index`, then you can refer to
  the index as `ilevel_0` as well, but at this point you should consider
  renaming your columns to something less ambiguous.

MultiIndex query() Syntax        *user_guide-indexing-multiindex-query-syntax*

You can also use the levels of a `DataFrame` with a |pandas.MultiIndex| as
if they were columns in the frame:

>python
    In [264]: n = 10

    In [265]: colors = np.random.choice(['red', 'green'], size=n)

    In [266]: foods = np.random.choice(['eggs', 'ham'], size=n)

    In [267]: colors
    Out[267]: 
    array(['green', 'green', 'red', 'green', 'red', 'red', 'red', 'red',
           'green', 'green'], dtype='<U5')

    In [268]: foods
    Out[268]: 
    array(['ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'eggs', 'eggs',
           'eggs'], dtype='<U4')

    In [269]: index = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([colors, foods], names=['color', 'food'])

    In [270]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(n, 2), index=index)

    In [271]: df
    Out[271]: 
                       0         1
    color food                    
    green ham  -1.087664 -0.883833
          ham  -1.554827 -0.118953
    red   ham  -1.460084 -0.020351
    green ham  -0.256125  0.358575
    red   ham   1.112033 -0.200521
          ham  -0.508784 -0.327758
          ham   0.627056  0.067058
          eggs -1.376511  1.162330
    green eggs -0.482120 -0.455309
          eggs -0.985682  1.383438

    In [272]: df.query('color == "red"')
    Out[272]: 
                       0         1
    color food                    
    red   ham  -1.460084 -0.020351
          ham   1.112033 -0.200521
          ham  -0.508784 -0.327758
          ham   0.627056  0.067058
          eggs -1.376511  1.162330
<
If the levels of the `MultiIndex` are unnamed, you can refer to them using
special names:

>python
    In [273]: df.index.names = [None, None]

    In [274]: df
    Out[274]: 
                       0         1
    green ham  -1.087664 -0.883833
          ham  -1.554827 -0.118953
    red   ham  -1.460084 -0.020351
    green ham  -0.256125  0.358575
    red   ham   1.112033 -0.200521
          ham  -0.508784 -0.327758
          ham   0.627056  0.067058
          eggs -1.376511  1.162330
    green eggs -0.482120 -0.455309
          eggs -0.985682  1.383438

    In [275]: df.query('ilevel_0 == "red"')
    Out[275]: 
                     0         1
    red ham  -1.460084 -0.020351
        ham   1.112033 -0.200521
        ham  -0.508784 -0.327758
        ham   0.627056  0.067058
        eggs -1.376511  1.162330
<
The convention is `ilevel_0`, which means “index level 0” for the 0th level
of the `index`.

query() Use Cases  *user_guide-indexing-query-use-cases*

A use case for |pandas.DataFrame.query| is when you have a collection of
|pandas.DataFrame| objects that have a subset of column names (or index
levels/names) in common. You can pass the same query to both frames without
having to specify which frame you're interested in querying

>python
    In [276]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(n, 3), columns=list('abc'))

    In [277]: df

              a         b         c

    7  0.258647  0.655096  0.654920
    8  0.452594  0.454307  0.918260
    9  0.581556  0.470410  0.417434

    In [278]: df2 = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(n + 2, 3), columns=df.columns)

    In [279]: df2
    Out[279]: 
               a         b         c
    0   0.552021  0.483125  0.807046
    1   0.277950  0.213500  0.471524

    In [280]: expr = '0.0 <= a <= c <= 0.5'

    In [281]: map(lambda frame: frame.query(expr), [df, df2])
    Out[281]: <map at 0x7fa21b2fcfa0>

query() Python versus pandas Syntax Comparison  *user_guide-indexing-query-python-versus-pandas-syntax-comparison*

Full numpy-like syntax:

>python
    In [282]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randint(n, size=(n, 3)), columns=list('abc'))

    In [283]: df
    Out[283]: 
       a  b  c
    0  6  2  2
    1  2  6  3
    2  3  8  2
    3  1  7  2
    4  5  1  5
    5  9  8  0
    6  1  5  0
    7  4  9  6
    8  2  3  0
    9  6  5  4

    In [284]: df.query('(a < b) & (b < c)')
    Out[284]: 
    Empty DataFrame
    Columns: [a, b, c]
    Index: []

    In [285]: df[(df['a'] < df['b']) & (df['b'] < df['c'])]
    Out[285]: 
    Empty DataFrame
    Columns: [a, b, c]
    Index: []
<
Slightly nicer by removing the parentheses (comparison operators bind
tighter than `&` and `|`):

>python
    In [286]: df.query('a < b & b < c')
    Out[286]: 
    Empty DataFrame
    Columns: [a, b, c]
    Index: []
<
Use English instead of symbols:

>python
    In [287]: df.query('a < b and b < c')
    Out[287]: 
    Empty DataFrame
    Columns: [a, b, c]
    Index: []
<
Pretty close to how you might write it on paper:

>python
    In [288]: df.query('a < b < c')
    Out[288]: 
    Empty DataFrame
    Columns: [a, b, c]
    Index: []
<

                             *user_guide-indexing-the-in-and-not-in-operators*
The `in` and `not in` operators

|pandas.DataFrame.query| also supports special use of Python's `in` and
`not in` comparison operators, providing a succinct syntax for calling the
`isin` method of a `Series` or `DataFrame`.

>python
    # get all rows where columns "a" and "b" have overlapping values
    In [289]: df = pd.DataFrame({'a': list('aabbccddeeff'), 'b': list('aaaabbbbcccc'),
       .....:                    'c': np.random.randint(5, size=12),
       .....:                    'd': np.random.randint(9, size=12)})
       .....: 

    In [290]: df
    Out[290]: 
        a  b  c  d
    0   a  a  2  3
    1   a  a  0  0
    2   b  a  1  6
    3   b  a  2  2
    4   c  b  1  7
    5   c  b  2  7
    6   d  b  3  6
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    10  f  c  3  3
    11  f  c  1  3

    In [291]: df.query('a in b')
    Out[291]: 
       a  b  c  d
    0  a  a  2  3
    1  a  a  0  0
    2  b  a  1  6
    3  b  a  2  2
    4  c  b  1  7
    5  c  b  2  7

    # How you'd do it in pure Python
    In [292]: df[df['a'].isin(df['b'])]
    Out[292]: 
       a  b  c  d
    0  a  a  2  3
    1  a  a  0  0
    2  b  a  1  6
    3  b  a  2  2
    4  c  b  1  7
    5  c  b  2  7

    In [293]: df.query('a not in b')
    Out[293]: 
        a  b  c  d
    6   d  b  3  6
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    10  f  c  3  3
    11  f  c  1  3

    # pure Python
    In [294]: df[~df['a'].isin(df['b'])]
    Out[294]: 
        a  b  c  d
    6   d  b  3  6
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    10  f  c  3  3
    11  f  c  1  3
<
You can combine this with other expressions for very succinct queries:

>python
    # rows where cols a and b have overlapping values
    # and col c's values are less than col d's
    In [295]: df.query('a in b and c < d')
    Out[295]: 
       a  b  c  d
    0  a  a  2  3
    2  b  a  1  6
    4  c  b  1  7
    5  c  b  2  7

    # pure Python
    In [296]: df[df['b'].isin(df['a']) & (df['c'] < df['d'])]
    Out[296]: 
        a  b  c  d
    0   a  a  2  3
    2   b  a  1  6
    4   c  b  1  7
    5   c  b  2  7
    6   d  b  3  6
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    11  f  c  1  3
<
  Note: ~

  Note that `in` and `not in` are evaluated in Python, since `numexpr` has
  no equivalent of this operation. However, only the `in`/`not in`
  expression itself is evaluated in vanilla Python. For example, in the
  expression

  >python
      df.query('a in b + c + d')
<
  `(b + c + d)` is evaluated by `numexpr` and then the `in` operation is
  evaluated in plain Python. In general, any operations that can be
  evaluated using `numexpr` will be.

           *user_guide-indexing-special-use-of-the-operator-with-list-objects*
Special use of the `==` operator with `list` objects

Comparing a `list` of values to a column using `==`/`!=` works similarly to
`in`/`not in`.

>python
    In [297]: df.query('b == ["a", "b", "c"]')
    Out[297]: 
        a  b  c  d
    0   a  a  2  3
    1   a  a  0  0
    2   b  a  1  6
    3   b  a  2  2
    4   c  b  1  7
    5   c  b  2  7
    6   d  b  3  6
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    10  f  c  3  3
    11  f  c  1  3

    # pure Python
    In [298]: df[df['b'].isin(["a", "b", "c"])]
    Out[298]: 
        a  b  c  d
    0   a  a  2  3
    1   a  a  0  0
    2   b  a  1  6
    3   b  a  2  2
    4   c  b  1  7
    5   c  b  2  7
    6   d  b  3  6
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    10  f  c  3  3
    11  f  c  1  3

    In [299]: df.query('c == [1, 2]')
    Out[299]: 
        a  b  c  d
    0   a  a  2  3
    2   b  a  1  6
    3   b  a  2  2
    4   c  b  1  7
    5   c  b  2  7
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    11  f  c  1  3

    In [300]: df.query('c != [1, 2]')
    Out[300]: 
        a  b  c  d
    1   a  a  0  0
    6   d  b  3  6
    10  f  c  3  3

    # using in/not in
    In [301]: df.query('[1, 2] in c')
    Out[301]: 
        a  b  c  d
    0   a  a  2  3
    2   b  a  1  6
    3   b  a  2  2
    4   c  b  1  7
    5   c  b  2  7
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    11  f  c  1  3

    In [302]: df.query('[1, 2] not in c')
    Out[302]: 
        a  b  c  d
    1   a  a  0  0
    6   d  b  3  6
    10  f  c  3  3

    # pure Python
    In [303]: df[df['c'].isin([1, 2])]
    Out[303]: 
        a  b  c  d
    0   a  a  2  3
    2   b  a  1  6
    3   b  a  2  2
    4   c  b  1  7
    5   c  b  2  7
    7   d  b  2  7
    8   e  c  2  8
    9   e  c  2  8
    11  f  c  1  3
<

Boolean operators                      *user_guide-indexing-boolean-operators*

You can negate boolean expressions with the word `not` or the `~` operator.

>python
    In [304]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(n, 3), columns=list('abc'))

    In [305]: df['bools'] = np.random.rand(len(df)) > 0.5

    In [306]: df.query('~bools')
    Out[306]: 
              a         b         c  bools
    4  0.580078  0.620439  0.434445  False
    7  0.260776  0.290751  0.462080  False
    9  0.165948  0.902260  0.825007  False

    In [307]: df.query('not bools')
    Out[307]: 
              a         b         c  bools
    4  0.580078  0.620439  0.434445  False
    7  0.260776  0.290751  0.462080  False
    9  0.165948  0.902260  0.825007  False

    In [308]: df.query('not bools') == df[~df['bools']]
    Out[308]: 
          a     b     c  bools
    4  True  True  True   True
    7  True  True  True   True
    9  True  True  True   True
<
Of course, expressions can be arbitrarily complex too:

>python
    # short query syntax
    In [309]: shorter = df.query('a < b < c and (not bools) or bools > 2')

    # equivalent in pure Python
    In [310]: longer = df[(df['a'] < df['b'])
       .....:             & (df['b'] < df['c'])
       .....:             & (~df['bools'])
       .....:             | (df['bools'] > 2)]
       .....: 

    In [311]: shorter
    Out[311]: 
              a         b        c  bools
    7  0.260776  0.290751  0.46208  False

    In [312]: longer
    Out[312]: 
              a         b        c  bools
    7  0.260776  0.290751  0.46208  False

    In [313]: shorter == longer
    Out[313]: 
          a     b     c  bools
    7  True  True  True   True
<

Performance of query()              *user_guide-indexing-performance-of-query*

`DataFrame.query()` using `numexpr` is slightly faster than Python for large
frames.

You will only see the performance benefits of using the `numexpr` engine
with `DataFrame.query()` if your frame has more than approximately 100,000
rows.

This plot was created using a `DataFrame` with 3 columns each containing
floating point values generated using `numpy.random.randn()`.

>python
    In [314]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(8, 4),
       .....:                   index=dates, columns=['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'])
       .....: 

    In [315]: df2 = df.copy()
<

DUPLICATE DATA                            *user_guide-indexing-duplicate-data*

If you want to identify and remove duplicate rows in a DataFrame, there are
two methods that will help: `duplicated` and `drop_duplicates`. Each takes
as an argument the columns to use to identify duplicated rows.

- `duplicated` returns a boolean vector whose length is the number of rows,
  and which indicates whether a row is duplicated.
- `drop_duplicates` removes duplicate rows.

By default, the first observed row of a duplicate set is considered unique,
but each method has a `keep` parameter to specify targets to be kept.

- `keep='first'` (default): mark / drop duplicates except for the first
  occurrence.
- `keep='last'`: mark / drop duplicates except for the last occurrence.
- `keep=False`: mark / drop all duplicates.

>python
    In [316]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({'a': ['one', 'one', 'two', 'two', 'two', 'three', 'four'],
       .....:                     'b': ['x', 'y', 'x', 'y', 'x', 'x', 'x'],
       .....:                     'c': np.random.randn(7)})
       .....: 

    In [317]: df2
    Out[317]: 
           a  b         c
    0    one  x -1.467157
    1    one  y  0.113937
    2    two  x -1.428572
    3    two  y  0.337109
    4    two  x  0.052469
    5  three  x -2.294560
    6   four  x  2.148507

    In [318]: df2.duplicated('a')
    Out[318]: 
    0    False
    1     True
    2    False
    3     True
    4     True
    5    False
    6    False
    dtype: bool

    In [319]: df2.duplicated('a', keep='last')
    Out[319]: 
    0     True
    1    False
    2     True
    3     True
    4    False
    5    False
    6    False
    dtype: bool

    In [320]: df2.duplicated('a', keep=False)
    Out[320]: 
    0     True
    1     True
    2     True
    3     True
    4     True
    5    False
    6    False
    dtype: bool

    In [321]: df2.drop_duplicates('a')
    Out[321]: 
           a  b         c
    0    one  x -1.467157
    2    two  x -1.428572
    5  three  x -2.294560
    6   four  x  2.148507

    In [322]: df2.drop_duplicates('a', keep='last')
    Out[322]: 
           a  b         c
    1    one  y  0.113937
    4    two  x  0.052469
    5  three  x -2.294560
    6   four  x  2.148507

    In [323]: df2.drop_duplicates('a', keep=False)
    Out[323]: 
           a  b         c
    5  three  x -2.294560
    6   four  x  2.148507
<
Also, you can pass a list of columns to identify duplications.

>python
    In [324]: df2.duplicated(['a', 'b'])
    Out[324]: 
    0    False
    1    False
    2    False
    3    False
    4     True
    5    False
    6    False
    dtype: bool

    In [325]: df2.drop_duplicates(['a', 'b'])
    Out[325]: 
           a  b         c
    0    one  x -1.467157
    1    one  y  0.113937
    2    two  x -1.428572
    3    two  y  0.337109
    5  three  x -2.294560
    6   four  x  2.148507
<
To drop duplicates by index value, use `Index.duplicated` then perform
slicing. The same set of options are available for the `keep` parameter.

>python
    In [326]: df3 = pd.DataFrame({'a': np.arange(6),
       .....:                     'b': np.random.randn(6)},
       .....:                    index=['a', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'b', 'a'])
       .....: 

    In [327]: df3
    Out[327]: 
       a         b
    a  0 -0.293144
    a  1 -1.596615
    b  2  0.149716
    c  3  0.173897
    b  4 -0.049440
    a  5  1.394590

    In [328]: df3.index.duplicated()
    Out[328]: array([False,  True, False, False,  True,  True])

    In [329]: df3[~df3.index.duplicated()]
    Out[329]: 
       a         b
    a  0 -0.293144
    b  2  0.149716
    c  3  0.173897

    In [330]: df3[~df3.index.duplicated(keep='last')]
    Out[330]: 
       a         b
    c  3  0.173897
    b  4 -0.049440
    a  5  1.394590

    In [331]: df3[~df3.index.duplicated(keep=False)]
    Out[331]: 
       a         b
    c  3  0.173897
<

DICTIONARY-LIKE GET() METHOD  *user_guide-indexing-dictionary-like-get-method*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-dictionarylike*

Each of Series or DataFrame have a `get` method which can return a default
value.

>python
    In [332]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=['a', 'b', 'c'])

    In [333]: s.get('a')  # equivalent to s['a']
    Out[333]: np.int64(1)

    In [334]: s.get('x', default=-1)
    Out[334]: -1
<

                *user_guide-indexing-looking-up-values-by-index-column-labels*
LOOKING UP VALUES BY INDEX/COLUMN LABELS

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-lookup*

Sometimes you want to extract a set of values given a sequence of row labels
and column labels, this can be achieved by `pandas.factorize` and NumPy
indexing.

For heterogeneous column types, we subset columns to avoid unnecessary NumPy
conversions:

>python
    def pd_lookup_het(df, row_labels, col_labels):
       rows = df.index.get_indexer(row_labels)
       cols = df.columns.get_indexer(col_labels)
       sub = df.take(np.unique(cols), axis=1)
       sub = sub.take(np.unique(rows), axis=0)
       rows = sub.index.get_indexer(row_labels)
       values = sub.melt()["value"]
       cols = sub.columns.get_indexer(col_labels)
       flat_index = rows + cols * len(sub)
       result = values[flat_index]
       return result
<
For homogeneous column types, it is fastest to skip column subsetting and go
directly to NumPy:

>python
    def pd_lookup_hom(df, row_labels, col_labels):
        rows = df.index.get_indexer(row_labels)
        df = df.loc[:, sorted(set(col_labels))]
        cols = df.columns.get_indexer(col_labels)
        result = df.to_numpy()[rows, cols]
        return result
<
Formerly this could be achieved with the dedicated `DataFrame.lookup` method
which was deprecated in version 1.2.0 and removed in version 2.0.0.

INDEX OBJECTS                              *user_guide-indexing-index-objects*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-class*

The pandas |pandas.Index| class and its subclasses can be viewed as
implementing an ordered multiset. Duplicates are allowed.

|pandas.Index| also provides the infrastructure necessary for lookups, data
alignment, and reindexing. The easiest way to create an |pandas.Index|
directly is to pass a `list` or other sequence to |pandas.Index|:

>python
    In [335]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'])

    In [336]: index
    Out[336]: Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype='str')

    In [337]: 'd' in index
    Out[337]: True
<
or using numbers:

>python
    In [338]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12])

    In [339]: index
    Out[339]: Index([1, 5, 12], dtype='int64')

    In [340]: 5 in index
    Out[340]: True
<
If no dtype is given, `Index` tries to infer the dtype from the data. It is
also possible to give an explicit dtype when instantiating an
|pandas.Index|:

>python
    In [341]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype="string")

    In [342]: index
    Out[342]: Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype='string')

    In [343]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12], dtype="int8")

    In [344]: index
    Out[344]: Index([1, 5, 12], dtype='int8')

    In [345]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12], dtype="float32")

    In [346]: index
    Out[346]: Index([1.0, 5.0, 12.0], dtype='float32')
<
You can also pass a `name` to be stored in the index:

>python
    In [347]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], name='something')

    In [348]: index.name
    Out[348]: 'something'
<
The name, if set, will be shown in the console display:

>python
    In [349]: index = pd.Index(list(range(5)), name='rows')

    In [350]: columns = pd.Index(['A', 'B', 'C'], name='cols')

    In [351]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(5, 3), index=index, columns=columns)

    In [352]: df
    Out[352]: 
    cols         A         B         C
    rows                              
    0     0.698035  0.631397  0.816412
    1     0.709404 -1.193616 -0.263520
    2    -0.878602  0.035458 -0.285808
    3    -0.957431  2.243279 -1.124957
    4    -1.994374  0.050270  0.512794

    In [353]: df['A']
    Out[353]: 
    rows
    0    0.698035
    1    0.709404
    2   -0.878602
    3   -0.957431
    4   -1.994374
    Name: A, dtype: float64
<

Setting metadata                        *user_guide-indexing-setting-metadata*

*user_guide-indexing-indexing-set-metadata*

Indexes are “mostly immutable”, but it is possible to set and change their
`name` attribute. You can use the `rename`, `set_names` to set these
attributes directly, and they default to returning a copy.

See |user_guide-advanced-advanced| for usage of MultiIndexes.

>python
    In [354]: ind = pd.Index([1, 2, 3])

    In [355]: ind.rename("apple")
    Out[355]: Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='int64', name='apple')

    In [356]: ind
    Out[356]: Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='int64')

    In [357]: ind = ind.set_names(["apple"])

    In [358]: ind.name = "bob"

    In [359]: ind
    Out[359]: Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='int64', name='bob')
<
`set_names`, `set_levels`, and `set_codes` also take an optional `level`
argument

>python
    In [360]: index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([range(3), ['one', 'two']], names=['first', 'second'])

    In [361]: index
    Out[361]: 
    MultiIndex([(0, 'one'),
                (0, 'two'),
                (1, 'one'),
                (1, 'two'),
                (2, 'one'),
                (2, 'two')],
